M15 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-97

Separately Billed Services/Tests Have Been Bundled

Bundling / NCCI · All Claim Types · CMS-1500 Box 24D / UB-04 FL44 · Professional & Facility Claims
Common CARC Pairing
CO-97 / 234 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 24D FL44 NCCI Edits Modifier 59 / XE/XS/XP/XU
What This Means
📦
What This Means

RARC M15 means the payer has bundled two or more separately billed services or tests into a single payment because, under established coding rules, those services are considered included in — or incidental to — another procedure already billed on the same claim. The payer is not denying that the services were performed; it is denying separate reimbursement for them because they are expected to be part of a larger, already-paid procedure.

The primary bundling authority is NCCI — the National Correct Coding Initiative — a CMS-maintained set of procedure-to-procedure (PTP) edits that define which CPT/HCPCS codes cannot be billed together without a valid modifier indicating they were truly distinct, separate services. Payers also maintain their own proprietary bundling edits beyond NCCI.

ℹ️
Important Distinction
M15 does not mean the services were not performed or are not covered. It means they cannot be paid separately from the primary procedure. If the services were genuinely distinct and separate (different anatomical site, different session, different indication), a valid NCCI-associated modifier such as 59, XE, XS, XP, or XU may allow separate reimbursement. Always verify the NCCI edit table before applying a modifier — not all edits are modifier-bypassable.
Where to Address Bundling on the Claim
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Professional claim bundling resolution
  • Box 24D — Procedures / Modifier: The unbundling modifier (59, XE, XS, XP, or XU) is appended to the procedure code in Box 24D to indicate the service was distinct and separate
  • Enter the modifier in the modifier fields immediately to the right of the CPT/HCPCS code in Box 24D — up to four modifiers per line
  • EDI 837P equivalent: Loop 2400 SV1 segment — modifier appended after the procedure code in the composite medical procedure identifier
  • The modifier must accurately reflect why the service was separate — do not default to modifier 59 when a more specific X-modifier (XE, XS, XP, XU) is applicable
  • Ensure medical documentation supports the modifier used — payers may request records to validate the distinct service claim
CMS-1500 Box 24D
Field Label: Procedures / Modifier
Modifier Entry: 59, XE, XS, XP, or XU
EDI 837P: Loop 2400 SV1 composite modifier field
🏥
UB-04 (Facility / Hospital Claims)
Facility claim bundling resolution
  • FL44 — HCPCS / Accommodation Rate / HIPPS Rate Code: Procedure codes and their modifiers are entered in FL44 on the UB-04 — append the appropriate unbundling modifier here
  • Up to two modifiers can be appended after the HCPCS/CPT code in FL44 (e.g., 99213-59 or 27447-XS)
  • EDI 837I equivalent: Loop 2400 SV2 segment — modifier appended in the composite medical procedure identifier
  • Hospital outpatient claims subject to OPPS are also subject to NCCI PTP edits — verify bundling edits apply to the facility's OPPS setting
  • For ASC claims, NCCI edits apply differently — always check the ASC-specific NCCI tables before adding an unbundling modifier
UB-04 FL44 Entry
Field Label: HCPCS / Rate / HIPPS
Modifier Entry: Appended after procedure code
EDI 837I: Loop 2400 SV2 composite modifier field
⚠️
Modifier 59 vs. X-Modifiers — Use the Most Specific One
CMS guidance directs providers to use the most specific X-modifier (XE, XS, XP, XU) rather than the generic modifier 59 when one of the X-modifiers accurately describes why the service was distinct. Modifier 59 should only be used when none of the X-modifiers apply. Using 59 when XE/XS/XP/XU is the correct choice may trigger additional review or denial under some payer edits.
Why This Happens
⚠️
BUNDLING / NCCI EDIT TRIGGERED
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
M15 bundling denials occur when two or more codes are billed together but are considered part of the same service under NCCI PTP edits, medically unlikely edits (MUEs), or payer-proprietary bundling logic — and no valid modifier was submitted to indicate the services were genuinely separate.
1
NCCI PTP Edit — No Modifier
Two codes billed together hit an NCCI Procedure-to-Procedure edit and no unbundling modifier was appended to indicate a distinct service.
2
Component Included in Comprehensive Code
A component code was billed alongside its comprehensive code — NCCI treats the component as already included in the higher-value comprehensive procedure.
3
Wrong or Missing Modifier
Modifier 59 or an X-modifier was required to bypass the edit but was not added, or the wrong modifier was used (e.g., modifier 25 instead of 59).
4
Duplicate / Redundant Test Billing
A panel code and its individual component tests were both billed — payer bundled the individual tests into the panel already paid.
5
Payer Proprietary Bundling Edit
Payer applies their own bundling logic beyond NCCI — codes that are separately payable under Medicare may still be bundled by a commercial payer per their own policies.
6
Evaluation & Management + Procedure Same Day
E/M service billed on the same day as a procedure without modifier 25, causing the E/M to bundle into the global surgical or procedure package.
7
Global Surgery Package Inclusion
A procedure billed separately was already included in the global surgical package of another procedure on the claim (pre-op, intra-op, or post-op service).
8
Modifier 59 Not Modifier-Bypassable Edit
A modifier was added, but the NCCI edit for this code pair has a "0" indicator — meaning no modifier can override it; the codes simply cannot be billed together.
9
Outdated Billing Template / Charge Master
Charge master or billing template includes both a comprehensive and component code without modifiers — updated quarterly NCCI tables were not reflected in the system.
10
Medically Unlikely Edit (MUE) Exceeded
Units billed for a single code exceeded the CMS Medically Unlikely Edit threshold for that code — excess units were bundled or denied as unlikely for a single encounter.
How to Fix It — RARC M15: Separately Billed Services/Tests Have Been Bundled
💡 What is RARC M15?
Your claim was denied because the payer bundled two or more services you billed separately. Think of bundling like ordering a combo meal — if you order the combo, the sides are included; you can't charge for them separately. Payers use NCCI edits to define which CPT/HCPCS codes are "combos" — services that are part of a larger procedure and not separately reimbursable unless they were truly independent. The fix is either to add the correct modifier to prove the service was separate, or to confirm the bundling was correct and remove the unbundleable code.
CMS-1500
Box 24D
Modifier field
UB-04
FL 44
HCPCS / modifier field
EDI
Loop 2400
SV1/SV2 modifier composite
1
Identify the Bundled Code Pair
Find which codes triggered the NCCI edit
🔍 Review the remittance advice — M15 will be tied to a specific line item. Identify which procedure code was bundled into which other code.
  • Check the NCCI PTP edit tables at cms.gov — search the column-one (comprehensive) and column-two (component) code pair to confirm the edit exists
  • Note the modifier indicator for the edit: "1" = modifier can bypass the edit; "0" = modifier cannot bypass — bundling is absolute
  • If the modifier indicator is "0", the codes cannot be billed together regardless of circumstances — remove the component code from the claim
  • If the modifier indicator is "1", proceed to verify whether the services were truly distinct and the correct modifier applies
  • Also check for MUE violations if units were denied — look up the MUE value for the code at cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/ncci-medically-unlikely-edits
2
Verify the Services Were Truly Separate
Documentation must support the modifier before adding it
✅ A modifier is only valid when the services genuinely meet the criteria for separation. Confirm in the clinical documentation before adding any modifier.
  • XE (Separate Encounter): Were the services performed at a different encounter or visit on the same day?
  • XS (Separate Structure): Were the services performed on a different anatomical site or organ system?
  • XP (Separate Practitioner): Were the services performed by a different practitioner?
  • XU (Unusual Non-Overlapping Service): Does the service not overlap with the usual components of the main procedure?
  • Modifier 59: Use only when none of the above X-modifiers accurately describe the distinction
  • ⚠️ If documentation does not support any of these distinctions, do not add a modifier — the bundling was correct and the code should be removed
3
Add Correct Modifier & Resubmit as Corrected Claim
Fastest resolution path when services were genuinely separate
📝 Once documentation confirms the service was distinct, add the appropriate modifier and resubmit as a corrected claim — not a new claim.
  • CMS-1500: Add modifier in Box 24D on the bundled service line. Use Resubmission Code "7" in Box 22 with the original ICN
  • UB-04: Add modifier in FL44 on the affected revenue line. TOB frequency digit "7" + original TCN in FL64
  • 837P/837I EDI: Add modifier to the Loop 2400 SV1/SV2 composite procedure code element
  • If multiple lines were bundled, correct each line individually — do not batch all under a single modifier without verifying each separately
  • ⚠️ Monitor timely filing deadlines — corrected claims must be submitted within the payer's corrected claim filing window
4
Still Denied? Call the Payer
Clarify whether a proprietary edit — not NCCI — is the cause
📞 If the corrected claim with a valid modifier still denies with M15, the issue may be a payer-proprietary bundling edit, not NCCI. Call provider relations to confirm.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, DOS, CPT codes billed, the modifier applied, and both remittance advices
  • Ask: "Is the denial based on an NCCI PTP edit or a proprietary bundling policy? Is this edit modifier-bypassable under your guidelines?"
  • Request the payer's bundling edit documentation and their provider companion guide reference for the code pair in question
  • If the payer's edit is more restrictive than NCCI and contracts don't permit it, this may be a contract compliance issue — escalate to your contracting team
  • 📝 Document the call: reference number, rep name, date, time, and the specific payer edit or policy cited
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Charge Master & Billing Templates
One system fix stops M15 across every affected claim type
🔁 Recurring M15 denials indicate that bundling edits are not built into your pre-submission claim scrubber or that charge master code combinations haven't been updated to reflect current NCCI tables.
  • Implement a claim scrubber with NCCI PTP edit tables loaded — it should flag bundled code pairs before the claim reaches the payer
  • Update NCCI tables quarterly — CMS updates NCCI edits four times per year; stale edit tables cause newly-bundled pairs to slip through
  • Audit your charge master for code combinations that routinely appear together and confirm each pair is NCCI-compliant or requires a standing modifier
  • Train clinical and coding staff on NCCI modifier indicators — specifically the difference between indicator "0" (no bypass) and "1" (modifier allowed)
  • Review payer companion guides annually — commercial payer bundling policies change and may differ from NCCI; each payer's rules must be checked separately
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Adding a modifier to bypass an NCCI edit without documentation support constitutes improper billing and creates False Claims Act exposure. Never add modifier 59/X-modifier without clinical evidence of a distinct service.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common bundling billing and compliance mistakes that trigger M15 denials
These errors cause repeat M15 denials, corrected-claim failures, and compliance risk under the False Claims Act.
  • Do not add modifier 59 or X-modifiers without verifying the clinical documentation supports a genuinely distinct service
  • Do not attempt to bypass an NCCI edit with indicator "0" — no modifier can override it; the codes simply cannot be billed together
  • Do not resubmit the corrected claim with the same code combination and no modifier if a modifier was the fix needed
  • Do not use modifier 25 (significant, separately identifiable E/M) in place of modifier 59 to separate procedure codes — modifier 25 is only for E/M + same-day procedure situations
  • Do not appeal before first checking the NCCI modifier indicator — if the edit allows a modifier, correct the claim first; appealing without the modifier will fail
  • Do not bill both a comprehensive code and its component codes on the same claim without confirming the component was performed at a distinct anatomical site or encounter
  • Do not assume NCCI rules apply equally across all payers — commercial payers may have additional proprietary bundling edits that modifier 59 will not override
  • Do not leave NCCI edit tables unupdated in your claim scrubber — CMS updates them quarterly; stale tables generate systematic M15 denials
  • Do not bill individual panel component tests when the panel code has already been billed and paid for the same date of service
⚠️
Critical Compliance Reminder
Appending modifier 59 or X-modifiers to bypass NCCI bundling edits without documented clinical justification constitutes improper unbundling and creates exposure under the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3729). CMS and OIG actively audit unbundling patterns. Always ensure documentation in the medical record clearly supports the distinct nature of each separately billed service before submitting a modifier.
BUNDLING VALIDATION CHECKLIST
✅
BUNDLING VALIDATION CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist for M15 prevention

Before submitting any claim with multiple procedure codes, confirm all bundling validations are completed

  • ✅ NCCI PTP edit table checked for each code pair billed on the same claim and same date of service
  • ✅ Modifier indicator confirmed — "1" = modifier allowed; "0" = codes cannot be billed together under any circumstance
  • ✅ Clinical documentation reviewed and confirms the service was distinct before any unbundling modifier is added
  • ✅ Most specific modifier selected — XE, XS, XP, or XU used instead of 59 wherever one accurately applies
  • ✅ E/M billed same day as procedure has modifier 25 on the E/M code to indicate a significant, separately identifiable service
  • ✅ No panel code and its component individual tests billed simultaneously on the same claim
  • ✅ Claim scrubber NCCI tables updated to the current quarter's version — verified before submission batch
  • ✅ Payer companion guide checked — payer's proprietary bundling edits do not restrict the code pair beyond NCCI
  • ✅ MUE threshold checked for any code billed with units greater than 1 — units do not exceed the CMS MUE limit
  • ✅ Global surgical package reviewed — no pre-op, intra-op, or post-op services separately billed within the global period
  • ✅ Charge master reviewed for standing code combinations that routinely trigger NCCI edits — corrected or flagged for manual review
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅
Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True
Use only after corrected claim submission fails
Appeal only when a corrected claim with the proper modifier was submitted and the denial persists due to a payer-side system or policy issue — not a claim data problem.
  • A corrected claim with the appropriate modifier (59, XE, XS, XP, or XU) has already been submitted and denied again
  • The NCCI PTP edit's modifier indicator is confirmed as "1" (modifier-bypassable) for this code pair
  • Clinical documentation clearly supports the distinct, separate nature of the service — records are ready to attach
  • The payer's provider relations team confirmed the denial is a system validation issue, not a documentation problem
  • Timely filing window for the appeal is still open — deadline is confirmed before proceeding
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)
Recommended first action for most M15 denials
Most M15 denials are resolved by adding the correct unbundling modifier to the affected claim line and resubmitting as a corrected claim.
  • The vast majority of M15 denials resolve when the correct modifier is added to Box 24D (CMS-1500) or FL44 (UB-04)
  • Do not appeal as a first step — check the NCCI edit, verify documentation, add the modifier, and resubmit
  • If the NCCI indicator is "0", do not attempt to unbundle at all — remove the component code instead
  • Use Resubmission Code 7 on the corrected claim and include the original claim number
  • If the bundling was correct (no distinct service), write off the component — do not resubmit without justification

CARC 151 CONTRACTUAL CO-151

Payment Adjusted — Information Submitted Does Not Support This Many/Frequency of Services

Frequency & Quantity Limitation · Professional & Facility Claims · CMS-1500 & UB-04
Common RARC Pairing & Claim Fields
CO-151 N115 M86 M127 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 24G Box 24D FL42 FL46 LCD / NCD
What This Means
📊
What This Means

CARC 151 means the payer reviewed the quantity, units, or frequency of services billed on the claim and determined that the information submitted — diagnoses, clinical notes, medical necessity documentation, or prior authorization — does not clinically justify billing that many services, that many units, or that often within the defined time period. The payer is not denying that the service was performed or that it is a covered benefit — it is specifically denying or reducing payment because the volume or frequency of the service exceeds what the submitted documentation supports for the patient's condition.

ℹ️
Think of it this way — What Is a Frequency or Quantity Limit?
Payers — including Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurers — set clinical limits on how many times a service can be billed within a given time window (per day, per month, per year, or per lifetime). These limits come from Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs), National Coverage Determinations (NCDs), plan benefits, or prior authorization criteria. Think of it like a prescription with a refill limit — even if you need the medication, the payer only authorizes a defined number of refills per period without additional justification. CARC 151 fires when the number of units or dates of service billed exceeds the payer's defined frequency limit and the submitted information does not override that limit.
⚠️
CARC 151 Is NOT Always a Billing Error — Sometimes It Is a Missing Documentation Problem
The service may have been clinically necessary and appropriately performed the number of times billed. CARC 151 fires when the payer's system cannot find sufficient documentation in the submitted information to justify that frequency. The solution is often not changing the claim — it is supplying the missing medical necessity documentation, treatment plan, or prior authorization that the payer required and did not receive.
💡
Important: CO-151 Means the Patient Generally Cannot Be Billed
CARC 151 is a Contractual Obligation (CO) adjustment. Under participation agreements, providers have agreed that amounts denied as CO are not billable to the patient. The provider may not balance-bill the patient for CO-151 denied units or dates of service unless a valid Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN) or equivalent advance written notice of non-coverage was signed by the patient before the services were rendered. Billing patients without a valid ABN for CO-151 denials may violate payer contracts and, for Medicare, the False Claims Act.
Where Frequency, Units, and Service Counts Are Reported on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Frequency and units reporting fields — professional claims
  • Box 24G — Days or Units: The number of units, visits, or services billed for the procedure on each service line. This is the primary field the payer cross-checks against its frequency policy for the CPT/HCPCS code. Must reflect the actual number of units performed and documented.
  • Box 24D — Procedure Code + Modifier: The CPT/HCPCS code being billed. The payer retrieves the frequency limit for this code from its LCD, NCD, or plan benefit table. Modifiers such as -76 (Repeat procedure by same physician), -77 (Repeat procedure by another physician), or -59 (Distinct procedural service) may be required to override frequency edits when the clinical scenario justifies additional units.
  • Box 24A — Dates of Service: The from and through dates define the timeframe of the services. Payers evaluate how many times the same CPT code appears across all service lines and claim submissions within the defined frequency window (per day, per week, per month, per year).
  • Box 21 — Diagnosis Codes: The supporting ICD-10-CM codes must be specific and consistent with the number of services billed. A single acute diagnosis rarely justifies high-frequency billing; a chronic, complex, or progressive condition may.
  • Box 19 — Additional Claim Information / Notes: Some payers allow or require clinical justification text here to override frequency limitations. Check payer-specific guidelines before using this field.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility / Hospital Claims)
Frequency and units reporting fields — facility claims
  • FL46 — Service Units: The number of units of service provided for each revenue code line. This is the primary quantity field on facility claims. Payers validate FL46 against the frequency limit associated with the revenue code or HCPCS code billed. Incorrect units here directly trigger CO-151.
  • FL42 — Revenue Code: The revenue code classifies the type of facility service. Each revenue code has payer-specific frequency thresholds. Repeated revenue codes across multiple billing dates are flagged when total utilization exceeds the limit.
  • FL44 — HCPCS / CPT Code: When HCPCS or CPT codes are reported alongside revenue codes on outpatient facility claims, the payer applies frequency edits at the procedure code level in addition to the revenue code level.
  • FL45 — Service Date: The date each service line was rendered. The payer reviews all service dates across FL45 to calculate total frequency of the service within the review window.
  • FL63 — Treatment Authorization Code: If a prior authorization was obtained for a specific number of services, the auth code and authorized quantity must match FL46. A mismatch between authorized units and billed units is a common CO-151 trigger on facility claims.
  • EDI 837I — Loop 2400 SV2 / QTY Segment: Service units and quantity are transmitted in the SV2 segment. Frequency edits run against these values in the payer's adjudication engine.
✅
Units vs. Frequency — Quick Distinction
Units refer to the quantity billed on a single claim service line (e.g., 4 units of a timed therapy code in one session). Frequency refers to how many times a service is billed across multiple claims within a defined period (e.g., physical therapy 3× per week). CARC 151 can fire for either or both. Always identify which limit was exceeded — per-session units or per-period frequency — before determining the correct resolution path.
Why This Happens
⚠️
FREQUENCY & QUANTITY DENIAL ROOT CAUSES
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
CO-151 denials occur when the total number of units billed on a single service line, or the number of times a service was billed within a defined review period, exceeds the limit established by the payer's LCD, NCD, benefit plan, or prior authorization — and the submitted claim documentation does not provide sufficient clinical justification to override that limit.
1
Units Exceed Per-Day Maximum
More units were billed on a single service line than the payer allows per date of service for that CPT/HCPCS code. Common with timed therapy codes (e.g., CPT 97110) where the number of 15-minute units billed exceeds what is medically reasonable in a single visit given the documented treatment time.
2
Service Billed Too Frequently Within the Review Period
The same CPT code was billed more times than the payer's LCD or benefit policy allows within a defined window — for example, more than the allowed number of chiropractic manipulations per month, or more than the allowed number of echocardiograms per year, without clinical documentation justifying exception.
3
Missing or Expired Prior Authorization for Additional Services
An authorization was obtained for a set number of visits or units (e.g., 20 PT visits), the provider rendered additional services beyond the authorized quantity, and no extension or new auth was obtained. Claims for services beyond the authorized quantity deny with CO-151.
4
No Treatment Plan or Plan of Care Submitted
Payers require a current, signed treatment plan or plan of care to support ongoing or high-frequency services (e.g., physical therapy, home health, DME). When only the claim is submitted — without the supporting plan — the payer cannot validate that the frequency is clinically indicated and denies CO-151.
5
Diagnosis Does Not Support High-Frequency Billing
The ICD-10-CM diagnosis reported is a minor, acute, or self-limiting condition that the payer's clinical editing engine does not recognize as justifying a high number of visits or units. Example: billing 30 PT visits with a diagnosis of a simple muscle strain typically does not pass automated frequency edits without additional documentation showing complexity or lack of expected progress.
6
Units Billed Don't Match Documented Service Time
For time-based CPT codes (e.g., therapeutic exercise, psychotherapy, infusion), the number of units billed implies a total service duration. If the documented session time in the clinical note is shorter than the time implied by the units billed, the payer reduces units to match documented time.
7
Same Service Billed by Multiple Providers in the Same Period
The payer's system detects that another provider already billed and was paid for the same or a similar service within the same frequency window for the same patient. When the combined total across providers exceeds the allowed frequency, subsequent claims deny with CO-151.
8
Required Modifier Omitted to Override Frequency Edit
Some frequency limitations can be overridden when a procedure is repeated for a clinically distinct reason or on a separate anatomical site. Missing modifiers such as -76 (Repeat procedure, same physician), -77 (Repeat procedure, different physician), -RT/-LT (bilateral), or -59 (Distinct service) prevent the payer from recognizing the exception and trigger CO-151.
9
DME or Supply Quantity Exceeds Coverage Allowance
Durable medical equipment, orthotics, prosthetics, or supplies (DMEPOS) are billed with quantities that exceed the payer's allowed replacement or replenishment schedule — for example, billing 90 days of supply before the prior supply period has ended, or billing replacement quantities beyond the scheduled benefit allowance.
10
Billing System or Template Defaulting Incorrect Unit Count
A billing system template, charge capture default, or EHR order set is automatically populating an incorrect unit count — often a legacy value from a prior configuration — which does not reflect the actual service documented. The claim submits with inflated units on every encounter without anyone catching the default error.
How to Fix It — CARC 151: Payment Adjusted for Frequency / Quantity of Services
💡 What is CARC 151?
Your claim was denied or reduced because the payer determined that the number of units billed on a service line or the total frequency of the service across claims exceeds what is clinically supported by the submitted information for the patient's condition. The fix requires confirming the payer's applicable frequency limit, reviewing documentation for clinical justification, adding required modifiers, supplying missing authorization or treatment plan documentation, and resubmitting or appealing with the supporting clinical record.

1
Identify the Exact Service, Units, and Frequency Period That Denied
The RA will identify which CPT code, which date(s), and what quantity triggered CO-151
🔍 Review the remittance advice carefully. CO-151 may be a full denial (all units or all dates denied) or a partial reduction (the payer paid some units and denied the excess). Identify exactly which units, dates, or quantity amount was denied before taking any action.
  • Pull the original claim and identify the CPT/HCPCS code on the denied line, the units billed in Box 24G (CMS-1500) or FL46 (UB-04), and the date(s) of service.
  • Note whether the denial is for a single date (per-day unit limit exceeded) or spans multiple dates (per-period frequency limit exceeded).
  • Check if RARC N115 (decision based on LCD), M86 (service denied not authorized), or M127 (missing information) is paired with CO-151 — this indicates the specific policy or documentation gap driving the denial.
  • Determine whether a prior authorization was in place for this service and what quantity was authorized.
2
Look Up the Payer's Frequency Limit for This CPT/HCPCS Code
You must know the limit before you can determine whether the denial is correct or disputable
📋 Find the frequency policy that applies to this service. Different payers — and even different plans within the same payer — may have different limits for the same CPT code.
  • Medicare: Go to cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database, search by CPT/HCPCS code, locate the applicable LCD or NCD, and review the coverage criteria and frequency limitations section.
  • Commercial payers: Log into the payer's provider portal and search for the clinical policy or coverage criteria document for the denied CPT code. Alternatively, call provider relations and ask specifically: "What is the frequency limit for CPT [XXXXX] under this plan, and what documentation is required to exceed it?"
  • Confirm the frequency window: is the limit per day, per week, per month, per rolling 12 months, or per benefit year?
  • Confirm whether the limit is a hard cap (cannot be exceeded regardless of documentation) or a soft edit (can be overridden with clinical documentation or prior authorization).
  • 📝 Save a copy of the policy, LCD, or the call note with the frequency limit confirmed — you will need this for the corrected claim or appeal.
3
Review the Medical Record — Can the Frequency Be Clinically Justified?
Documentation is the key to overriding a frequency edit
📋 Review the clinical notes for the dates in question. The medical record must document why the patient required services at the frequency billed. The more specific and measurable the documentation, the stronger the case for overriding the limit.
  • For therapy services: notes must document the patient's condition severity, functional deficits, measurable goals, progress (or lack of expected progress requiring continued treatment), and the clinical rationale for the prescribed frequency.
  • For diagnostic services: notes must document why a repeat study was medically necessary — for example, a new symptom, a change in condition, or a failed prior intervention that requires reassessment.
  • For timed CPT codes: confirm the total direct treatment time documented in the note supports the number of units billed under the 8-minute rule. Correct Box 24G if units exceed documented time.
  • For DME/supplies: confirm the clinical need documentation (physician order, CMN, prior authorization) supports the quantity billed and that the resupply interval has been met.
  • If the record does not support the frequency — correct the claim to reflect actual documented services and resubmit. Do not resubmit the same unsupported frequency.
4
Still Denied? File a Formal Appeal with Clinical Documentation
Use when documentation fully supports the frequency and the corrected or original claim re-denies
⚖️ If the clinical record fully supports the frequency of service and the claim still denies after correction, file a formal appeal attaching the complete medical record, treatment plan, and the payer's own frequency policy that the documentation satisfies.
  • Appeal must include: Patient name, member ID, claim number, DOS, denied CPT code, units denied, and both EOBs (original and corrected claim if applicable).
  • Key statement: "The clinical documentation attached supports the medical necessity of [X units/visits] of CPT [XXXXX] for this patient. The applicable [LCD/NCD/plan policy] permits this frequency when supported by documentation of [specific clinical criteria]. We appeal the CO-151 denial as the attached record satisfies all required clinical criteria."
  • Attach: Signed clinical notes for all denied dates, current treatment plan or plan of care, physician orders, prior authorization confirmation (if applicable), payer LCD/NCD or policy printout with criteria highlighted, and both EOBs.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with your MAC within 120 days. Commercial: check EOB for deadline — typically 30–180 days from the denial date.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Authorization, Units, and Documentation Workflows
Stop CO-151 before it reaches the payer
🔁 If CO-151 is appearing across multiple claims, your practice has a systemic gap in authorization tracking, unit calculation, documentation specificity, or frequency policy awareness that is causing repeated overbilling relative to documented or authorized limits.
  • Build a payer-by-payer frequency limit reference table for your top CPT codes. Document the allowed units per day, visits per month, and annual caps for every high-volume CPT code billed to each payer. Update it whenever LCDs or commercial policies are revised. Make it accessible at point of charge capture.
  • Implement authorization tracking with visit count alerts. Track every authorization: authorized quantity, used quantity, and remaining balance. Set alerts at 80% utilization to trigger a re-authorization request before the limit is exhausted — not after claims start denying.
  • Audit timed therapy unit calculations regularly. Pull a sample of therapy claims monthly and verify that units billed in Box 24G match the total direct treatment time documented in the notes under the 8-minute rule. A systematic unit calculation error will generate CO-151 on every therapy claim.
  • Train clinical staff to document frequency rationale explicitly. Therapists, physicians, and treating providers must document why the patient needs the specific frequency of service prescribed — not just what service was done. Functional deficits, severity scores, and measurable treatment response data are what payers look for to override frequency edits.
  • Check billing system defaults for unit fields quarterly. Confirm no CPT code template in your billing system is defaulting to a fixed unit count that does not match actual documented service time or quantities. Default unit values that do not match reality cause every claim from that template to deny with CO-151.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Billing units or visit counts that are not documented in the clinical record — even if the service was genuinely provided — constitutes unsupported billing under the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3729). Documentation must support every unit billed.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these critical mistakes that cause repeat CO-151 denials, compliance violations, and improper patient billing
These mistakes commonly cause repeat CO-151 denials, corrected claim failures, audit exposure, and violations of payer contracts and the False Claims Act.
  • Do not resubmit with the same unit count or frequency that was denied without first correcting the units to match documented service time, or supplying clinical documentation that justifies the original frequency — resubmitting an identical claim will re-deny with CO-151 every time
  • Do not assume the denial is an error before checking the payer's LCD, NCD, or benefit policy frequency limit for the specific CPT code — many CO-151 denials are correct and the appropriate resolution is writing off the overage, not resubmitting
  • Do not bill the patient for CO-151 denied units or visit overages without confirming a valid ABN or advance written notice of potential non-coverage was signed before the services that exceeded the limit were rendered
  • Do not add a modifier (-59, -76, -77) to the resubmitted claim to override a frequency edit unless the clinical record genuinely documents a distinct or repeat service scenario that the modifier is meant to describe — modifier abuse to bypass frequency edits is a compliance violation and an audit flag
  • Do not appeal as a first step without first correcting the claim to match documented services and resubmitting — an appeal without a prior corrected claim or without clinical documentation attached will be dismissed, and the appeal opportunity may be lost
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Billing units or visit frequencies that are not supported by the clinical record — even when the services were genuinely performed — constitutes unsupported billing under the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3729). Every unit billed must be documented in the medical record. CO-151 denials that result from chart reviews or RAC audits carry recoupment risk beyond the initial denied amount.
FREQUENCY & UNITS VALIDATION CHECKLIST
✅
FREQUENCY & UNITS VALIDATION CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist to prevent CO-151 denials

Before submitting any claim with multiple units or recurring services, confirm all frequency and quantity validations are completed

  • ✅ Units billed in Box 24G (CMS-1500) or FL46 (UB-04) match the actual documented service time or quantity in the clinical record for that date of service
  • ✅ Total frequency of the service across all claim submissions within the payer's review window has been checked against the applicable LCD, NCD, or commercial policy frequency limit before claim is sent
  • ✅ Prior authorization is active, covers the date(s) of service billed, and the authorized quantity has not been exhausted — if near the limit, extension request has been submitted before this claim
  • ✅ Clinical notes document the medical necessity and rationale for the specific frequency of service prescribed — including functional deficits, severity, and measurable treatment response data
  • ✅ For timed CPT codes, total direct treatment time in the note has been converted to units using the 8-minute rule and the result matches Box 24G before submission
  • ✅ Any required modifier (-76, -77, -59, -RT, -LT, -AT) needed to identify a distinct or repeated service has been added to the claim line and is supported by the clinical record
  • ✅ For services approaching or exceeding a payer's soft frequency edit, a current treatment plan, physician order, or clinical justification letter has been prepared and is available to submit with the claim or on request
  • ✅ For DME and supplies, the resupply interval since the last billing date has been confirmed to meet the payer's minimum replacement period before the claim is submitted
  • ✅ Billing system CPT code templates have been audited and no unit field is defaulting to a fixed value that does not reflect actual documented service quantities
  • ✅ If frequency will exceed the payer's coverage limit for this patient, and service was rendered, confirm whether a valid ABN or equivalent advance written notice was obtained before the services beyond the limit were performed
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Use only after documentation fully supports the frequency and a corrected claim has already been denied
Appeal only when the clinical record fully documents the medical necessity of the frequency or units billed, the service meets the payer's coverage criteria, and a corrected claim with complete documentation was denied again with CO-151.
  • The clinical notes for all denied dates document specific medical necessity for the frequency or unit count billed
  • The ICD-10-CM diagnosis and service type are confirmed to meet the payer's coverage criteria for the frequency billed
  • A corrected claim with all supporting documentation has already been submitted and denied again with CO-151
  • Always attach the complete clinical record, treatment plan, payer policy criteria, and both EOBs to the appeal
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most CO-151 Cases)
Recommended first action when units or frequency can be corrected to match documentation
Most CO-151 denials resolve by correcting the units in Box 24G or FL46 to match documented service time or quantity, adding a required modifier, or supplying a missing treatment plan or prior authorization — and resubmitting with Resubmission Code 7.
  • If units billed exceeded documented service time — correct Box 24G to match the record and resubmit
  • If a required modifier was missing — add it (confirm the clinical scenario supports it) and resubmit
  • If a prior authorization was in place but the auth number was missing from the claim — add it to Box 23 (CMS-1500) or FL63 (UB-04) and resubmit
  • If the frequency exceeds a hard coverage limit that cannot be overridden by documentation, do not resubmit — evaluate write-off or patient billing options based on ABN status
  • Do not appeal as a first step — correct the root cause first and escalate to appeal only after the corrected claim is also denied

N846 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

NDC Does Not Correspond to HCPCS/CPT Billed

Drug Billing / Data Mismatch · Professional & Facility Claims ·
Common CARC Pairing
CMS-1500 Box 24 & UB-04 (FL43-FL44) CO-16 Claim/service lacks information
What This Means
💡
What This Means

The National Drug Code (NDC) reported on the claim does not match the HCPCS/CPT drug code (typically a J-code) billed on the same service line.

ℹ️
Important Distinction
N846 does not automatically mean the drug is not covered or the claim is permanently denied. It means the NDC and J-code need to match up before processing can continue.
Where to Report This Information
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional)
Professional claim reporting guidance
  • Box 24D — HCPCS/CPT drug code (J-code)
  • Shaded area 24A–24G — N4 qualifier + 11-digit NDC + unit of measure + quantity
✅ Correct: N412345678901
❌ Incorrect: N4 12345678901
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims)
Facility claim reporting guidance
  • FL - 44 — HCPCS/CPT code
  • FL - 43 — N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM + Quantity
Format: N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM + Qty
Example: ✅ Correct: N412345678901
⚠️
N4 Qualifier Format — Common Sub-Error
The N4 qualifier must appear as a single uninterrupted prefix directly before the 11-digit NDC number. Any spaces, punctuation, or formatting characters between N4 and the NDC value will trigger clearinghouse edits and payer format rejection.
#
11-Digit NDC Format (5-4-2) — Conversion Guide
Original Format Add Zero To Example Conversion
4-4-2 Front of Labeler Code 1234-5678-90 → 01234-5678-90
5-3-2 Front of Product Code 12345-678-90 → 12345-0678-90
5-4-1 Front of Package Code 12345-6789-0 → 12345-6789-00
Unit of Measure (UOM) Misalignment
💊
Valid UOM Codes — When to Use Each
Reference guide for selecting the correct billing unit of measure
UOM Code Name When to Use Billing Unit
UN Unit Powder-form drugs in a vial that must be reconstituted before administration One unit per vial used
ML Milliliter Liquid-form drugs supplied in a vial or pre-filled syringe Actual milliliters administered
GR Gram Ointments, creams, inhalers, or bulk powders dispensed by weight Actual grams dispensed — primarily retail pharmacy
F2 International Unit Factor VIII Antihemophilic Factor and similar biologics billed in international units Per IU administered
📌
Key Rule
The UOM must match the physical form of the drug as supplied on the date of service — not how you prefer to bill it, and not what a prior claim used.
Why This Happens
⚠️
DATA ENTRY & SELECTION ISSUES
Most common root causes behind NDC mismatch denials
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
NDC mismatch denials typically happen when the submitted NDC does not align with the drug administered, HCPCS code billed, or payer drug file requirements.
1
Wrong NDC Selected
The NDC entered does not belong to the drug actually administered or references a different manufacturer version.
2
10-Digit NDC Not Converted
A 10-digit NDC was submitted without converting it into the required 11-digit billing format.
3
HCPCS and NDC Misalignment
The HCPCS or J-code billed does not correspond with the NDC submitted on the claim.
4
Expired or Inactive NDC
The submitted NDC is expired, discontinued, or no longer active in the payer's drug file.
5
Missing NDC on Claim
The drug was billed using only a J-code or HCPCS code without attaching the required NDC information.
6
Supplier Change Not Captured
A new supplier or manufacturer was used, but the updated NDC was not captured during administration or claim entry.
How to Fix It — RARC N846: NDC Does Not Correspond to HCPCS/CPT Billed
💡 What is RARC N846?
Your claim was denied because the NDC (National Drug Code) on the claim does not match the HCPCS or CPT drug code billed. Think of it like ordering a specific product by catalog number — the NDC is the exact barcode of the drug vial administered, and the HCPCS/CPT is the billing code for that drug. If the barcode and the catalog number describe two different drugs, the payer flags the mismatch and denies the claim. Both codes must point to the exact same drug, strength, and form.
CMS-1500
Box 24A–J
NDC in shaded area
837P EDI
Loop 2410
LIN / CTP segments
NDC Format
11 Digits
5-4-2 or 5-3-2 padded
📋 Common Reasons NDC and HCPCS/CPT Don't Match
Root Cause
What Happened
Wrong NDC entered
A different drug's NDC was typed in — the HCPCS maps to a different molecule
Generic vs. brand NDC
Generic administered but brand HCPCS billed (or vice versa)
Different strength / concentration
NDC is 10mg vial but HCPCS maps to 20mg — same drug, wrong dose
Wrong dosage form
NDC is oral tablet but HCPCS is for injectable — different forms of same drug
Stale NDC in billing system
Drug repackaged / reformulated — old NDC no longer maps to the HCPCS
1
Verify What Was Actually Administered
Go back to the medication record first
🔍 Pull the medication administration record (MAR) or drug log for the date of service. The NDC on the claim must match the exact vial or package administered — not the drug name, not the order — the actual product given to the patient.
  • Check the drug label / vial barcode scanned or recorded at administration — the 10- or 11-digit NDC is printed on every drug package.
  • Confirm the NDC on the claim matches the exact manufacturer, strength, and dosage form administered — same drug name is not enough if the NDC points to a different concentration or route.
  • Cross-reference the NDC against the HCPCS code billed using the FDA NDC Directory (ndclist.com or fda.gov/drugs) — confirm the NDC maps to the drug described by the HCPCS code.
  • Check if the drug was substituted at dispensing — pharmacy may have dispensed a different manufacturer's NDC than what was ordered, and the billing system still carries the original NDC.
  • If a compounded drug was administered, note that compounded drugs do not have FDA-assigned NDCs — confirm with the payer how they require compounded drug reporting.
2
Correct the NDC or HCPCS & Resubmit
Fix the mismatch — then send corrected claim
✅ Once you confirm what was administered, correct whichever side of the pair is wrong — the NDC, the HCPCS, or both — and resubmit as a corrected claim. Never submit as a new claim.
  • CMS-1500 (paper): Enter the corrected 11-digit NDC in the shaded portion of Box 24A using the qualifier N4 followed by the NDC, unit of measure qualifier, and quantity administered.
  • 837P electronic: Update Loop 2410, LIN segment (qualifier N4 + NDC) and CTP segment (NDC unit price, unit of measure, and quantity). All three fields must be correct — a partial fix re-denies.
  • NDC must be 11 digits — if the package shows a 10-digit NDC, add a leading zero to the correct segment (5-4-2 format). Never use hyphens in electronic submission.
  • Corrected claim: CMS-1500 → Box 22, Resubmission Code "7" + original ICN. UB-04 → TOB frequency digit "7" + original TCN in Box 64.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits before resubmitting — do not lose the claim window while resolving the NDC discrepancy internally.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
Payer crosswalk may not recognize the NDC
📞 If the corrected claim still gets N846, call the payer's provider relations or pharmacy/drug billing line. The payer's internal NDC-to-HCPCS crosswalk may not include your drug's NDC — especially for newer drugs, repackaged products, or specialty biologics.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, date of service, NDC submitted, HCPCS code billed, drug name, strength, manufacturer, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask the rep: "Is NDC [XXXXXXXXXXX] in your crosswalk for HCPCS [XXXXX]? If not, what NDC or alternate HCPCS code does your system recognize for [drug name / strength]?"
  • Ask if the payer requires a specific NDC from an approved formulary or contracted manufacturer — some payers only accept NDCs from preferred suppliers even when the drug is the same molecule.
  • Ask if the denial is a crosswalk gap vs. a true mismatch — if the payer's table simply hasn't been updated to include a newer NDC, they may reprocess manually or advise a workaround HCPCS.
  • 📝 Document: reference number, rep name, date, time, and any alternate NDC or HCPCS they advise using.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Prove NDC and HCPCS describe the same drug
⚖️ If the payer upholds the N846 denial, file a formal appeal with FDA drug labeling and crosswalk documentation proving the NDC submitted correctly corresponds to the HCPCS code billed.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, NDC submitted, HCPCS code billed, drug name, strength, route, and manufacturer.
  • Key statement: "NDC [XXXXXXXXXXX] is the FDA-assigned National Drug Code for [Drug Name, Strength, Form] manufactured by [Manufacturer]. This NDC correctly corresponds to HCPCS [XXXXX] per the FDA NDC Directory and [CMS / payer] drug crosswalk. We appeal the N846 denial as the NDC-to-HCPCS pairing was accurate at submission."
  • Attach: FDA NDC Directory printout for the NDC, drug package label or insert confirming drug name/strength, medication administration record confirming what was given, original and corrected claims, and both remittance advices.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with the MAC within 120 days. Reference CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Pub 100-04, Chapter 17 (Drugs and Biologicals).
  • Commercial: check EOB for appeal deadline — typically 30–180 days. Include the payer's own NDC crosswalk reference if the drug is listed there under the HCPCS billed.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Drug Crosswalk & Templates
One crosswalk update stops N846 across your entire drug claim volume
🔁 If N846 is appearing on multiple claims, your NDC-to-HCPCS crosswalk table in your billing system is outdated, incomplete, or incorrectly mapped. Drug NDCs change when manufacturers repackage or reformulate — a crosswalk that was correct last quarter may already be stale.
  • Audit your NDC-to-HCPCS crosswalk table quarterly. For every drug billed, verify the NDC in your system still maps to the correct HCPCS — especially after formulary changes, new supplier contracts, or manufacturer switches.
  • Capture the NDC at point of administration, not at billing. The actual vial barcode scanned by nursing or pharmacy at administration time is the source of truth — build a workflow that passes that NDC directly into the claim, not a pre-set billing system value.
  • Maintain a drug substitution log. When pharmacy substitutes a different manufacturer's NDC at dispensing, that change must flow through to the claim. A silent substitution with no billing update is the #1 cause of repeat N846 denials.
  • Add a pre-submission edit that validates each NDC against its paired HCPCS code before the claim is released — flag any pair where the NDC does not appear in the FDA directory under the drug described by the HCPCS.
  • Update crosswalks for new drugs immediately upon formulary addition. When a new drug or biosimilar is added to your formulary, map its NDC to the correct HCPCS before the first claim is submitted — not after the first denial.
  • 🔒 Train your billing and nursing teams: NDC reporting is a clinical accuracy requirement, not just a billing field. The NDC must reflect the exact product administered — substituting a similar drug's NDC because it's "close enough" is a false claims risk.
Modifier to Know
🏷️
Modifier Reference Guide
Common modifiers and proper usage guidelines
Modifier Description Usage Notes
KO Single drug unit dose formulation Use for single-drug unit-dose packaging.
KP First drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation First drug when multiple drugs are in one unit-dose.
KQ Second or subsequent drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation Each additional drug after KP in multi-drug unit-dose.
JW Drug amount discarded or not administered to the patient Requires a separate line on the same claim. Primary line must show >0 units administered. JW line shows wasted/discarded quantity. Both lines must reflect the same NDC and J-code.
JZ Zero wastage — no drug was discarded Use when no drug was discarded. Required by some payers when JW is not applicable.
💊
JW Modifier — Correct Billing Structure Example
Line 1
Line 1: J-code | 2 ML administered | same NDC | same DOS
Line 2
Line 2: J-code + JW | 0.5 ML discarded | same NDC | same DOS If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
Important: If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that lead to repeat denials
  • Do not appeal before correcting the NDC/J-code mismatch
  • Do not reuse old, default, or copied NDCs from previous claims without verification
  • Do not guess at the manufacturer, quantity, or drug lot always Verify with MR
  • Do not submit a corrected claim with the same incorrect NDC
  • Do not appeal a N846 denial if you have not yet submitted a corrected claim first
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting the underlying NDC error wastes timely filing days and may forfeit your right to correct the claim. Always correct first, then appeal only if the corrected claim is also denied.
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
✅
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist

Before submitting any drug claim, confirm:

  • ✅ NDC captured directly from the administered vial or package label
  • ✅ J-code validated against NDC using a current, reliable crosswalk
  • ✅ 10-digit NDC converted to 11-digit format (5-4-2) if applicable
  • ✅ N4 qualifier formatted with no space before the NDC number
  • ✅ Manufacturer-specific NDC confirmed (not from a different lot or supplier)
  • ✅ JW modifier applied on a separate line with administered quantity on primary line (if wastage applies)
  • ✅ NDC confirmed as active on the date of service
  • ✅ Claim run through edits before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅

Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True

Use only when the claim has already been corrected and still denied
  • A corrected claim has already been submitted and denied again
  • All billing data (NDC, J-code, UOM, quantity, manufacturer) has been confirmed correct against the MAR and vial label
  • The denial reason after correction still cites N846 — indicating a payer-side processing error
🔄

Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)

Recommended first step for most denials
  • Most N846 denials resolve by correcting and resubmitting the claim
  • Do not appeal as a first step - Verify NDC ↔ J-code crosswalk, 11-digit format, N4 qualifier, UOM, and quantity before resubmission
  • Use Resubmission Code 7 on the corrected claim

CARC 11 CONTRACTUAL CO-11

The Diagnosis Is Inconsistent with the Procedure

Diagnosis–Procedure Mismatch · Professional & Facility Claims · CMS-1500 & UB-04
Common RARC Pairing & Claim Fields
CO-11 N30 N115 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 21 Box 24E FL67 FL44 ICD-10-CM
What This Means
🩺
What This Means

CARC 11 means the payer's claims editing system compared the diagnosis code (ICD-10-CM) reported on the claim against the procedure code (CPT/HCPCS) billed and determined they are clinically incompatible — in other words, the diagnosis does not support or justify the procedure performed. The payer cannot adjudicate the claim because the clinical story told by the diagnosis does not logically connect to the service billed. This is a Contractual Obligation (CO) denial, meaning the contractual agreement between the provider and the payer requires the denial and the patient generally cannot be billed.

ℹ️
Think of it this way — What is a Diagnosis–Procedure Relationship?
Every procedure code has a clinical purpose — a reason a provider would perform it. Payers use automated editing engines (such as ClaimLogic, ClaimsXten, or McKesson InterQual) that cross-reference every CPT/HCPCS code against the ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes on the same claim. If the diagnosis reported does not appear on the payer's approved list of supporting diagnoses for that procedure, the claim is denied CO-11. Think of it like a prescription — a pharmacist won't fill a medication unless the condition matches. CO-11 means the "prescription" (diagnosis) does not match the "medication" (procedure) you billed.
⚠️
CO-11 Is NOT Always a Coding Error — Sometimes It Is a Missing Diagnosis
In many CO-11 cases, the procedure was medically appropriate — but the coder selected a diagnosis that is too vague, too broad, or simply not on the payer's approved cross-reference list for that CPT code. Before assuming a miscoded claim, review the full encounter documentation. The correct, more specific ICD-10-CM code may already exist in the medical record but was not reported on the original claim.
💡
Important: CO-11 Means the Patient Cannot Be Billed
Because CARC 11 is a Contractual Obligation (CO) adjustment, the provider has contractually agreed to write off amounts that do not meet payer billing requirements. Unlike a PR (Patient Responsibility) denial, the provider may not bill the patient for CO-11 denied amounts unless a valid Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN) or equivalent waiver was signed before the service. Billing patients for CO-11 denials without a waiver violates payer contracts and, for Medicare, the False Claims Act.
Where the Diagnosis and Procedure Pointer Go on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Diagnosis and procedure linkage fields — professional claims
  • Box 21 (A–L) — Diagnosis Codes: Up to 12 ICD-10-CM codes that describe why the patient was seen. Must be as specific as possible — unspecified codes are a primary CO-11 trigger. Report the most relevant diagnosis first in position A.
  • Box 24E — Diagnosis Pointer: One or more letters (A–L) linking each service line in Box 24 to the diagnosis codes in Box 21 that justify that specific procedure. If the pointer references the wrong letter or a diagnosis that does not support the CPT code on that line, CO-11 fires.
  • Box 24D — CPT / HCPCS Procedure Code: The procedure being billed. This is the code the payer cross-checks against the diagnosis pointer in Box 24E.
  • Box 24B — Place of Service: Some payers restrict certain diagnosis–procedure combinations by POS. Confirm the POS is consistent with the clinical setting documented for the service.
  • Box 19 / 24 Modifier: Modifiers such as -59, -25, or -KX can sometimes override CO-11 editing when the clinical scenario justifies a separate, distinct service — but only when fully supported by documentation.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility / Hospital Claims)
Diagnosis and procedure linkage fields — facility claims
  • FL67 (A–Q) — Principal & Other Diagnosis Codes: ICD-10-CM codes explaining why the patient received inpatient or outpatient facility services. FL67 (Principal Diagnosis) is the primary reason for the encounter — it must be specific, valid for the date of service, and clinically linked to the revenue code and procedure.
  • FL44 — Revenue Code: Revenue codes describe the type of service provided at the facility level. Revenue codes are cross-matched against the diagnosis codes in FL67. Mismatched revenue code and diagnosis combinations trigger CO-11 on facility claims.
  • FL74 (a–e) — Principal & Other Procedure Codes: ICD-10-PCS procedure codes (inpatient) or CPT/HCPCS codes (outpatient). Must be supported by the diagnoses in FL67. On outpatient facility claims, each CPT/HCPCS line must map to an appropriate diagnosis.
  • FL68 — Admitting Diagnosis: Required for inpatient claims. Must reflect the condition that led to the admission, and should be consistent with the principal diagnosis and procedures performed.
  • EDI 837I — Loop 2300 HI Segment: Carries all diagnosis codes. Loop 2400 SV2 carries the revenue code and procedure. Diagnosis pointer linkage on facility claims must be consistent across both loops.
✅
Diagnosis Pointer Rule — Quick Reminder
On CMS-1500, Box 24E must reference only the letter(s) from Box 21 that directly and specifically justify the procedure on that service line. Do not point every procedure to the principal diagnosis (position A) by default — if the procedure is for a secondary condition, point to the appropriate secondary diagnosis letter. Incorrect pointers are one of the top five CO-11 causes even when the correct diagnosis code is present on the claim.
Why This Happens
⚠️
DIAGNOSIS–PROCEDURE MISMATCH ROOT CAUSES
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
CO-11 denials occur when payer claim-editing software determines that the ICD-10-CM diagnosis code(s) reported on the claim do not clinically support, justify, or match the CPT/HCPCS procedure code billed on the same claim or service line.
1
Wrong or Unspecified Diagnosis Code
A vague, unspecified, or non-specific ICD-10-CM code was reported when a more specific code exists and is required to justify the procedure. Example: billing J06.9 (Acute upper respiratory infection, unspecified) for a sinus surgery procedure instead of J32.0 (Chronic maxillary sinusitis).
2
Incorrect Diagnosis Pointer (Box 24E)
The correct diagnosis is on the claim in Box 21 but the pointer in Box 24E references a different diagnosis letter that does not support the procedure on that specific service line. The code is right — the pointer is wrong.
3
Diagnosis Not on Payer's Approved LCD/NCD List
Medicare and many commercial payers publish Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs) and National Coverage Determinations (NCDs) that list the exact ICD-10-CM codes that support coverage for a given CPT code. A diagnosis not on that list causes automatic CO-11 denial, even if it is clinically valid.
4
Diagnosis Laterality or Specificity Mismatch
A procedure performed on the right knee was billed with a left-sided diagnosis, or a unilateral procedure was billed with a bilateral diagnosis code. ICD-10-CM requires laterality specificity — payers match it against the procedure code's anatomical scope.
5
Diagnosis Is Excluded from CPT Coverage Criteria
Some CPT codes are explicitly excluded for certain diagnoses. Example: Certain lab tests are not covered when the only diagnosis is a screening (Z) code rather than an active disease diagnosis, or a surgical procedure is excluded for a benign vs. malignant diagnosis mismatch.
6
Secondary Diagnosis Used as Primary
The supporting or secondary diagnosis (e.g., a symptom or comorbidity) was placed in position A (principal diagnosis) instead of the active condition that drove the procedure. Payer edits prioritize the principal diagnosis pointer when adjudicating medical necessity.
7
Age, Sex, or POS Conflict with Diagnosis
Some ICD-10-CM codes are age- or sex-specific. A male patient billed with a female-specific diagnosis, or a pediatric diagnosis coded on an adult encounter, will trigger CO-11. Similarly, certain diagnoses are only payable in specific place-of-service settings.
8
Screening vs. Diagnostic Diagnosis Conflict
A procedure was billed with a diagnostic CPT code (e.g., 45378 – colonoscopy) but the diagnosis was a screening Z code (Z12.11). This combination triggers CO-11 because the procedure type (diagnostic) and the indication (screening) are clinically inconsistent in the payer's editing engine.
9
ICD-10-CM Code Invalid for Date of Service
ICD-10-CM codes are updated annually each October 1. A diagnosis code that was valid in a prior fiscal year but was deleted, revised, or replaced in the current fiscal year will cause a CO-11 denial when billed for services on or after the effective date of the code set change.
10
EHR Default or Copy-Forward Diagnosis Error
A default, carry-forward, or pre-populated diagnosis from a prior encounter was submitted without clinical review. The diagnosis may have been appropriate for a previous visit but is not consistent with the procedures performed at the current encounter — a common EHR workflow problem.
How to Fix It — CARC 11: The Diagnosis Is Inconsistent with the Procedure
💡 What is CARC 11?
Your claim was denied because the payer's claim editing system determined that the ICD-10-CM diagnosis code(s) on the claim do not clinically support the CPT/HCPCS procedure code(s) billed. The fix requires reviewing the medical record, identifying the correct and most specific supporting diagnosis, correcting the diagnosis code and pointer, and resubmitting as a corrected claim. This is almost always correctable at the coding level before any appeal is needed.
CMS-1500
Box 21 / 24E
Diagnosis Codes & Pointer
UB-04
FL67 / FL44
Diagnosis & Revenue Code
837P / 837I
Loop 2300 HI
Diagnosis Segment
📋 CO-11 Most Common Diagnosis–Procedure Mismatch Scenarios
Scenario
✅ Correct Approach
❌ What Triggers CO-11
Sinus surgery billed
J32.0 Chronic maxillary sinusitis
J06.9 Acute URI, unspecified
Knee arthroscopy billed
M23.211 Derangement of anterior cruciate ligament, right knee
M79.3 Panniculitis (unrelated to knee)
Diagnostic colonoscopy billed
K92.1 Melena (diagnostic indication)
Z12.11 Screening for colon cancer (screening code)
Cardiac stress test billed
I25.10 Atherosclerotic heart disease
Z00.00 Encounter for general exam (no cardiac indication)
Mastectomy billed (female-specific)
C50.911 Malignant neoplasm of breast, female
Incorrect laterality or sex-conflicting code
1
Pull the Remittance & Identify the Denied Service Line
The RA will identify which procedure triggered CO-11
🔍 Review the remittance advice (ERA/835 or paper EOB). Identify the exact CPT/HCPCS code on the denied service line and the diagnosis pointer letter referenced in Box 24E for that line. Note the ICD-10-CM code that pointer references in Box 21.
  • Write down the CPT code that denied and the ICD-10-CM code the pointer referenced.
  • Pull the original claim image or 837P/837I transaction for the exact codes submitted.
  • Note if RARC N30 ("Patient ineligible for this service") or N115 ("This decision was based on a Local Coverage Determination") was also present — this changes the approach.
  • Confirm whether other service lines on the same claim paid — a partial CO-11 means only certain procedure–diagnosis combinations failed.
2
Review the Medical Record for a Supporting Diagnosis
Source of truth — the clinical documentation drives the correct ICD-10-CM code
📋 Go to the medical record for the date of service. The correct supporting diagnosis may already be documented — it simply was not coded or was coded incorrectly on the original claim.
  • Review the provider's assessment/plan and final diagnosis in the encounter note.
  • Confirm the documented condition is clinically consistent with the procedure performed — if so, identify the most specific ICD-10-CM code for that condition.
  • Check laterality, acuity (acute vs. chronic), and episode of care qualifiers in the documentation — these drive ICD-10-CM specificity.
  • If the correct diagnosis is documented but was not coded, a corrected claim is appropriate. If the documentation does not support any valid diagnosis for the procedure, a physician query or addendum may be needed before resubmitting.
  • Do not code a diagnosis that is not documented — that is upcoding and creates False Claims Act exposure.
3
Check the Payer's LCD / NCD or Coverage Policy for This CPT Code
Your corrected diagnosis must appear on the payer's approved list
📑 Even if your corrected ICD-10-CM code is accurate, CO-11 will re-deny if that code is not on the payer's approved coverage list for the CPT code billed. Always verify against the LCD or commercial coverage policy before resubmitting.
  • Medicare: Go to cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database → search by CPT/HCPCS code → locate the applicable LCD or NCD → review the "ICD-10-CM Codes That Support Medical Necessity" table.
  • Commercial payers: Go to the payer's provider portal or call provider relations to request the clinical editing policy or coverage criteria for the denied CPT code.
  • If your documented diagnosis is clinically correct but not on the approved list, this is a coverage limitation — document this carefully. You may need to bill the patient if a valid ABN was signed, or write off the amount if it was not.
  • If the correct ICD-10-CM code IS on the approved list, proceed to Step 4 and resubmit with the corrected diagnosis and pointer.
  • 📝 Save a copy of the LCD/NCD or coverage policy you reviewed — attach it to the corrected claim or any subsequent appeal.
4
Still Denied? File a Formal Appeal with Medical Records
Use when the corrected claim re-denies and documentation fully supports medical necessity
⚖️ If the corrected claim with a specific, documented, LCD-supported diagnosis still re-denies with CO-11, the payer's editing engine may have an incorrect crosswalk or the clinical documentation supports coverage on its merits. File a formal appeal with the medical record attached.
  • Appeal must include: Patient name, member ID, claim number, DOS, denied CPT code, corrected ICD-10-CM code, and both EOBs (original denial + corrected claim denial).
  • Key statement: "ICD-10-CM code [XXX.XX] — [Diagnosis Name] — is documented in the attached encounter note and is listed on the applicable LCD/NCD as a covered indication for CPT [XXXXX]. We appeal the continued CO-11 denial as a payer-side clinical editing error."
  • Attach: Signed encounter note with documented diagnosis, LCD/NCD printout with the ICD-10-CM code highlighted, original and corrected EOBs, and any prior authorization documentation if applicable.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with your MAC within 120 days of the denial date. Commercial: check EOB for the appeal deadline — typically 30–180 days.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Coding Workflow and LCD Crosswalk
Stop CO-11 before it reaches the payer
🔁 If CO-11 is appearing across multiple claims, your diagnosis coding workflows, EHR templates, or coder training have systematic gaps in ICD-10-CM specificity, diagnosis pointer accuracy, or LCD compliance.
  • Build and maintain an LCD/NCD crosswalk table by CPT code. For every high-volume CPT code your practice bills, maintain an internal reference table of ICD-10-CM codes approved by each payer. Update it every October 1 when ICD-10-CM codes change.
  • Implement pre-submission diagnosis–procedure edit checks. Configure your billing system or clearinghouse to flag any claim where the diagnosis pointer does not map to an LCD-approved ICD-10-CM code for the corresponding CPT code before the claim transmits.
  • Conduct quarterly coder audits on CO-11 patterns. Pull all CO-11 denials for the prior quarter, group by CPT code, and identify which diagnoses are triggering the most denials. Use findings to update EHR templates and coder education.
  • Update EHR diagnosis templates and smart sets annually. Remove ICD-10-CM codes deleted in the annual October 1 update and replace with the new equivalents. Outdated codes in EHR drop-down templates are the most common source of systemic CO-11 denials.
  • Train clinical staff on diagnosis specificity at point of documentation. Providers who document "knee pain" instead of the specific derangement allow coders only a nonspecific code — which will not pass LCD edits. Documentation improvement reduces CO-11 at the source.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Coding a diagnosis purely to satisfy a payer's LCD crosswalk — without clinical documentation — is fraudulent upcoding under the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3729). The diagnosis must be documented in the medical record first.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these critical mistakes that trigger repeat CO-11 denials, compliance violations, and patient billing errors
These mistakes commonly cause repeat CO-11 denials, corrected claim failures, compliance risk under the False Claims Act, and improper patient billing under the payer contract.
  • Do not change the diagnosis code without reviewing the medical record — coding a diagnosis to satisfy a payer crosswalk without clinical documentation is upcoding and violates the False Claims Act
  • Do not bill the patient for a CO-11 denied amount without confirming a valid ABN or equivalent written advance notice was signed before the service was rendered
  • Do not resubmit without checking the payer's LCD or coverage policy — if the corrected diagnosis is not on the approved list for the CPT code, the claim will re-deny with CO-11 regardless of how accurate the code is
  • Do not assume the diagnosis pointer in Box 24E is correct just because the correct ICD-10-CM code is present in Box 21 — if the pointer references the wrong letter, the payer reads the wrong diagnosis and CO-11 fires
  • Do not appeal before first correcting the diagnosis, confirming LCD support, updating the pointer, and resubmitting as a corrected claim — an appeal without a prior corrected claim submission will generally be dismissed
⚠️
Critical Reminder
CO-11 is a Contractual Obligation denial. Providers who have signed participation agreements with payers have contractually agreed not to bill patients for amounts denied as CO. Billing a patient for a CO-11 denied amount without a valid pre-service ABN or waiver may constitute a breach of your payer contract and, for Medicare, a violation of the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3729).
DIAGNOSIS–PROCEDURE CONSISTENCY CHECKLIST
✅
DIAGNOSIS–PROCEDURE CONSISTENCY CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist to prevent CO-11 denials

Before submitting any claim, confirm all diagnosis–procedure linkage validations are completed

  • ✅ ICD-10-CM code(s) are valid for the date of service — confirmed against the current fiscal year code set (updated October 1 annually)
  • ✅ Diagnosis is documented in the medical record for the date of service — not assumed, inferred, or carried forward from a previous encounter
  • ✅ Most specific ICD-10-CM code used — laterality, acuity, episode of care, and any applicable 7th character extension included as required
  • ✅ Box 24E (CMS-1500) diagnosis pointer references the correct letter(s) in Box 21 that directly justify the procedure on each specific service line
  • ✅ ICD-10-CM code verified against payer's LCD/NCD or commercial coverage policy as an approved indication for the CPT/HCPCS code billed
  • ✅ Diagnosis type is consistent with the procedure type — diagnostic procedure billed with a diagnostic (condition) code, not a screening Z-code
  • ✅ Patient age and sex are consistent with the ICD-10-CM code selected — age-specific and sex-specific codes confirmed against patient demographics
  • ✅ Place of service is consistent with both the diagnosis and the procedure — certain payers restrict diagnosis–procedure combinations by POS
  • ✅ EHR smart sets and diagnosis templates reviewed and updated after October 1 annual ICD-10-CM code set update — no deleted or inactive codes remain in claim templates
  • ✅ If the correct diagnosis is not on the payer's approved LCD list and service was rendered, confirm whether a valid ABN or written advance notice was signed by the patient before billing them
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Use only after a corrected claim with documented, LCD-supported diagnosis was denied again
Appeal only when the corrected claim with the correct, documented, most specific ICD-10-CM code — confirmed on the payer's LCD/coverage list — was resubmitted and denied again with CO-11.
  • The diagnosis is fully documented in the encounter note for the date of service
  • The ICD-10-CM code is confirmed on the payer's LCD, NCD, or commercial coverage policy as an approved indication for the CPT code billed
  • A corrected claim with the updated code and pointer has already been submitted and denied again with CO-11
  • Always attach the encounter note, LCD/NCD printout, and both EOBs to the appeal letter
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most CO-11 Cases)
Recommended first action for the vast majority of CO-11 denials
Most CO-11 denials resolve by identifying the correct, specific ICD-10-CM code from the medical record, confirming it against the payer's LCD or coverage policy, correcting the diagnosis pointer, and resubmitting with Resubmission Code 7.
  • Most CO-11 denials are caused by unspecified diagnosis codes, incorrect diagnosis pointers, or codes not on the LCD/NCD list — all correctable at the coding level
  • Review the medical record first — do not change the code without clinical documentation supporting the correction
  • If the documentation does not support any valid covered diagnosis for the procedure, do not resubmit — evaluate write-off or patient billing (with valid ABN) options
  • Do not appeal as a first step — correct the root cause first and escalate to appeal only after the corrected claim is also denied
