119 CARC CO-119

Benefit Maximum for This Time Period or Occurrence Has Been Reached

Benefit Limit Exhaustion · Professional & Facility Claims · CMS-1500 & UB-04
Common RARC Pairings & Claim Form References
CO-119 N130 N362 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 24A (DOS) Box 21 (DX) Box 24D (CPT) FL42 (Revenue Code) FL44 (HCPCS)
What This Means
🚧
What This Means

CARC 119 means the member's health plan benefit for the billed service has been fully consumed for the applicable time period (calendar year, plan year, benefit period) or for the maximum number of allowed occurrences (visits, days, units). The payer is denying payment — not because the service was medically inappropriate, but because the patient has already received the maximum covered amount under their specific plan. The member is responsible for any remaining balance unless secondary insurance, a waiver, or a plan exception applies.

ℹ️
Think of it this way — What is a Benefit Maximum?
Every insurance plan has a cap on how much it will pay for specific categories of care within a defined time window. Think of it like a prepaid debit card for a specific service — once the balance is zero, no further charges go through. Common examples include: 20 outpatient therapy visits per year, 60 inpatient hospital days per benefit period, $500 in durable medical equipment per calendar year, or 3 chiropractic adjustments per month. CARC 119 fires the moment the plan's counter for that bucket hits its limit.

⚠️
CARC 119 Is Not Always Final — Payer Counts May Be Wrong
Before writing off a CARC 119 denial, always verify the payer's visit or unit count against your own records. Payers frequently include visits from other providers that were billed under the same plan, cross-plan visits from a previous insurer, or improperly counted units. If your internal count differs from the payer's, request an itemized benefits utilization report from the payer and reconcile before accepting the denial.
Understanding the Three Limit Types: Time Period · Occurrence · Dollar Cap
📅
Time Period Maximum
Resets on a fixed date

The plan allows a set number of visits, units, or dollar amount within a defined calendar window — most commonly a calendar year (Jan 1–Dec 31) or a plan/policy year. Once that window closes, the counter resets to zero.

  • Calendar Year: resets January 1 each year
  • Plan Year: resets on the member's enrollment anniversary date
  • Benefit Period (Medicare): resets after 60 consecutive days without hospitalization
  • Example: 20 outpatient PT visits per calendar year — visit 21 in the same year triggers CO-119
🔢
Occurrence Maximum
Does not automatically reset

The plan allows a service to occur a fixed number of times — not tied to a time window. Once the count is exhausted, the benefit is permanently closed under that plan or episode unless medically exceptional circumstances are met.

  • Example: 1 bariatric surgery per lifetime
  • Example: 2 hearing aids per 36 months
  • Example: 3 cortisone injections per joint, per year
  • These require a medical necessity exception or plan override to override the occurrence cap
💲
Dollar Cap Maximum
Tracks cumulative plan payments

The plan pays up to a defined dollar amount for a benefit category per time period. Once the plan's payment total reaches the cap, subsequent claims for that category deny under CO-119 — even if the visit count has not been reached.

  • Example: $500/year for durable medical equipment
  • Example: $1,200/year for vision care
  • Example: $2,000/year for mental health services
  • Dollar caps are independent of visit limits — either can trigger CO-119 first
✅
Key Rule — Always Identify WHICH Limit Type Was Reached
The resolution path differs depending on limit type. A time period maximum may require waiting for the counter to reset or obtaining a medical necessity exception. An occurrence maximum requires plan override documentation. A dollar cap exhaustion requires verifying plan payments are accurate before accepting the denial. Call the payer's provider relations line and ask: "What is the specific benefit limit that triggered the CO-119 and how many visits/units/dollars remain?"
Why This Happens
⚠️
BENEFIT LIMIT & UTILIZATION TRACKING ISSUES
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
CO-119 denials occur when a patient's plan-defined benefit limit has been reached — whether by time period, occurrence count, or dollar cap. Root causes range from legitimate plan exhaustion to payer-side counting errors and benefits verification failures.
1
Legitimate Benefit Exhaustion
Patient genuinely used all covered visits, units, or dollars for the benefit period. No error — the plan limit was consumed by prior authorized services.
2
Benefits Verification Not Performed Before Service
Provider did not verify remaining benefit balance before scheduling or delivering the service. No pre-service check — denial avoidable with a simple eligibility call.
3
Payer's Visit Counter Includes Other Providers
Payer is counting visits from another provider in the same specialty toward the patient's shared benefit limit — common with PT, behavioral health, and chiropractic benefits.
4
Benefit Year Not Aligned with Calendar Year
Provider assumed a calendar-year reset but the member's plan year runs July–June or another cycle. Service billed in January is still in the prior plan year for this member.
5
Payer Counted Denied or Reversed Claims
Payer's system is counting previously denied or reversed claims against the benefit limit — inflating the utilization count and triggering premature CO-119 denials.
6
Mid-Year Plan Change or Benefit Reduction
Member changed plans mid-year or employer modified the benefit structure. New plan has a lower limit and inherited the prior plan's utilization history.
7
Incorrect CPT / Revenue Code Triggered Wrong Benefit Bucket
Claim was submitted with a CPT code that maps to a benefit category with a tighter limit than the service actually falls under — consuming from the wrong bucket.
8
Mental Health Parity Violation (Behavioral Health)
For behavioral health or substance use disorder benefits, visit limits that are more restrictive than medical/surgical limits may violate the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA).
9
Authorization Not Obtained for Continued Services
Initial authorization covered a limited number of visits. Additional services beyond the authorization are being denied as benefit maximum — but root cause is lack of continued authorization.
10
Medicare Skilled Care / 3-Day Stay Rule Not Met
For Medicare SNF benefit, CO-119 may trigger when the qualifying 3-day inpatient stay requirement was not met, the SNF benefit days are exhausted, or the benefit period has not reset.
How to Fix It — CARC 119: Benefit Maximum Reached
💡 What is CARC 119?
Your claim was denied because the patient's plan benefit limit has been fully used for the applicable period or occurrence. Resolution depends on whether the denial is legitimate (limit genuinely exhausted), a payer counting error (incorrect utilization count), or a plan exception opportunity (medical necessity override or MHPAEA parity challenge). Always verify the count before accepting the denial.
STEP 1
Verify the Count
Compare payer's tally to your records
STEP 2
Determine Path
Error → correct; Exhausted → exception or appeal
STEP 3
Notify Patient
ABN / financial liability communication
1
Obtain and Reconcile the Payer's Utilization Count
Do this before any other action — payer counts are frequently inaccurate
🔍 Call the payer and request an itemized benefit utilization report showing every visit, unit, or dollar counted toward the limit that triggered CO-119. Do not accept "the benefit is exhausted" without seeing the line-by-line count.
  • Ask: "Can you provide a list of all dates of service and claim numbers counted toward this benefit limit?"
  • Compare each date and claim on the payer's list against your own remittance history and appointment records.
  • Flag any claim on the payer's list that was denied, voided, or reversed — these should not count against the limit.
  • Flag any dates of service that are from a different provider or facility — confirm whether the plan shares limits across providers.
  • Document the payer rep name, reference number, call date, and the exact count they provided.
2
If Payer Count Is Wrong — Reprocess & Correct & Resubmit
Payer counting errors are common and correctable
✅ If the payer's utilization list includes denied claims, other providers' visits, or dates that belong to a different benefit year, document the discrepancy and submit a corrected claim or informal dispute immediately.
  • Call Payer provide the information that still patient has left the visit This should be send back for Reprocessing Take the TAT time and follow up accordingly.
  • If payer denied to reprocess advise to resubmit a corrected claim (Resubmission Code 7) with a cover letter identifying the specific overcounted dates.
  • Attach your RA history showing which prior claims were denied or reversed and should not count toward the limit.
  • If the payer is counting another provider's visits, attach the member's plan document verifying the shared vs. per-provider benefit structure.
  • Request the payer recalculate the limit and reprocess the denied claim within the same submission cycle.
3
If Limit Is Legitimately Exhausted — Seek a Medical Necessity Exception
For medically necessary continued care beyond the plan limit
📋 Many plans allow exceptions to visit limits when continued care is medically necessary. The treating provider must document why additional visits are clinically required beyond the standard limit.
  • Submit a medical necessity exception or prior authorization request to the payer for visits beyond the benefit maximum.
  • Include: current clinical notes, functional assessment, treatment plan with goals, and a physician statement of medical necessity.
  • Clearly document why the patient's condition requires continuation beyond the standard limit (e.g., post-surgical complexity, acute deterioration, neurological injury).
  • Some payers have a formal Benefit Exception Request form — ask provider relations if one is available.
  • Do not deliver additional services before the exception is approved — services delivered without approval remain patient liability.
4
Evaluate MHPAEA Parity Violation (Behavioral Health Only)
Behavioral health visit limits are legally regulated under federal parity law
⚖️ If the CO-119 denial is for mental health, behavioral health, or substance use disorder services, the plan's visit limit may be an unlawful violation of the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA).
  • Under MHPAEA, plans may not impose more restrictive visit limits on behavioral health services than on analogous medical/surgical services.
  • Ask the payer: "What is the comparable visit limit for medical/surgical outpatient services under this plan?" If behavioral health limits are tighter, this is a potential MHPAEA violation.
  • File a formal MHPAEA parity appeal with the payer. Attach the denial, the plan's stated behavioral health limit, and a request for the comparative medical/surgical benefit limit.
  • If the payer does not resolve the parity issue, file a complaint with the DOL Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA) for employer-sponsored plans or your state insurance commissioner for individual/small group plans.
  • Document all communications — MHPAEA violations can result in payer audits and retroactive payment.
5
Notify the Patient and Issue ABN / Financial Liability Notice
Required before collecting from patient — do not skip this step
📣 Once you determine the benefit limit is genuinely exhausted and no exception or parity challenge applies, the patient must be formally notified of their financial liability before additional services are delivered. For Medicare patients, an Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN) is legally required.
  • For Medicare patients: Issue a valid ABN (Form CMS-R-131) before delivering non-covered services. Without an ABN, you cannot bill the patient for services denied as benefit maximum exceeded. The ABN must clearly state the specific service and reason coverage may be denied.
  • For commercial patients: Issue a financial responsibility notice informing the patient their benefit maximum has been reached and they will be personally responsible for any further services. Get written acknowledgment before proceeding.
  • Check for secondary insurance: Verify whether the patient carries a secondary or supplemental policy (Medigap, commercial secondary) that may cover services beyond the primary plan's benefit limit.
  • Offer financial assistance options: If the patient cannot afford out-of-pocket services, discuss: sliding scale fees, payment plans, charity care, or referral to a community health center with grant-funded services.
  • Document the conversation: Keep a signed copy of the ABN or financial liability notice in the patient record. This is your legal protection if a collections dispute arises later.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Providing services after benefit maximum exhaustion without proper patient notification and consent can result in inability to collect the balance and potential audit findings under the False Claims Act if Medicare is involved.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these mistakes that lead to write-offs, compliance risk, and repeat CO-119 denials
These mistakes commonly cause uncollectable balances, ABN violations, missed appeal windows, and preventable future CO-119 denials.
  • Do not accept CO-119 without first verifying the payer's utilization count — counting errors are common and frequently result in premature limit exhaustion denials
  • Do not deliver services past the benefit maximum without issuing an ABN (Medicare) or written financial liability notice — you will be unable to collect from the patient without prior documented consent
  • Do not appeal CO-119 without first requesting the payer's itemized utilization list — appealing without evidence of a counting error will be rejected and wastes your appeal window
  • Do not assume the benefit maximum resets on January 1 for every patient — many employer-sponsored plans run non-calendar benefit years; always confirm the specific member's plan year before scheduling additional services
  • Do not ignore MHPAEA parity for behavioral health denials — a visit limit that is stricter than the medical/surgical limit may be an illegal plan design, and the benefit restriction may be challengeable
  • Do not bill the patient for Medicare-covered services denied as CO-119 without a valid ABN on file — this is a civil money penalty violation under the Medicare program
⚠️
Critical Reminder — Medicare ABN Requirement
For Medicare patients, delivering services after the benefit maximum is exhausted without a signed Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN) means you cannot bill the patient for those services. The ABN must be issued before the service is delivered, must explain the specific service and reason for potential non-coverage, and must be signed by the patient. Retroactive ABNs are not valid.
BENEFIT MAXIMUM PREVENTION CHECKLIST
✅
BENEFIT MAXIMUM PREVENTION CHECKLIST
Pre-service and ongoing benefit tracking validation

Perform these checks before scheduling services and at each benefit period milestone to prevent CO-119 denials

  • ✅ Benefits verified for the specific member and plan year — including confirmed visit/unit limit and remaining balance — before scheduling any service with known caps (PT, OT, behavioral health, chiro)
  • ✅ Plan year type confirmed for each member — calendar year vs. plan/policy year vs. Medicare benefit period — so remaining benefit is calculated against the correct reset date
  • ✅ Internal visit or unit counter maintained in the scheduling/EHR system for each patient's benefit-capped services — updated after every visit and checked before each appointment
  • ✅ Patient notified in writing when they have 2–3 visits remaining in their benefit — giving time for medical necessity exception requests or financial planning before limit is hit
  • ✅ ABN or financial liability notice issued and signed before delivering any service that may exceed the benefit maximum — retroactive ABNs are not valid for Medicare
  • ✅ Medical necessity exception or extended authorization submitted to payer before the final covered visit — not after the denial — to maintain continuity of care without payment gaps
  • ✅ Secondary insurance checked for all benefit-capped services — many Medigap and commercial secondary plans cover services beyond the primary plan's visit limit
  • ✅ For behavioral health: plan's BH visit limit cross-referenced against medical/surgical outpatient limit to identify potential MHPAEA parity violations before accepting CO-119 as final
  • ✅ CPT and revenue codes audited to confirm services are mapping to the correct benefit bucket — miscoded claims can prematurely exhaust the wrong benefit category
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit vs. When to Write Off
✅
Appeal When These Are True
Payer count error OR MHPAEA parity violation
Appeal when the payer's utilization count is wrong, includes invalid claims, or when a behavioral health limit violates federal parity law.
  • Payer's utilization list includes denied, reversed, or voided claims that should not count toward the limit
  • Payer is counting visits from other providers against a per-practice limit when the plan allows per-provider counting
  • Behavioral health visit cap is more restrictive than the analogous medical/surgical benefit (MHPAEA violation)
  • Attach: itemized utilization discrepancy summary, RA records showing denied/voided claims, and payer call documentation
🔄
Correct & Resubmit When
CPT coding error mapped service to wrong benefit bucket
Correct and resubmit when the denial is caused by coding errors that mapped the service to a depleted benefit bucket instead of the correct, still-available one.
  • Service was billed with the wrong CPT code that maps to a capped benefit — recode to the correct CPT and resubmit
  • Resubmit with Resubmission Code 7 and a cover note identifying the coding correction and the correct benefit bucket
  • Confirm the corrected code maps to a benefit with remaining balance before resubmitting
  • Do not resubmit identical claims — payer will re-deny CO-119 on the same coding
📋
Bill Patient / Write Off When
Benefit genuinely exhausted and no exception available
When the limit is legitimately exhausted, no counting error exists, no exception applies, and MHPAEA does not apply — patient responsibility applies (with proper ABN/notice).
  • Confirm ABN or financial liability notice was signed before service — required to bill patient
  • Check for secondary insurance before billing patient directly
  • Bill patient for the allowed amount, not the full billed charge, per contract terms
  • If no ABN was obtained for a Medicare patient, you may not bill the patient — this becomes a provider write-off

M57 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

Missing/Incomplete/Invalid Provider Identifier

Provider Identifier Data Mismatch · Professional & Facility Claims · CMS-1500 & UB-04
Common CARC Pairing
CO-16 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 25 Box 33a Box 33b Box 24J FL56 FL81
What This Means
🔐
What This Means

M57 means the payer's system could not identify or validate the billing provider, rendering provider, or group identifier on the claim. Either the NPI is missing entirely, incorrectly formatted, inactive in the NPPES registry, belongs to the wrong provider type, or does not match the provider information the payer has on file from enrollment. The payer cannot adjudicate the claim until it can verify who submitted and who performed the service.

ℹ️
Think of it this way — What is a Provider Identifier?
Every provider who bills insurance must have a unique 10-digit National Provider Identifier (NPI) — think of it like a license plate number for your practice. The payer uses that number to look you up in their system and confirm you are credentialed, enrolled, and authorized to bill them. M57 fires when that number is missing, incorrectly formatted, inactive, or does not match what the payer has on file from your credentialing or enrollment records.
⚠️
M57 Is NOT Always a Data Entry Error
Sometimes the NPI on the claim is correct but the payer's credentialing or enrollment file has not been updated — for example after a group merger, provider join date, or recent re-enrollment. Always confirm what NPI the payer has on file before assuming the claim data is wrong.
Where the Provider Identifier Goes on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Professional provider identifier reporting guidance
  • Box 33a — Billing Provider NPI: 10-digit NPI of the billing entity (individual or group). Must be Type-1 or Type-2 NPI exactly as enrolled with the payer. No hyphens or spaces.
  • Box 33b — Billing Provider Taxonomy Code: Required by most payers. Must match the healthcare provider taxonomy listed in the NPPES registry.
  • Box 24J (shaded) — Rendering Provider NPI: 10-digit NPI of the individual provider who performed the service. Must be associated with the billing provider in the payer's network file.
  • Box 25 — Tax ID / EIN: Must match the Tax ID the payer has on file for this billing provider. EIN for organizations; SSN for individual providers.
  • Box 17 — Referring Provider NPI (if applicable): Valid, active 10-digit NPI required when referral-based services are billed.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility / Hospital Claims)
Facility provider identifier reporting guidance
  • FL56 — Billing Provider NPI: 10-digit NPI of the billing facility, group, or organization. Most common source of M57 on facility claims. No hyphens.
  • FL56a — Billing Provider Organization Name: Legal business name exactly as registered with the payer during credentialing or enrollment.
  • FL81 — Attending / Supervising Provider NPI: 10-digit NPI of the physician overseeing care. Required by most payers on facility claims. Must be active in NPPES.
  • FL81a — Attending Provider Organization Name: Physician's legal practice name or business name.
  • EDI 837I — Loop 2010AA: Billing Provider NPI and Taxonomy Code must be reported. Loop 2310A carries Attending Provider NPI.
✅
NPI Format — Quick Rule
NPI must be submitted as exactly 10 digits with no hyphens, no spaces, and no special characters in electronic claims. If the NPI in your system shows as 1234-567-890 or 123456789 (9 digits), it will fail payer validation every time. Always confirm NPI is Active in NPPES at npiregistry.cms.hhs.gov before resubmitting.
Why This Happens
⚠️
PROVIDER IDENTIFIER DATA & REGISTRATION ISSUES
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
M57 denials occur when provider identification data is missing, incorrectly formatted, inactive in NPPES, or does not match what the payer has on file from enrollment or credentialing.
1
Missing NPI Entirely
Billing or rendering provider NPI field left completely blank on the claim — most common cause.
2
NPI Format Error
NPI submitted with hyphens, spaces, or wrong digit count — often 9 digits instead of the required 10.
3
Inactive / Deactivated NPI
Provider's NPI has been deactivated, closed, or retired in NPPES — was valid before but no longer active.
4
NPI Not Enrolled with Payer
Valid NPI exists but provider is not registered or credentialed with this specific payer or plan.
5
Wrong Tax ID / NPI Combination
NPI and Tax ID on the claim do not match together as a pair in the payer's enrollment records.
6
Billing ≠ Rendering Mismatch
Rendering provider NPI in Box 24J is not affiliated with or linked to the billing provider NPI in Box 33a in the payer's system.
7
Type-1 vs. Type-2 NPI Confusion
Individual Type-1 NPI submitted where a group Type-2 organization NPI is required by the payer for billing.
8
Rendering Provider Not Credentialed
Individual provider's NPI is valid but not listed under the billing group in the payer's network file.
9
Claim Sent to Wrong Payer Entity
Submitted to a national or wrong regional payer entity where the provider is not enrolled — e.g., wrong state Blue Cross affiliate.
10
Billing System Legacy / Default NPI
Billing system or claim template carrying an outdated, placeholder, or retired NPI from a previous configuration or provider merge.
How to Fix It — RARC M57: Missing/Incomplete/Invalid Provider Identifier
💡 What is RARC M57?
Your claim was denied because the payer cannot identify the billing provider, rendering provider, or group from the information on the claim. The provider identifier — NPI, Tax ID, taxonomy, or group affiliation — is missing, incorrectly formatted, not enrolled with the payer, or does not match payer records. This is a pure administrative fix: verify the correct provider data, correct the claim, and resubmit.

FL 56 / FL 81
Billing & Attending NPI
CMS-1500
Box 33a / 24J
Billing & Rendering NPI
837P / 837I
Loop 2010AA
NPI + Taxonomy

1
Identify Which Provider Field Is Wrong
The RA will tell you which identifier triggered M57
🔍 Review the remittance advice — M57 is always tied to a specific provider field. Identify whether the payer flagged the Billing Provider, Rendering Provider, Tax ID, or Taxonomy Code before taking any action.
  • Pull the original claim and locate the exact provider field mentioned in the denial.
  • Compare the NPI on the claim against your billing system's current provider master file.
  • Confirm all NPIs are exactly 10 digits with no hyphens or spaces.
  • Confirm the Tax ID is exactly 9 digits and matches the type of entity (EIN for groups, SSN for individuals).
  • Confirm the taxonomy code in Box 33b or FL 81 matches the provider's NPPES classification.
2
Verify NPI Is Active in NPPES
Takes 60 seconds — must be confirmed before resubmission
✅ Go to npiregistry.cms.hhs.gov/search and search the NPI from the claim. This is a required step before correcting any claim with M57.
  • Confirm NPI Status = Active — not Deactivated, Retired, or Delinquent.
  • Verify the effective date covers the date of service on the denied claim.
  • Note the Healthcare Provider Taxonomy Code — required for Box 33b (CMS-1500) and FL 81a (UB-04).
  • If the NPI is inactive, do not resubmit until a valid active NPI is obtained and enrolled with the payer.
  • If the NPI is not found at all, the provider may need to apply for a new NPI at nppes.cms.hhs.gov.
3
Confirm Provider Is Enrolled with the Payer
Active NPI ≠ enrolled with this specific payer
📞 An active NPI in NPPES does not automatically mean the provider is enrolled with this payer. Call the payer's provider relations or credentialing line to confirm.
  • Ask: "Is NPI [XXXXXXXXXX] for [Provider Name] currently enrolled with your plan?"
  • Ask: "What Tax ID do you have on file for this provider?"
  • Ask: "Is [Rendering Provider] listed under group [Group Name] in your network file?"
  • If not enrolled: ask for the credentialing or provider enrollment department and the process to register.
  • 📝 Document the call: reference number, rep name, date, time, and what NPI/Tax ID the payer has on file.
4
Still Denied? File a Formal Appeal
Use when corrected claim is denied and payer confirms enrollment
⚖️ If the corrected claim with a verified, active, enrolled NPI still denies with M57, the payer has a system-side issue. File a formal appeal with NPPES and enrollment documentation.
  • Appeal must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, DOS, and both remittance advices.
  • Key statement: "NPI [XXXXXXXXXX] is Active in the NPPES registry and confirmed enrolled with [Payer Name] per provider relations call on [date]. We appeal the continued M57 denial as a payer-side processing error."
  • Attach: NPPES printout showing Active status, provider enrollment confirmation letter or portal screenshot, call note with payer reference number, original and corrected claims.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with MAC within 120 days. Commercial: check EOB — typically 30–180 days.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Provider Master File
Stop M57 before it reaches the payer
🔁 If M57 is appearing across multiple claims, your provider master file or billing system templates contain outdated, incorrectly formatted, or unenrolled NPI data that is being passed to claims without validation.
  • Audit your provider master file quarterly. Pull every billing and rendering provider in your system and verify each NPI against NPPES. Any inactive or wrong-format NPI must be corrected before the next claim run.
  • Implement NPI format validation at data entry. Your billing system should reject any NPI entry that is not exactly 10 digits with no special characters — block bad data before it reaches a claim.
  • Build a payer-specific provider configuration table. Different payers may require different NPI/Tax ID combinations. Store the correct pair per payer and auto-populate at claim creation.
  • Add a pre-submission provider audit edit. Before any claim reaches the clearinghouse, validate: (1) Billing NPI is Active in NPPES, (2) Rendering NPI is Active and linked to billing group, (3) NPI + Tax ID pair matches payer enrollment file.
  • Update provider templates after any credentialing event. Provider join, leave, group merge, EIN change — any of these events must trigger an immediate update to all affected billing templates.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Submitting claims with unverified, inactive, or fabricated NPIs creates False Claims Act exposure. Provider identifiers must reflect actual enrolled, credentialed providers.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common provider identifier mistakes that trigger repeat M57 denials
These mistakes commonly cause repeat M57 denials, corrected claim failures, and compliance risk under the False Claims Act.
  • Do not resubmit without correcting the NPI format — hyphens, spaces, or wrong digit count will re-deny with M57 every time
  • Do not assume clearinghouse acceptance means the NPI is valid with the payer — clearinghouses check format only, not payer enrollment
  • Do not use an inactive or deactivated NPI from NPPES — payers will not pay any claim submitted with an inactive provider identifier
  • Do not submit a different NPI than what the payer has on file, even if both are technically "valid" in NPPES — the enrolled NPI must match exactly
  • Do not appeal before first verifying NPPES status, confirming payer enrollment, correcting the claim, and resubmitting — an appeal without a prior corrected claim submission will be rejected
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Submitting a claim with an unverified, inactive, or fabricated NPI is a violation of the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3729). All provider NPIs must be confirmed Active in NPPES and enrolled with the payer before any claim is submitted or resubmitted.
PROVIDER IDENTIFIER CHECKLIST
✅
PROVIDER IDENTIFIER CHECKLIST
Pre-submission provider validation checklist

Before submitting any claim, confirm all provider identifier validations are completed

  • ✅ Billing Provider NPI is exactly 10 digits with no hyphens or spaces
  • ✅ Billing Provider NPI verified as Active in NPPES registry before submission
  • ✅ Billing Provider NPI confirmed enrolled with this specific payer
  • ✅ Rendering Provider NPI is exactly 10 digits, active in NPPES, and associated with billing group in payer's network file
  • ✅ Tax ID is exactly 9 digits — no hyphens in electronic submission — and matches payer enrollment records
  • ✅ Billing Provider Taxonomy Code (Box 33b / FL 81a) matches NPPES classification
  • ✅ NPI type is correct — Type-2 organization NPI used for group billing; Type-1 individual NPI for solo providers
  • ✅ Claim submitted to the correct payer entity — not to a national affiliate where the provider is not enrolled
  • ✅ Provider master file reviewed and no placeholder, legacy, or retired NPIs remain in claim templates
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Use only after provider data is fully verified and corrected claim is denied
Appeal only when provider NPI is confirmed active in NPPES, confirmed enrolled with the payer, correctly formatted on the corrected claim — and the payer denied it anyway.
  • A corrected claim with a verified, active, enrolled NPI has already been submitted and denied again with M57
  • NPPES confirms the NPI is Active as of the date of service
  • Payer provider relations confirmed the NPI is enrolled and on file — this is a payer-side processing error
  • Always attach the NPPES printout and enrollment confirmation letter to the appeal
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most M57 Cases)
Recommended first action for most M57 denials
Most M57 denials resolve by correcting the NPI format, updating the Tax ID, or adding the missing rendering provider NPI and resubmitting as a corrected claim.
  • Most M57 denials are caused by missing, incorrectly formatted, or unenrolled provider NPIs — verify, correct, and resubmit with Resubmission Code 7
  • If the provider is not enrolled with the payer, work with your credentialing team before resubmitting — submitting again with the same unenrolled NPI will re-deny
  • If the NPI is inactive, obtain the current active NPI and confirm enrollment before resubmitting
  • Do not appeal as a first step — correct the root cause first and escalate to appeal only after the corrected claim is also denied

M77 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

Missing/Incomplete/Invalid/Inappropriate Place of Service

Place of Service / Claim Form Data Error · Professional Claims · CMS-1500 Only
Common CARC Pairing
CO-16 CO-5 CMS-1500 Box 24B 837P CLM05-1 837P SV105
What This Means
📍
What This Means

M77 means the Place of Service (POS) code in Box 24B of the CMS-1500 is either missing entirely, contains an invalid two-digit code not recognized by CMS, is incomplete, or is inappropriate for the procedure billed on that service line. The POS code tells the payer exactly where the service was physically performed — and that location directly determines which fee schedule applies, whether the service is covered in that setting, and how much the payer will pay. A missing or wrong POS code makes the claim unprocessable.

ℹ️
Think of it this way — What is a Place of Service Code?
Every service billed on a professional claim must declare where it happened. The Place of Service code is a mandatory two-digit number — entered in Box 24B of the CMS-1500 — that identifies the physical setting where care was provided. POS 11 = physician office. POS 22 = hospital outpatient. POS 23 = emergency room. Payers use this code to apply the correct fee schedule, verify coverage for that setting, and confirm the service makes clinical sense in that location. M77 fires when that two-digit code is blank, wrong, or doesn't match the service billed.
⚠️
M77 Applies to CMS-1500 Professional Claims Only
POS codes and Box 24B exist only on CMS-1500 professional claims. UB-04 institutional claims do not use POS codes — they use Type of Bill (TOB) in FL4 and Revenue Codes in FL42 to define the care setting. If M77 appears on a facility claim, verify the claim was submitted on the correct claim form before investigating POS data.
Where the Place of Service Code Goes on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Professional POS reporting guidance
  • Box 24B — Place of Service: Mandatory two-digit POS code entered on every service line. Each line in Box 24 (A–J) must have its own POS code if the services were rendered in different settings on the same claim.
  • POS code must match the actual physical location where the service was rendered — not the billing address and not where the order was written.
  • Box 24D — Procedure Code: The CPT/HCPCS billed must be clinically appropriate for the POS entered. Payers cross-validate the two — an office-only code billed with an inpatient POS will deny.
  • Box 32 — Service Facility Location: The address of the location where services were rendered must be consistent with the POS code entered in Box 24B.
  • 837P EDI: POS code is submitted in Loop 2300, CLM05-1 (claim level) and Loop 2400, SV105 (service line level). Line-level SV105 takes priority over claim-level in payer adjudication.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims) — No POS Code
Facility claims do not use Box 24B or POS codes
  • UB-04 does NOT use POS codes. Place of service on institutional claims is defined by the Type of Bill (TOB) in FL4 — the first digit identifies the facility type and the second identifies the care classification.
  • FL4 — Type of Bill: Replaces the function of POS on facility claims. Digit 1 = facility type (1=Hospital, 2=SNF, 3=HHA). Digit 2 = bill classification (1=Inpatient, 3=Outpatient).
  • FL42 — Revenue Codes: Revenue codes define the department or service category and indirectly communicate care setting to the payer.
  • If M77 appears on a UB-04 submission, the claim was likely submitted on the wrong form — a professional service was billed institutionally, or the form type itself requires correction.
⚠️ Key Rule: If a physician provides services inside a hospital setting, they submit a CMS-1500 with the appropriate facility POS code (e.g., POS 22 for outpatient hospital). The hospital separately submits a UB-04. Two separate claims — two separate forms.

✅
POS Code vs. Reimbursement Rate — Critical Billing Impact
The POS code directly controls which fee schedule the payer applies. POS 11 (office) pays the non-facility rate — typically 18–30% higher than the facility rate. POS 22 (outpatient hospital) pays the lower facility rate. Entering the wrong POS code is not just a denial risk — it is a reimbursement accuracy issue that can cause systematic overpayment or underpayment on every claim it touches.
Why This Happens
⚠️
MISSING / INVALID / INAPPROPRIATE POS CODE
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
M77 denials occur when the POS code in Box 24B is blank, contains a non-existent two-digit code, or does not match the clinical setting, the procedure billed, or the service facility address on the claim.
1
POS Code Left Blank
Box 24B not populated on one or more service lines — most common cause of M77.
2
Invalid POS Code
A code was entered that does not exist in the CMS POS code set — e.g., a 3-digit number, a letter, or a retired code.
3
POS Does Not Match Procedure
CPT/HCPCS billed is not clinically valid in the setting indicated — e.g., office E/M code billed with inpatient POS 21.
4
POS Does Not Match Service Facility Address
Box 32 service facility address indicates a hospital but POS 11 (office) was entered — the address and POS conflict.
5
Telehealth POS Error
Telehealth service billed with POS 11 (office) instead of POS 02 or POS 10, or submitted without required Modifier 95 or GT.
6
Facility vs. Non-Facility Confusion
Service rendered in a hospital outpatient department but billed with POS 11 — triggering both a denial and a reimbursement rate error.
7
Copy/Paste from Prior Claim
POS code copied from a previous claim where the service was in a different setting — not updated to match the current date of service location.
8
Wrong POS for Service Type
ASC procedure billed with POS 22 (outpatient hospital) instead of POS 24 (ASC) — or SNF service billed with POS 21 instead of POS 31.
9
Billing System Default POS
Billing template has a hardcoded default POS code that was not overridden for a service rendered at a different location.
10
Payer-Specific POS Restriction
Some payers restrict certain CPT codes to specific POS settings per their coverage policy — a valid POS/CPT pair under Medicare may deny under a commercial payer.
How to Fix It — RARC M77: Missing/Incomplete/Invalid/Inappropriate Place of Service
💡 What is RARC M77?
Your claim was denied because the Place of Service code in Box 24B is missing, contains an invalid code, or does not match the service, procedure, or facility address on the claim. The POS code is not optional — it is a mandatory two-digit field that must accurately reflect the physical setting where each service was rendered. Wrong POS = wrong fee schedule = wrong payment or denial.
CMS-1500
Box 24B
Place of Service Code
837P — Claim Level
Loop 2300

SV105 (takes priority)

✅ Correct POS
Office E/M (CPT 99213)

1
Confirm Where the Service Was Actually Rendered
The medical record and appointment location are the source of truth
🔍 The POS code must reflect the physical location where the service was performed on the date of service — not the billing address, not the ordering location, not where the claim was created.
  • Pull the medical record or appointment documentation for the date of service — confirm the physical address where care was delivered.
  • Cross-reference that address against the CMS POS code list to identify the correct two-digit code.
  • Confirm whether the location is a provider-based department of a hospital — if so, POS 22 is required even if it physically looks like a clinic.
  • For telehealth: confirm whether the patient was at home (POS 10) or at a distant site (POS 02) and whether Modifier 95 or GT was appended to the CPT code.
  • Check the Box 32 service facility address — it must logically correspond with the POS code entered in Box 24B.
2
Correct the POS Code & Resubmit
Fastest fix — correct Box 24B and resubmit as corrected claim
✅ Once you confirm the correct POS code from the medical record, update Box 24B on every affected service line and resubmit as a corrected claim — not a new claim.
  • CMS-1500: Update Box 24B on every affected service line. Use Resubmission Code "7" in Box 22 + original ICN.
  • 837P EDI: Update Loop 2400, SV105 (line-level) — this takes adjudication priority over the claim-level CLM05-1. Correct both if needed.
  • Verify Box 32 service facility address is consistent with the corrected POS code — fix both in the same corrected claim if needed.
  • If telehealth, confirm Modifier 95 or GT is present on the CPT code — missing modifier with telehealth POS will re-deny.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits — corrected claim deadlines vary by payer (Medicare: 12 months from DOS).
3
POS Is Correct But Still Denied? Call the Payer
Payer may have a coverage restriction for this CPT + POS combination
📞 If the POS code is confirmed correct against the medical record but the claim still denies with M77, call the payer's provider relations line — the denial may be a payer-specific CPT/POS restriction, not a data error.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, date of service, CPT code billed, POS code submitted, service facility address, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask: "Is CPT [XXXXX] covered under POS [XX] per your coverage policy? If not, which POS is required?"
  • Ask if the denial is a payer-side restriction beyond CMS guidelines — commercial payers may restrict certain procedures to specific POS settings even when CMS allows them broadly.
  • Ask whether a modifier is required to override the restriction (e.g., modifier 22, 52, or a place-of-service override modifier specific to that payer).
  • 📝 Document the call: reference number, rep name, date, time, and the specific CPT/POS policy cited by the payer.
4
Still Denied? File a Formal Appeal
Attach documentation proving the service setting was correct
⚖️ If the corrected claim with a verified POS code is still denied, file a formal appeal with medical record documentation proving the service was rendered in the setting indicated by the POS code.
  • Appeal must include: Provider name, NPI, patient name, member ID, claim number, DOS, CPT billed, POS submitted, service facility address, and both remittance advices.
  • Key statement: "The Place of Service code [XX] submitted on the corrected claim accurately reflects the physical setting where [service] was rendered on [DOS], as documented in the medical record and consistent with the service facility address in Box 32. We appeal the continued M77 denial."
  • Attach: Medical record confirming the service location, appointment scheduling record, service facility address documentation, and both remittance advices.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with MAC within 120 days. Reference CMS Claims Processing Manual, Pub 100-04, Chapter 26. Commercial: check EOB — typically 30–180 days.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your POS Workflow & Templates
Stop M77 before it reaches the payer
🔁 If M77 is appearing across multiple claims, your billing system has a POS default or data capture gap — either the wrong POS is hardcoded in templates, the clinical documentation workflow is not passing the service location to billing, or billers are not verifying POS before submission.
  • Map POS codes to service locations in your scheduling system. Every appointment location in your system should be configured with the correct POS code so it auto-populates onto the claim — eliminating manual entry errors at billing time.
  • Build a CPT-to-POS validation table. Identify which CPT codes your practice routinely bills and map the valid POS settings for each. Add a pre-submission edit that flags any CPT/POS pairing that falls outside the valid range.
  • Train billers on facility vs. non-facility POS distinction. The most common and costly M77 error is billing POS 11 for services rendered in a hospital outpatient department — this causes both denial and systematic underpayment.
  • Add a Box 32 / Box 24B cross-validation edit. Before any claim is released, confirm that the service facility address in Box 32 is logically consistent with the POS code in Box 24B — a hospital address with POS 11 should be flagged automatically.
  • Build a telehealth POS rule. All telehealth claims must fire an edit: (1) Is POS 02 or 10 present? (2) Is Modifier 95 or GT appended to the CPT? If either is missing, hold the claim for review.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Billing POS 11 when services were rendered in a hospital outpatient department (POS 22) constitutes upcoding — the non-facility rate is higher than the facility rate. This creates False Claims Act exposure on every affected claim.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common POS mistakes that trigger repeat M77 denials
These mistakes commonly cause repeat M77 denials, reimbursement rate errors, corrected claim failures, and compliance risk.
  • Do not resubmit without verifying the actual service location from the medical record — guessing the POS code will re-deny with M77
  • Do not use POS 11 (office) for services rendered in any hospital-based setting — this is the most common M77 cause and creates a False Claims Act risk from overbilling the non-facility rate
  • Do not copy POS codes from prior claims without confirming the service location was the same on the current date of service
  • Do not submit telehealth services with POS 11 — use POS 02 (telehealth, other than home) or POS 10 (telehealth, patient home) and always append Modifier 95 or GT
  • Do not appeal before correcting the POS code and resubmitting as a corrected claim — an appeal without a prior corrected claim submission will be rejected
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Billing POS 11 for services rendered in a hospital outpatient department (where POS 22 is correct) means the claim captures the higher non-facility fee schedule rate. This constitutes upcoding under the False Claims Act. CMS and commercial payers actively audit POS 11 vs. POS 22 patterns — systematic misuse can result in post-payment audits, recoupment, and exclusion.
PLACE OF SERVICE CHECKLIST
✅
PLACE OF SERVICE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission POS validation checklist

Before submitting any professional claim, confirm all POS validations are completed

  • ✅ Box 24B populated with a valid two-digit CMS POS code on every service line
  • ✅ POS code verified against the actual physical location where care was rendered on the date of service
  • ✅ CPT/HCPCS codes on the claim are clinically valid in the setting indicated by the POS code
  • ✅ Box 32 service facility address is logically consistent with the POS code in Box 24B
  • ✅ Hospital outpatient department services use POS 22 — not POS 11
  • ✅ Telehealth services use POS 02 or POS 10 — not POS 11 — and Modifier 95 or GT is appended
  • ✅ ASC procedures use POS 24 — not POS 22 or POS 11
  • ✅ SNF services use POS 31 for inpatient skilled nursing — not POS 21 (inpatient hospital)
  • ✅ POS code was not copied from a prior claim without confirming the location is the same
  • ✅ Payer-specific CPT/POS coverage policy reviewed — commercial payer restrictions confirmed before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Use only after POS accuracy is confirmed and corrected claim denied
Appeal only when the POS code is confirmed correct per the medical record and the corrected claim was denied again — indicating a payer-side processing or coverage policy issue.
  • A corrected claim with the verified POS code has already been submitted and denied again with M77
  • The medical record and Box 32 service facility address both confirm the service was rendered in the setting indicated by the POS
  • Payer provider relations confirmed the CPT/POS pairing is valid under their coverage policy — this is a payer-side adjudication error
  • Always attach medical record documentation confirming the service location when appealing M77
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most M77 Cases)
Recommended first action for most M77 denials
Most M77 denials resolve by confirming the correct POS code from the medical record, updating Box 24B, and resubmitting as a corrected claim with Resubmission Code 7.
  • Most M77 denials are caused by a missing, invalid, or mismatched POS code in Box 24B — verify the service location, correct the code, and resubmit with Resubmission Code 7
  • If the POS was wrong because the service location changed (e.g., moved from office to hospital outpatient), correct both Box 24B and Box 32 in the same corrected claim
  • If telehealth, correct both the POS code (02 or 10) and ensure Modifier 95 or GT is present before resubmitting
  • Do not appeal as a first step — correct the root cause first and escalate to appeal only after the corrected claim is also denied

Referral — Missing / Incomplete / Invalid / Unauthorized

Referral & Physician Authorization · Professional & Facility Claims · CMS-1500 Box 17 / UB-04 FL17
Common CARC Pairing
CO-16 CO-243 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 17 / 17b Box 23 UB-04 FL17
All 6 Referral RARC Codes — At a Glance

All six codes relate to referral documentation failures. They differ only in which element of the referral is missing, incomplete, invalid, or unauthorized. The root causes, claim fields, and resolution steps overlap significantly — this guide covers all six together.

N335 Missing/incomplete/invalid referral date

The referral date on the form is blank, uses an incorrect format, falls outside the service date range, or is missing the month, day, or year.

N475 Missing completed referral form

A fully completed referral form was required but was not attached to or submitted with the claim.

N476 Incomplete/invalid completed referral form

A referral form was submitted but is missing required fields, has illegible data, contains incorrect information, or lacks a required signature.

N489 Missing referral form

No referral form of any kind was submitted. The claim was processed without any referral documentation attached or on file with the payer.

N490 Incomplete/invalid referral form

A referral form was submitted but is incomplete, invalid, or does not satisfy the payer's referral documentation requirements for the service billed.

N630 Referral not authorized by attending physician

The referral was not issued by the patient's attending or designated PCP, was issued by a provider outside the plan's gatekeeper rules, or the attending physician did not authorize the referred service.

⚠️ N475 vs. N489 / N476 vs. N490 — Key Distinction: N475 and N476 refer specifically to a completed referral form (one that was submitted but had issues). N489 and N490 refer to a referral form in the broader sense — including situations where no referral documentation was submitted at all. In practice, all four require the same resolution: obtain, complete, and submit valid referral documentation.
What This Means
📋
What This Means

All six of these codes indicate a referral documentation failure. The payer cannot process or pay the claim because the referral — the formal permission from the patient's primary care physician or attending physician to see a specialist or receive a specific service — is either missing from the claim, incomplete, invalid, contains an error in the referral date, or was not issued by the correct authorizing physician. On managed care plans (HMO, certain PPO and Medicaid plans), a referral from the PCP is a required gate before the specialist can be paid. Without valid referral documentation, the claim cannot be adjudicated.

ℹ️
Think of it this way — What is a Referral?
On managed care plans — especially HMOs — the patient's Primary Care Physician (PCP) acts as a gatekeeper. Before a patient can see a specialist, the PCP must formally refer them. The payer issues or recognizes a referral number or form that proves the PCP approved the specialist visit. That referral must be on the claim, valid, unexpired, and issued by the correct physician. These six RARC codes fire when any element of that referral chain breaks down — missing date, missing form, incomplete form, wrong authorizing physician, or no authorization at all.
⚠️
These Codes Do NOT Apply to All Plan Types
Referral requirements vary by plan type. HMO plans always require PCP referrals. PPO plans typically do not. EPO plans vary. Medicare fee-for-service does not require referrals (though Medicare Advantage HMO plans do). Always verify the patient's specific plan type and referral requirement at time of scheduling — not at time of billing — before rendering specialist services.
Where Referral Information Goes on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Professional referral reporting guidance
  • Box 17 — Referring/Ordering Provider Name: Full name of the PCP or attending physician who issued the referral. Must match the CMS Ordering and Referring file exactly — no titles (Dr., MD) or middle initials.
  • Box 17a — Qualifier: Enter the qualifier identifying the type of provider number: DN = Referring Provider, DK = Ordering Provider, DQ = Supervising Provider.
  • Box 17b — Referring Provider NPI: 10-digit NPI of the referring or ordering physician. Must be active in NPPES and match the provider named in Box 17.
  • Box 23 — Prior Authorization / Referral Number: Enter the referral number issued by the payer or PCP authorization system. Required when payer issues referral tracking numbers.
  • Referral Date (N335): The date the referral was issued must be on file and must pre-date or match the date of service. Format: MM DD CCYY.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims)
Facility referral reporting guidance
  • FL17 — Referring Provider Name: Full name of the referring physician who directed the patient to the facility. Required on inpatient and many outpatient facility claims.
  • FL17a — Referring Provider NPI: 10-digit NPI of the referring physician, entered in the unshaded portion of FL17.
  • FL63 — Treatment Authorization Code: When the payer issues a referral tracking or authorization number, it is reported here — same field as prior authorization on UB-04.
  • FL67 — Principal Diagnosis: Payers validate that the diagnosis used to justify the referral matches the diagnosis on the claim.
  • EDI 837I: Referring provider is reported in Loop 2310F — NM101 qualifier = DN, NM109 = referring provider NPI.
✅
Referral Date Rule (N335) — Format & Validity
The referral date must be in MM DD CCYY format and must be on or before the date of service — a referral dated after the appointment was rendered is invalid. Most payers require the referral date to be within a specific validity window (commonly 30–90 days from date of referral to date of service). A referral issued 6 months before the DOS will often deny even if both dates are valid individually.
Why This Happens
⚠️
REFERRAL DOCUMENTATION & AUTHORIZATION FAILURES
Most common root causes behind all six referral denial codes
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Referral denials almost always originate before the claim is submitted — at the scheduling or intake stage. By the time the denial reaches billing, the referral opportunity has already passed. The root causes below span the full patient encounter workflow.
1
No Referral Obtained Before Service
Patient seen by specialist before PCP issued a referral. Most common cause of N489 and N630 — service rendered without any referral on file.
→ Triggers: N489, N630
2
Referral Not Submitted with Claim
Referral exists on file but was not attached to or reported on the claim at time of submission.
→ Triggers: N475, N489
3
Referral Date Missing or Invalid
Referral form has no date, an incomplete date (e.g., missing year), an incorrect format, or a date that falls after the date of service.
→ Triggers: N335
4
Incomplete Referral Form
Referral form submitted but is missing required fields — no diagnosis, no procedure/service type, no PCP signature, or no patient demographics.
→ Triggers: N476, N490
5
Expired Referral
Referral was valid when issued but the date of service falls outside the referral's approved validity period (commonly 30–90 days).
→ Triggers: N335, N489, N630
6
Referral from Non-Attending / Wrong Physician
Referral was issued by a covering provider, urgent care physician, or someone other than the patient's designated PCP or attending physician for the plan year.
→ Triggers: N630
7
Wrong Service Type on Referral
Referral was issued for a different specialty or service than what was billed — e.g., referred for cardiology but billed for orthopedic services.
→ Triggers: N476, N490, N630
8
Visit Count Exceeded
Referral authorized a specific number of visits (e.g., 6 PT visits). More visits were billed than the referral approved — excess visits deny with referral codes.
→ Triggers: N476, N490, N630
9
Communication Breakdown
Referral was obtained by the clinical team but the number or documentation was never communicated to the billing team before claim submission.
→ Triggers: N475, N489
10
Referral Not Required Per Plan — But Payer Denies Anyway
Payer system error or plan enrollment data mismatch causes the claim to deny for referral even though the patient's plan type (PPO, Medicare FFS) does not require one.
→ Triggers: N630 (payer-side error)
How to Fix It — N335 · N475 · N476 · N489 · N490 · N630: Referral Denials
💡 What Are These RARC Codes?
All six codes indicate the payer could not process payment because referral documentation was missing, incomplete, invalid, incorrectly dated, or not authorized by the correct physician. The fix always starts the same way: go back to the clinical record, locate or obtain the referral, verify it covers the service and date, and resubmit with the correct documentation.
CMS-1500
Box 17 / 17b
Referring Provider & NPI
CMS-1500
Box 23
Referral / Auth Number
UB-04
FL17 / FL63
Referring Provider / Auth
📋 Services Commonly Requiring PCP Referral on HMO Plans
Service Type
Why Referral Required
Specialist visits (all types)
HMO gatekeeper rule — PCP must direct patient to specialist
Physical / Occupational Therapy
Payer requires PCP order and visit count authorization
Mental health / Behavioral health
PCP referral and often separate behavioral health auth required
Diagnostic imaging (MRI, CT, PET)
Radiology management program requires order + referral
Elective surgical procedures
Requires both referral and prior authorization on HMO plans
1
Confirm Whether a Referral Was Obtained
The referral may exist — just not on the claim
🔍 Before taking any other action — check whether a referral was actually obtained. The denial may simply mean the referral was not attached to the claim, not that it doesn't exist.
  • Search your EHR, authorization management system, or practice management system for a referral on file for this patient, this specialist, and this date of service.
  • Check the payer's provider portal — many payers allow you to look up active referrals by member ID and service date.
  • Contact the referring PCP's office to confirm whether they entered a referral on the payer portal or issued a paper referral form.
  • Confirm the referral covers the exact service billed — specialty type, procedure, and date range must all match.
  • Confirm the referral was issued by the patient's designated PCP for the current plan year — a referral from a covering or different provider may be invalid under N630.
2
Add / Correct Referral Info & Resubmit
Fastest fix when referral exists but was missing from the claim
✅ If the referral exists and is valid, this is a data entry fix. Add the referral number, correct the referral date, attach the completed referral form, and resubmit as a corrected claim.
  • N335 (referral date): Correct Box 17 referral date in MM DD CCYY format — must be on or before the DOS and within the payer's validity window.
  • N475 / N489 (missing form): Attach the completed referral form to the corrected claim. Confirm your clearinghouse accepts referral attachments.
  • N476 / N490 (incomplete form): Complete all missing fields on the referral form — patient demographics, diagnosis, service type, date, and PCP signature — then reattach.
  • CMS-1500: Box 17 (referring provider name), Box 17b (NPI), Box 23 (referral number if issued). Resubmission Code "7" in Box 22 + original ICN.
  • UB-04: FL17 (referring provider), FL17a (NPI), FL63 (referral/auth number). TOB frequency digit "7" + original TCN in FL64.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits — act quickly, deadlines do not pause during referral research.
3
No Referral on File? Request Retro Referral from PCP
Some payers and PCPs allow backdated referral issuance
📞 If no referral was ever obtained, contact the patient's PCP immediately to request a retroactive referral. Many PCPs will issue one if the service was medically appropriate. Payer approval of retro referrals varies.
  • Call the patient's PCP office — explain the date of service, specialist seen, service rendered, and the denial received. Request they enter a referral retroactively on the payer portal.
  • Simultaneously call the payer's provider relations line and ask: "Does your plan accept retroactive referrals? What is the deadline and process?"
  • Have ready: Patient member ID, DOS, specialist name and NPI, service rendered, diagnosis, and the denial RA with the RARC code.
  • If the payer accepts retro referrals and PCP issues one, obtain the referral number in writing then resubmit the corrected claim immediately.
  • 📝 Document everything: PCP office contact, payer rep reference number, date, time, and outcome of retro referral request.
4
Retro Referral Denied? File a Formal Appeal
Fight it with medical necessity and plan language documentation
⚖️ If the payer denies the retro referral request or upholds the denial, file a formal appeal citing the medical necessity of the service and — for N630 — challenge the validity of the attending physician restriction.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, DOS, specialist name, service rendered, referring PCP name and NPI, and RARC code received.
  • For N630 specifically: "The service was medically necessary and rendered by an in-network specialist. The referral denial under N630 is disputed as the referring physician [Name, NPI] is the patient's designated attending physician under Plan ID [XXXXX] for plan year [XXXX]."
  • Attach: Medical record supporting medical necessity, referral documentation (if any), payer plan language on referral requirements, and both remittance advices.
  • For emergent services: Cite payer plan language — most plans cannot deny emergent specialist care solely for missing referral.
  • Medicare Advantage: File Reconsideration within 60 days. Commercial: check EOB — typically 30–180 days.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Referral Workflow
Referral denials start at scheduling — fix them there
🔁 If these referral codes appear repeatedly across claims, your practice has a front-end referral workflow gap. By the time the denial reaches billing, the referral window has often already closed. The fix must happen at scheduling — not at billing.
  • Build a plan-type referral requirement matrix. For every payer and plan type you see, document whether a referral is required, who must issue it, what the validity period is, and whether a referral number must be on the claim. Update it annually at open enrollment.
  • Make referral verification a scheduling checkpoint. Before any specialist appointment is confirmed for an HMO patient, a valid referral number must be on file. No referral = no appointment confirmation.
  • Store the referral number in the patient account at time of intake so it auto-populates onto the claim at billing — never rely on billers to manually locate and enter referral numbers at claim creation time.
  • Add a pre-submission referral edit. For all HMO plan claims, add a claim scrubber edit that flags any claim missing a referring provider NPI (Box 17b) or referral number (Box 23) before it reaches the payer.
  • Audit referral expiration dates. A referral in your system is only valid for the period the payer approved — confirm the referral date range covers the actual date of service, especially for recurring visits (PT, behavioral health).
  • 🔒 Train scheduling and front desk staff: Referral management is a revenue cycle responsibility that starts at patient intake — not in the billing department. The earlier the referral gap is caught, the easier it is to fix.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common referral mistakes that trigger repeat denials across all six codes
These mistakes cause repeat referral denials, corrected claim failures, appeal rejections, and in some cases patient balance billing errors.
  • Do not resubmit without first confirming whether a valid referral exists — submitting the same claim again without the referral will re-deny with the same code
  • Do not appeal a referral denial before correcting the claim — an appeal without the referral documentation attached will be denied for the same reason
  • Do not assume a referral from any physician is valid — for N630, the referral must come from the patient's designated attending PCP for the current plan year, not a covering provider
  • Do not use a referral number from a different service date, different patient, or a referral that has already expired
  • Do not bill the patient for referral-denied claims without first exhausting the retro referral and appeal process — the denial may be reversible
  • Do not let timely filing deadlines expire while pursuing retro referral or appeal — work both tracks simultaneously
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing a referral denial (especially N630) without attaching a copy of the referral form, referral number confirmation, or portal screenshot from the PCP's system is the most common reason referral appeals are rejected. Always include proof that the referral was valid, issued by the correct physician, and covered the service billed.
REFERRAL CHECKLIST
✅
REFERRAL CHECKLIST
Pre-submission referral validation checklist — all six codes

Before submitting any claim for a referred service on an HMO or referral-required plan, confirm all items below

  • ✅ Patient's plan type confirmed at scheduling — referral requirement verified (HMO requires; PPO typically does not)
  • ✅ Valid referral obtained from patient's designated PCP before date of service — not from covering or alternate provider (N630)
  • ✅ Referral date confirmed in MM DD CCYY format and falls on or before the date of service (N335)
  • ✅ Referral validity period covers the date of service — not expired (N335, N489)
  • ✅ Completed referral form attached to or on file with the claim — all required fields populated (N475, N476, N489, N490)
  • ✅ Referral form includes: patient demographics, diagnosis, service/specialty type, authorized visit count, PCP signature, and referral date
  • ✅ Referral covers the exact service or specialty billed — wrong specialty type will deny under N476 / N490 / N630
  • ✅ Number of visits billed does not exceed the number of visits approved on the referral
  • ✅ Box 17 (CMS-1500) or FL17 (UB-04) populated with referring PCP's full name and 10-digit NPI
  • ✅ Referral number entered in Box 23 (CMS-1500) or FL63 (UB-04) when payer issues referral tracking numbers
  • ✅ Referral number and documentation communicated from clinical team to billing team before claim is submitted
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Use only after referral validity is fully confirmed and corrected claim is denied
Appeal only when a valid referral existed, was issued by the correct physician, was correctly reported on the corrected claim — and the payer denied it anyway due to a system or processing error.
  • A valid referral was on file, issued by the patient's designated PCP, and the referral number was correctly entered on the claim — payer denied anyway
  • Payer provider relations confirmed the referral is valid in their system — this is a payer-side processing error
  • For N630: the referring physician is confirmed as the patient's designated attending/PCP for the plan year and payer record shows it
  • Always attach the referral form, referral number confirmation, or payer portal screenshot to the appeal
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)
Recommended first action for most referral denials
Most referral denials resolve by locating the existing referral, completing or correcting the referral form, adding it to the corrected claim, and resubmitting with Resubmission Code 7.
  • Most referral denials are caused by a referral that exists but was not submitted — add the referral number and documentation and resubmit with Resubmission Code 7
  • If the referral form was incomplete, complete all required fields and reattach before resubmitting
  • If no referral exists, request retro referral from PCP before resubmitting — do not resubmit without it
  • Do not appeal as a first step — correct the root cause first and escalate to appeal only after the corrected claim is also denied
