Authorization — Missing / Denied / Inconsistent / Unauthorized

Prior Authorization · Patient Signature · Workers' Comp · HIPPS TAC · Facility & Provider Authorization · CMS-1500 & UB-04
Common CARC Pairing
CO-16 CO-15 CO-167 CO-57 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 12/13 Box 23 FL63
All 11 Authorization RARC Codes — At a Glance

All eleven codes relate to authorization failures — spanning patient signature, prior auth denial, auth inconsistency, workers' compensation, HIPPS TAC, and facility/provider payment authorization. They are grouped into 4 logical sub-categories below.

📝 GROUP A — Patient Signature & Claim Authorization
MA75 Missing/incomplete/invalid patient or authorized representative signature

Patient's signature (Box 12 — release of information) or insured's signature (Box 13 — assignment of benefits) is missing, illegible, not on file, or provided by someone not legally authorized to sign on the patient's behalf.

🔐 GROUP B — Prior Authorization Status & Consistency
N41 Authorization request denied

The payer reviewed a prior authorization request and explicitly denied it — the service does not meet medical necessity criteria, is not covered, or was not approved for this patient under current plan benefits.

N45 Payment based on authorized amount

An informational code — payment was made, but the amount paid reflects the authorized amount only, which is less than the billed amount. The authorization limited the approved quantity, units, or dollar amount and payment was capped accordingly.

N54 Claim information is inconsistent with pre-certified/authorized services

Services were authorized but the claim billed something different — wrong CPT code, wrong diagnosis, different dates, different provider, different location, or more units than what was approved in the pre-certification.

N758 Adjusted based on the prior authorization decision

An informational adjustment code — payment amount or coverage decision was adjusted to align exactly with what was approved in the prior authorization decision. The auth decision controls the payment outcome.

🦺 GROUP C — Workers' Compensation & Injury-Specific Codes
N311 Missing/incomplete/invalid authorized to return to work date

On workers' compensation or disability claims, the physician-authorized return-to-work (RTW) date is missing, formatted incorrectly, or conflicts with other dates on the claim. Required on WC claims to validate the duration of disability and associated treatment period.

N596 Records reflect the injured party did not complete a Medical Authorization for this loss

Workers' compensation or personal injury claim — the injured party (claimant) did not sign and submit the required Medical Authorization form that permits the payer/insurer to access medical records related to the reported injury or loss. Without this signed authorization, the insurer cannot legally access or adjudicate the medical bill.

N612 Medical provider not authorized/certified to provide treatment to injured workers in this jurisdiction

Workers' compensation claims require providers to be specifically authorized or certified by the state's Workers' Compensation Board or Division of Workers' Compensation. This code means the treating provider is not registered, credentialed, or authorized within the WC system for the state where the injury occurred.

🏥 GROUP D — HIPPS TAC, Facility & Provider Payment Authorization
N752 Missing/incomplete/invalid HIPPS Treatment Authorization Code (TAC)

Post-acute facility claims (SNF, HHA, IRF) — the HIPPS (Health Insurance Prospective Payment System) Treatment Authorization Code is missing, incomplete, or invalid. The HIPPS TAC is a 5-character code derived from the patient assessment that drives payment rate under PPS (Prospective Payment System). Required on UB-04 FL44.

N760 This facility is not authorized to receive payment for the service(s)

The billing facility is not enrolled, credentialed, contracted, or authorized with the payer to receive payment for the services billed. Includes facilities that are excluded from Medicare/Medicaid, not enrolled in the payer's network, or billing for service categories outside their facility certification.

N761 This provider is not authorized to receive payment for the service(s)

The rendering or billing provider is not enrolled, credentialed, contracted, or authorized with the payer to receive payment for the services billed. Applies when the provider's NPI is not in the payer's network file, the provider is excluded, or the provider is not authorized to bill for that specific service category.

What This Means
🔐
What This Means

All eleven codes represent authorization-category failures — but they span four distinct authorization contexts: (A) the patient's own signature authorizing release of information and payment, (B) prior authorization status from the payer, (C) workers' compensation and injury-specific authorizations, and (D) facility and provider-level payment authorization from the payer system. The common thread is that payment cannot proceed until the appropriate authorization — from the right party, in the correct format, for the correct service — is in place and verified.

ℹ️
Think of it this way — Authorization in Four Contexts
Patient Signature (MA75): The patient must authorize release of their medical records and direct payment to the provider. Without this, the payer legally cannot process and pay the claim.

Prior Authorization (N41, N45, N54, N758): The payer must pre-approve certain services before they are rendered. Denial, cap, inconsistency, or adjustment based on auth decision controls whether and how much is paid.

Workers' Comp Authorization (N311, N596, N612): WC claims require specific injury-related documentation — return-to-work dates, claimant-signed medical release forms, and provider certification within the state WC system.

Facility/Provider Authorization (N752, N760, N761): The facility and provider must be enrolled, credentialed, and authorized with the payer. Post-acute claims additionally require the HIPPS TAC code that links the assessment to the payment rate.
⚠️
N45 and N758 Are Informational — Not Always Denials
N45 and N758 are adjustment notices, not necessarily denials. Payment was made — but was capped or adjusted to the authorized amount. Always compare the paid amount against the authorized amount before taking action. If the payment matches the authorization, these codes require no correction — they explain the payment difference. Only dispute if the paid amount is lower than what the authorization approved.
Where Authorization Information Goes on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Professional authorization field guidance
  • Box 12 — Patient Signature (MA75 — Release of Info): Patient or authorized representative's signature authorizing release of medical information. Enter "Signature on File" or actual signature. Must be on file and current.
  • Box 13 — Insured's Signature (MA75 — Assignment of Benefits): Insured's signature authorizing direct payment to provider. Enter "Signature on File" (SOF) if a valid signed authorization is stored in the patient's record.
  • Box 23 — Prior Authorization Number (N41, N54, N758): Enter the prior authorization number exactly as issued by the payer. Required when payer issues PA numbers. Missing = denial on auth-required services.
  • Box 16 — Return to Work Date (N311): On workers' comp claims, the dates the patient was unable to work. The authorized return-to-work date must be documented and consistent with physician orders.
  • EDI 837P — Loop 2300, REF segment (G1): Prior authorization number reported here. Loop 2300 PWK segment carries supporting documentation attachments including patient signature authorizations.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims)
Facility authorization field guidance
  • FL63 — Treatment Authorization Code (N41, N54, N752, N758): Prior authorization number or HIPPS TAC reported here. For post-acute (SNF, HHA, IRF) claims, FL63 carries the HIPPS 5-character TAC code. For all auth-required services, the auth number goes here.
  • FL44 — HCPCS / Rate / HIPPS Code (N752): The HIPPS code is entered in FL44 on post-acute institutional claims. The HIPPS TAC in FL63 must match the HIPPS code in FL44.
  • FL56 — Billing Provider NPI (N760, N761): Billing facility NPI must match a payer-enrolled, authorized provider. If the facility is not enrolled, N760 fires.
  • FL81 — Attending/Rendering Provider (N761): Rendering/attending provider NPI must be enrolled and authorized. If not in payer's network, N761 fires.
  • EDI 837I — Loop 2300, REF segment (G1): Prior authorization number. Loop 2300 CR3 carries the HIPPS TAC information for post-acute claims.
✅
Signature on File (SOF) — Valid Use Rule (MA75)
"Signature on File" is acceptable in Boxes 12 and 13 only when a valid, current, signed patient authorization is physically stored in the patient's record. SOF is not a substitute for an absent signature — it is a reference to a signature that actually exists. Payers may audit SOF claims and request the original signed authorization. If you cannot produce the signed document, the claim will be recouped. Always obtain and store patient signatures at registration.
Why This Happens
⚠️
AUTHORIZATION DOCUMENTATION & ENROLLMENT FAILURES
Root causes behind all eleven authorization denial codes
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Authorization denials span the full revenue cycle — from patient intake (signatures) to scheduling (prior auth) to claim submission (HIPPS TAC) to enrollment (N760/N761). The code identifies which layer of authorization failed.
1
Patient Signature Never Obtained at Intake
Patient registration forms with Box 12/13 authorizations were not completed or signed at the first appointment — or were signed but never entered into the system as "Signature on File."
→ Triggers: MA75
2
Prior Authorization Request Denied by Payer
Payer reviewed the PA request and determined the service does not meet their medical necessity criteria, is not a covered benefit, or the clinical information submitted was insufficient.
→ Triggers: N41
3
Claim Billed Differently from What Was Authorized
Auth was approved for CPT 27447 but claim billed CPT 27446. Or auth approved 10 PT visits but 14 were billed. Or auth approved inpatient but claim was outpatient. Any mismatch between authorized vs. billed service triggers N54.
→ Triggers: N54
4
Billed Amount Exceeds Authorized Amount
Authorization approved $3,000 but claim was billed at $5,000. Payer pays only the authorized amount and uses N45 or N758 to explain the reduction.
→ Triggers: N45, N758
5
Return to Work Date Missing on WC Claim
Workers' compensation claim submitted without the physician-authorized return-to-work (RTW) date, or the RTW date format is incorrect, missing the year, or conflicts with the disability period dates.
→ Triggers: N311
6
Injured Worker Did Not Sign Medical Authorization
Workers' compensation or personal injury claimant did not complete and submit the required Medical Authorization form permitting the insurer to access injury-related medical records. Without it, the insurer cannot legally review or pay the bill.
→ Triggers: N596
7
Provider Not Certified for Workers' Comp in This State
Treating provider is not registered, certified, or authorized within the state workers' compensation system where the injury occurred. Each state maintains its own WC provider authorization list — treating an injured worker without WC authorization = N612.
→ Triggers: N612
8
HIPPS TAC Missing or Invalid on Post-Acute Claim
SNF, HHA, or IRF claim submitted without a valid HIPPS TAC code, or the code in FL63 does not match or correspond to a completed patient assessment (MDS, OASIS, IRF-PAI) for the billing period.
→ Triggers: N752
9
Facility Not Enrolled / Authorized with Payer
Billing facility NPI is not enrolled with this payer, the facility has been excluded from Medicare/Medicaid, the facility is billing for services outside its certification type, or the facility contract lapsed.
→ Triggers: N760
10
Provider Not Enrolled / Authorized with Payer
Rendering or billing provider NPI is not enrolled, credentialed, or contracted with this payer. Includes providers excluded from Medicare/Medicaid, providers whose enrollment has lapsed, or providers billing for service categories outside their authorized scope.
→ Triggers: N761
How to Fix It — MA75 · N41 · N45 · N54 · N311 · N596 · N612 · N752 · N758 · N760 · N761
💡 Resolution Path by Code Group
📋 Quick Resolution Guide — Which Code, Which Action
Code
Primary Issue
First Action
MA75
Missing patient/insured signature
Obtain signature → update record → resubmit
N41
Auth request denied by payer
Appeal with clinical notes + medical necessity
N45
Payment capped at authorized amount
Compare paid vs. auth → dispute if underpaid
N54
Claim doesn't match authorized service
Reconcile claim vs. auth → correct → resubmit
N311
Missing RTW date on WC claim
Get physician RTW date → correct Box 16 → resubmit
N596
Injured party didn't sign medical auth
Contact claimant → obtain signed authorization
N612
Provider not certified for WC in this state
Register with state WC board → resubmit after cert
N752
Missing/invalid HIPPS TAC on post-acute claim
Verify assessment → correct FL63/FL44 HIPPS → resubmit
N758
Payment adjusted to auth decision
Verify paid = auth amount → if gap, dispute or appeal
N760
Facility not authorized to receive payment
Verify enrollment → enroll/correct → resubmit after
N761
Provider not authorized to receive payment
Verify enrollment/credentialing → enroll → resubmit
1
Identify the Exact Authorization Layer That Failed
Different codes need different resolution paths — identify first
🔍 Read the RARC code carefully — each code points to a specific authorization layer. The resolution path for N41 (auth denied) is completely different from N760 (facility not enrolled).
  • MA75: Check patient registration record — is a signed Box 12/13 authorization on file? If not, obtain patient signature immediately.
  • N41: Pull the prior authorization denial letter or payer portal denial notice — identify the stated reason for the PA denial before deciding to appeal.
  • N45 / N758: Compare the paid amount against the authorization approval amount — if they match, no action needed. If paid amount is less than authorized, dispute the underpayment.
  • N54: Pull the original authorization approval document. Compare authorized CPT, DOS, provider, site, and units against what was billed on the claim — identify all discrepancies.
  • N311: Pull the physician's clinical notes and WC disability documentation — obtain or correct the return-to-work date.
  • N596: Contact the WC carrier or claimant's attorney to obtain the signed Medical Authorization form from the injured party.
  • N612: Verify the provider's WC authorization status with the relevant state workers' compensation board.
  • N752: Pull the patient assessment (MDS, OASIS, or IRF-PAI) for the billing period — verify the HIPPS code is correctly derived and entered in FL63 and FL44.
  • N760 / N761: Verify facility/provider enrollment status with the payer and confirm no exclusion is on file.
2
Correct the Deficiency & Resubmit (Where Applicable)
Administrative fixes — fastest path for MA75, N54, N311, N752
✅ For administrative data issues, correct the deficiency and resubmit as a corrected claim — Resubmission Code 7 (CMS-1500 Box 22) or TOB frequency 7 (UB-04 FL64).
  • MA75: Obtain patient signature on authorization forms. Update patient record with "Signature on File." Add SOF to Box 12 and 13 on corrected claim. Resubmit.
  • N54: Reconcile the claim against the authorization — correct CPT code, units, DOS, or provider to match what was authorized. Resubmit corrected claim immediately. If additional services were rendered beyond what was authorized, obtain a supplemental auth first.
  • N311: Obtain the authorized return-to-work date from the treating physician. Correct Box 16 (CMS-1500) with accurate dates in MM DD CCYY format. Resubmit.
  • N752: Verify the HIPPS 5-character TAC code from the completed patient assessment. Update FL44 (HIPPS code) and FL63 (TAC) on the UB-04. Resubmit corrected claim.
  • ⚠️ N41, N596, N612, N760, N761 typically cannot be resolved by corrected claim alone — see Steps 3–4 for escalation paths.
  • ⚠️ Always check timely filing limits before resubmitting — deadlines do not pause during investigation.
3
For Auth Denials & WC Issues — Call the Payer / Board
N41 · N596 · N612 · N760 · N761 — escalation required
📞 These codes require direct payer contact or engagement with the WC board — a corrected claim submission alone will not resolve them.
  • N41 (auth denied): Call the payer's prior authorization department. Ask for the specific denial reason and whether peer-to-peer review is available. Peer-to-peer review between the treating physician and the payer's medical reviewer overturns N41 denials in a significant percentage of cases.
  • N596 (WC — no medical auth): Contact the WC claims adjuster or the injured party's attorney. Provide them with the medical authorization form and request they have the claimant sign and return it immediately.
  • N612 (WC — provider not certified): Contact the state's Workers' Compensation Board to determine the registration or certification process. Some states allow retroactive authorization for treatment already rendered — confirm this option before writing off the claim.
  • N760 / N761 (facility/provider not authorized): Call payer's provider enrollment or credentialing department. Confirm whether this is an enrollment gap, an exclusion issue, or a system error. If it's a system error (enrollment is actually on file), request manual reprocessing with a reference number.
  • 📝 Document all calls: payer or board representative name, reference number, date, time, and specific action required.
4
Still Denied? File a Formal Appeal
Especially critical for N41 — auth denial appeals are winnable with the right documentation
⚖️ File a formal appeal with supporting clinical and administrative documentation. N41 appeals with peer-to-peer review and strong clinical justification have high overturn rates.
  • N41 appeal: Include clinical notes supporting medical necessity, applicable clinical guidelines, peer-reviewed literature if applicable, and treating physician's written justification. Request expedited appeal for urgent clinical situations.
  • N54 appeal: If the inconsistency was a payer-side processing error (authorization was correct, claim was correct), appeal with the original auth approval document proving alignment.
  • N760 / N761 appeal: If enrollment is on file but payer system didn't recognize it, include PECOS enrollment confirmation, credentialing letter, or provider agreement number.
  • Appeal must include: Provider name, NPI, patient name, member ID, claim number, DOS, service billed, auth number, and RARC code received.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination within 120 days. Commercial: check EOB for appeal deadline — typically 30–180 days.
  • 📌 For emergent services denied under N41, cite the payer's plan language — most plans cannot deny medically necessary emergency services on the basis of an auth denial.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Authorization Workflows by Code Group
Each code group requires a different system-level prevention fix
🔁 Recurring authorization denials mean your pre-service, intake, or enrollment workflows have systematic gaps. The prevention fix depends entirely on which code group is repeating.
  • MA75 repeating: Audit patient intake process. Every patient must sign Box 12/13 authorization forms at registration. Build an EHR-level gate that blocks claim submission for any patient without "Signature on File" documented.
  • N41 repeating: Analyze which service types are being denied and why. Build a pre-authorization requirements matrix by payer and CPT. Submit richer clinical documentation with initial PA requests — include supporting clinical guidelines to reduce denial rates.
  • N54 repeating: Build a claim-vs-authorization reconciliation step before claim release. Every claim for an authorized service must be compared to the auth approval document — CPT, units, DOS, provider, and site — before submission.
  • N752 repeating: Build an MDS/OASIS/IRF-PAI to HIPPS TAC crosswalk validation. The HIPPS code entered in FL44 and FL63 must be generated from the completed assessment — add a pre-submission check that confirms the HIPPS code is present and matches the assessment on file.
  • N596 repeating: Add a WC medical authorization form requirement to your intake process for all workers' compensation patients. No WC claim should be submitted until the claimant's signed Medical Authorization form is on file.
  • N612 repeating: Audit all providers treating workers' compensation patients against the applicable state WC provider authorization list. Any provider not registered must be enrolled with the state WC board before treating WC patients.
  • N760 / N761 repeating: Conduct quarterly audits of facility and provider enrollment status across all payers. For each payer, confirm: (1) facility is enrolled and active, (2) all rendering providers are enrolled and active, (3) no exclusion flags exist. Use PECOS and state Medicaid enrollment portals as primary verification sources.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Submitting claims under a facility (N760) or provider (N761) that is excluded from Medicare or Medicaid is a False Claims Act violation. Exclusion screening must be performed monthly against the OIG exclusion list for every provider and employee involved in billing.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common authorization mistakes that trigger repeat denials across all eleven codes
These mistakes cause repeat authorization denials, claim recoupment, compliance violations, and in some cases False Claims Act liability.
  • Do not enter "Signature on File" in Box 12/13 unless a physically signed authorization is actually stored in the patient's record — SOF is a reference, not a substitute
  • Do not appeal an N41 prior auth denial without first pursuing peer-to-peer review — most N41 denials can be overturned through peer-to-peer before a formal appeal is needed
  • Do not resubmit an N54 claim without first reconciling the claim against the authorization approval document — resubmitting the same inconsistent claim will re-deny
  • Do not assume N45 or N758 require action if the paid amount matches the authorized amount — verify first before disputing
  • Do not submit WC claims under a provider who has not completed state workers' compensation board authorization — N612 claims will deny and the WC board may take compliance action
  • Do not submit claims under a facility (N760) or provider (N761) that is on the OIG exclusion list — this is a False Claims Act violation regardless of intent
  • Do not allow timely filing deadlines to expire while working N41 peer-to-peer reviews or WC board enrollment processes — file a protective corrected claim or appeal to preserve your filing window
⚠️
Critical Compliance Reminder — N760 / N761
Submitting claims under a facility or provider that is excluded from Medicare or Medicaid programs (N760/N761) constitutes a False Claims Act violation (31 U.S.C. § 3729) and violates the Anti-Kickback Statute. OIG exclusion screening must be performed monthly for every provider, employee, and contractor involved in billing. CMS PECOS enrollment and OIG exclusion list are the primary verification sources.
AUTHORIZATION CHECKLIST
✅
AUTHORIZATION CHECKLIST
Pre-submission authorization validation — all eleven codes

Before submitting any claim requiring authorization, confirm all validations below

  • ✅ Patient and insured signatures on file (Box 12 & 13) — actual signed document stored in patient record (MA75)
  • ✅ Prior authorization obtained and approved before date of service — auth number confirmed and entered in Box 23 / FL63 (N41, N54)
  • ✅ Claim CPT codes, units, DOS, provider, and site verified against the authorization approval — all elements match (N54, N758)
  • ✅ Billed amount does not exceed the authorized amount — if it does, verify whether supplemental auth is needed (N45, N758)
  • ✅ For workers' comp claims: physician-authorized return-to-work date documented and entered in correct format (N311)
  • ✅ For workers' comp claims: claimant's signed Medical Authorization form on file before claim is submitted (N596)
  • ✅ For workers' comp claims: treating provider confirmed as authorized/certified by the applicable state workers' compensation board (N612)
  • ✅ For post-acute claims (SNF/HHA/IRF): HIPPS 5-character TAC code derived from completed patient assessment — entered correctly in FL44 and FL63 (N752)
  • ✅ Billing facility NPI confirmed enrolled and active with this payer — no exclusion flag in OIG list or PECOS (N760)
  • ✅ All rendering and billing provider NPIs confirmed enrolled, active, and not excluded — monthly OIG exclusion screening completed (N761)
  • ✅ Authorization validity period covers the date of service — not expired and not used beyond approved visit count or dollar cap
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Primarily for N41, N54, N760/N761 payer errors
Appeal when the underlying authorization or enrollment is valid and the denial is due to a payer-side error, an auth that was denied inappropriately, or a data mismatch the payer is responsible for.
  • N41: Prior authorization was denied — appeal with clinical documentation and request peer-to-peer review. Most N41 appeals with supporting clinical notes are winnable
  • N54: Claim data matched the authorization but payer denied anyway — appeal with the original auth approval document proving alignment
  • N760 / N761: Facility or provider is enrolled and active but payer system didn't recognize it — appeal with PECOS enrollment confirmation and enrollment date
  • Always attach the relevant authorization document, enrollment confirmation, or clinical justification to the appeal
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (MA75, N54, N311, N752)
Recommended first action for administrative data issues
Administrative authorization issues — missing signature, inconsistent claim data, missing HIPPS TAC, missing RTW date — resolve through correction and resubmission, not appeals.
  • MA75: Obtain signature, update SOF record, correct Box 12/13, resubmit with Resubmission Code 7
  • N54: Reconcile claim vs. auth, correct all mismatched elements, resubmit corrected claim
  • N311: Obtain RTW date from physician, correct Box 16, resubmit corrected claim
  • N752: Verify HIPPS from assessment, correct FL44/FL63, resubmit corrected UB-04
  • Do not appeal administrative data issues — correct the data and resubmit; escalate to appeal only if corrected claim also denies

N816 does not mean the drug is not covered. NDC - Drug Look Reference Image

Important Distinction
N816 does not mean the drug is not covered. It means the UOM field needs to be corrected before the claim can process. In most cases this is a straightforward corrected claim — not an appeal.
Where to Report This Information
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional)
Professional claim reporting guidance
  • Box 24D — HCPCS/CPT drug code (J-code)
  • Shaded area 24A–24G — N4 qualifier + 11-digit NDC + unit of measure + quantity
✅ Correct: N412345678901
❌ Incorrect: N4 12345678901
🏥

Facility claim reporting guidance

Format: N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM + Qty
Example: ✅ Correct: N412345678901
⚠️
N4 Qualifier Format — Common Sub-Error
The N4 qualifier must appear as a continuous prefix immediately before the 11-digit NDC number. Including spaces or separators between N4 and the NDC value will trigger payer formatting edits and electronic claim rejection.
#
11-Digit NDC Format (5-4-2) — Conversion Guide
Original Format Add Zero To Example Conversion
4-4-2 Front of Labeler Code 1234-5678-90 → 01234-5678-90
5-3-2 Front of Product Code 12345-678-90 → 12345-0678-90
5-4-1 Front of Package Code 12345-6789-0 → 12345-6789-00
Unit of Measure (UOM) Misalignment
💊
Valid UOM Codes — When to Use Each
Reference guide for selecting the correct billing unit of measure
UOM Code Name When to Use Billing Unit
UN Unit Powder-form drugs in a vial that must be reconstituted before administration One unit per vial used
ML Milliliter Liquid-form drugs supplied in a vial or pre-filled syringe Actual milliliters administered
GR Gram Ointments, creams, inhalers, or bulk powders dispensed by weight Actual grams dispensed — primarily retail pharmacy
F2 International Unit Factor VIII Antihemophilic Factor and similar biologics billed in international units Per IU administered
📌
Key Rule
The UOM must match the physical form of the drug as supplied on the date of service — not how you prefer to bill it, and not what a prior claim used.
Why This Happens
⚠️
DATA ENTRY & SELECTION ISSUES
Most common root causes behind UOM-related denials
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Most UOM denials happen because the submitted unit of measure does not match the drug type, payer drug file, or claim formatting requirements.
1
Missing UOM Code
The UOM field was left blank or populated with a placeholder or default value.
2
Wrong UOM Selected
Example: billing UN for a liquid drug that should be billed using ML.
3
Drug Form Mismatch
The UOM submitted does not match the drug form listed in the payer's NDC drug file.
4
Expired or Inactive NDC
The NDC submitted is expired, discontinued, or no longer active in the payer's drug file.
5
Missing NDC on Claim
The drug was billed only with a J-code or HCPCS code, but no NDC value was attached to the claim.
6
Supplier Change Not Captured
A new supplier or manufacturer was used, but the updated NDC and UOM were never captured at the point of administration.
How to Fix It — RARC N816: Unit of Measure (UOM) Does Not Match
💡 What is RARC N816?
Your claim was denied because the Unit of Measure (UOM) on the claim does not match what the payer expects for the drug or service billed. Think of it like ordering coffee — if the menu prices it per ounce but you bill per cup, the register won't process it. Every drug HCPCS code has a CMS-defined UOM (mL, mg, units, grams) and your quantity must be reported in that exact unit — wrong UOM = wrong quantity = denial.
CMS-1500
Box 24G
Units / quantity field
837P EDI
Loop 2410
CTP segment
Reference
HCPCS Book
Each code defines its UOM
📋 Common UOM Qualifiers & What They Mean
Code
Meaning
Example Use
UN
Unit(s)
Biologics, vaccines, insulin
ML
Milliliter(s)
IV solutions, injectable drugs by volume
GR
Gram(s)
Topical agents, some antibiotics
ME
Milligram(s)
Chemo, specialty drugs dosed by mg
F2
Intl. Unit(s)
Clotting factors, some vitamins
1
Look Up the Correct UOM for the HCPCS Billed
UOM is defined by the code — not your choice
🔍 The UOM is not a free choice — every HCPCS drug code has a CMS-assigned billing unit. Look it up in the HCPCS Level II code book or CMS ASP Drug Pricing File before correcting anything.
  • Look up the HCPCS code in the CMS HCPCS Level II Drug Table or ASP Pricing File — each entry shows the billing unit descriptor (e.g., "per 10 mg", "per 0.5 mL").
  • Confirm the UOM qualifier in your claim matches exactly — UN, ML, GR, ME, or F2. A correct NDC with the wrong qualifier still fires N816.
  • Recalculate the quantity using the CMS formula: Total dose administered ÷ HCPCS billing unit = billable units. Round up to the nearest whole unit per CMS guidance.
  • For weight-based dosing (mg/kg), bill total dose given ÷ billing unit — not the per-kg amount alone.
  • For multi-dose vials, bill only the quantity actually administered unless the payer's policy allows wastage billing.
2
Correct UOM + Quantity Together & Resubmit
Fix both in the same corrected claim — one without the other re-denies
✅ UOM and quantity are a linked pair. Changing the UOM always means recalculating the quantity too. Fix both in the same corrected claim submission.
  • CMS-1500: Correct quantity in Box 24G. For NDC claims, update UOM qualifier + quantity in the shaded area of Box 24A (format: N4 + NDC + UOM + quantity).
  • 837P EDI: Update Loop 2410, CTP segment — fix CTP05-1 (UOM qualifier) and CTP04 (quantity). Both must be corrected in the same transaction.
  • Corrected claim: CMS-1500 → Box 22, Resubmission Code "7" + original ICN. UB-04 → TOB frequency digit "7" + original TCN in Box 64.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits — act within days of receiving N816, not weeks.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
Payer may require a different UOM than CMS
📞 If the corrected claim still gets N816, call the payer's pharmacy or drug billing line. Some payers have UOM requirements that differ from CMS — especially for specialty drugs, biosimilars, and infusion services.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, date of service, HCPCS billed, NDC, UOM qualifier used, quantity billed, drug name, total dose administered, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask: "Which UOM qualifier and quantity do you require for HCPCS [XXXXX]? Does your requirement differ from the CMS HCPCS billing unit definition?"
  • Ask whether they want dispensed vial quantity vs. administered dose — payers differ on this for multi-dose vials.
  • 📝 Document: reference number, rep name, date, time, and the exact UOM and quantity format required.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Prove UOM and quantity were correct per CMS
⚖️ If the payer upholds N816, file a formal appeal proving the UOM qualifier and quantity were correct per the CMS HCPCS billing unit definition and the actual dose administered.
  • Appeal must include: Provider NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, HCPCS, NDC, UOM used, quantity billed, drug name, total dose administered, and dosage calculation.
  • Key statement: "HCPCS [XXXXX] is defined as [billing unit per CMS]. Quantity of [X] billed with UOM [XX] correctly reflects the [total dose] administered per the CMS billing unit formula. We appeal the N816 denial as UOM and quantity were compliant."
  • Attach: CMS HCPCS drug table entry, MAR confirming dose given, dosage calculation worksheet, original + corrected claims, both remittance advices.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with MAC within 120 days. Reference CMS Pub 100-04, Chapter 17. Commercial: check EOB — typically 30–180 days.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Drug Billing Templates
Hardcode UOM per HCPCS — stop N816 at the source
🔁 If N816 recurs across multiple claims, your drug billing templates have incorrect or missing UOM mappings. The UOM qualifier for each HCPCS should be hardcoded — never manually entered by a biller who may not know the CMS billing unit definition.
  • Hardcode UOM per HCPCS in your billing system. For every drug code you bill, the correct UOM qualifier should auto-populate — billers should never select it manually from a dropdown.
  • Build a quantity calculation rule per HCPCS. Configure the system to auto-calculate billable units from the administered dose using the CMS formula — eliminate manual math that introduces N816.
  • Review templates every January. CMS updates drug HCPCS codes and billing unit definitions annually — a UOM correct under last year's code may be wrong under the new descriptor.
  • Add a pre-submission edit that validates the UOM qualifier against the expected value for each HCPCS code before the claim is released — flag any mismatch before it reaches the payer.
  • Document payer-specific UOM rules. If a payer requires a different UOM than CMS standard, save that as a payer rule in your system so it overrides the default for that payer's claims.
  • 🔒 Train your billing team: UOM is not a formatting detail — it directly drives the reimbursement calculation. A wrong UOM can cause overpayment, underpayment, or denial on every drug claim it touches.
Modifier to Know
🏷️
Modifier Reference Guide
Common modifiers and proper usage guidelines
Modifier Description Usage Notes
KO Single drug unit dose formulation Use for single-drug unit-dose packaging.
KP First drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation First drug when multiple drugs are in one unit-dose.
KQ Second or subsequent drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation Each additional drug after KP in multi-drug unit-dose.
JW Drug amount discarded or not administered to the patient Requires a separate line on the same claim. Primary line must show >0 units administered. JW line shows wasted/discarded quantity. Both lines must reflect the same NDC and J-code.
JZ Zero wastage — no drug was discarded Use when no drug was discarded. Required by some payers when JW is not applicable.
💊
JW Modifier — Correct Billing Structure Example
Line 1
Line 1: J-code | 2 ML administered | same NDC | same DOS
Line 2
Line 2: J-code + JW | 0.5 ML discarded | same NDC | same DOS If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
Important: If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that lead to repeat denials
  • Do not appeal before correcting the UOM (UN or ML) mismatch
  • Do not reuse old, default, or copied NDCs & UOM from previous claims without verification
  • Do not guess at the manufacturer, quantity, or drug lot always Verify with MR
  • Do not submit a corrected claim with the same incorrect NDC & UOM
  • Do not appeal a N816 denial if you have not yet submitted a corrected claim first
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting the underlying NDC & UOM error wastes timely filing days and may forfeit your right to correct the claim. Always correct first, then appeal only if the corrected claim is also denied.
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
✅
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist

Before submitting any drug claim, confirm:

  • ✅ NDC & UOM captured directly from the administered vial or package label
  • ✅ J-code validated against NDC & UOM using a current, reliable crosswalk
  • ✅ 10-digit NDC converted to 11-digit format (5-4-2) if applicable
  • ✅ N4 qualifier formatted with no space before the NDC number
  • ✅ Manufacturer-specific NDC & UOM confirmed (not from a different lot or supplier)
  • ✅ JW modifier applied on a separate line with administered quantity on primary line (if wastage applies)
  • ✅ NDC & UOM confirmed as active on the date of service
  • ✅ Claim run through edits before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅

Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True

Use only when the claim has already been corrected and still denied
  • A corrected claim has already been submitted and denied again
  • All billing data (NDC, J-code, UOM, quantity, manufacturer) has been confirmed correct against the MAR and vial label
  • The denial reason after correction still cites N816 — indicating a payer-side processing error
🔄

Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)

Recommended first step for most denials
  • Most N816 denials resolve by correcting and resubmitting the claim
  • Do not appeal as a first step - Verify NDC ↔ J-code crosswalk, 11-digit format, N4 qualifier, UOM, and quantity before resubmission
  • Use Resubmission Code 7 on the corrected claim

Missing / Deactivated / Withdrawn NDC

Drug Billing / Data Mismatch · Professional & Facility Claims ·
Common CARC Pairing
CMS-1500 Box 24 & UB-04 (FL43-FL44) CO-16 Claim/service lacks information
What This Means
💡
What This Means

M119 used by payers to flag that the (NDC) on the claim is one of the following: completely missing, incomplete (e.g., wrong digit count), formatted incorrectly, or the NDC has been deactivated or withdrawn from the FDA drug database.

ℹ️
Important Distinction
M119 covers four distinct problem types. Before taking any action, you must identify which of the four applies — each has a different resolution path. A missing NDC is a data entry fix. A withdrawn NDC may require a NOC code and clinical documentation. Treating all M119 denials the same way is the most common mistake.

Why This Happens

DATA ENTRY & SELECTION ISSUES
Most common root causes behind NDC-to-HCPCS mismatch denials
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Most denials occur because the submitted NDC does not align with the HCPCS or J-code billed, or the NDC itself is invalid or incomplete.
1
Wrong NDC Selected
The NDC entered does not belong to the drug actually administered or references a different manufacturer version.
2
10-Digit NDC Not Converted
A 10-digit NDC was submitted without converting it to the required 11-digit (5-4-2) billing format.
3
HCPCS and NDC Do Not Match
The HCPCS or J-code billed does not align with the NDC submitted on the claim.
4
Expired or Inactive NDC
The NDC submitted is expired, discontinued, or no longer active in the payer's drug file.
5
Missing NDC on Claim
The drug was billed using only a J-code or HCPCS code, but no NDC value was included on the claim.
6
Supplier Change Not Captured
The drug was purchased from a new supplier, but the updated NDC was not captured during administration or claim entry.
How to Fix It — RARC M119: Missing / Deactivated / Withdrawn NDC
💡 What is RARC M119?
Your claim was denied because the NDC is either missing, deactivated, or withdrawn from the payer’s recognized drug database or FDA NDC Directory. This means either no NDC was submitted, or the submitted NDC is no longer valid for billing due to being inactive, discontinued, or removed from use. Payers require an active and valid NDC tied to the exact administered product — anything missing or inactive will result in denial.
CMS-1500
Box 24A
Shaded area — NDC required
837P EDI
Loop 2410
LIN segment — qualifier N4
NDC Status
Active Only
Inactive = denial
📋 Common Reasons M119 Fires
Root Cause
What Happened
NDC missing
Drug billed without any NDC value
Inactive NDC used
Code no longer active in FDA directory
Withdrawn product
Drug discontinued or removed from market
Repackaged drug
Old NDC used instead of updated one
System default issues
Billing system storing outdated or blank NDC
1
Find the Correct NDC for the Drug Administered
Go back to the actual vial or package label
🔍 Pull the medication administration record (MAR) or drug log for the date of service. The valid NDC must come from the exact vial or package administered — not the drug name, not the order, not a lookup table guess.
  • Check the drug label or barcode scanned at administration — the NDC is printed on every FDA-regulated drug package in a 10- or 11-digit format.
  • Verify the NDC is active and valid in the FDA NDC Directory at fda.gov/drugs or ndclist.com — search by NDC number and confirm the listing is not inactive or retired.
  • If the package shows a 10-digit NDC, pad it to 11 digits by adding a leading zero to the correct segment. The three NDC formats are 4-4-2, 5-3-2, and 5-4-1 — each pads differently to reach 11 digits (5-4-2).
  • Confirm the NDC is for the exact manufacturer and package size dispensed — same drug from a different manufacturer has a different NDC and must be reported correctly.
  • If a reference lab or specialty pharmacy provided the drug, obtain the NDC from them directly — do not guess or substitute a similar product's NDC.
2
Add the Valid NDC & Resubmit
Correct format is critical — not just the number
✅ Once you have the valid 11-digit NDC, add it in the correct field and format, then resubmit as a corrected claim. Format errors are just as likely to re-deny as a missing NDC.
  • CMS-1500 (paper): Enter in the shaded area of Box 24A using format: qualifier N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM qualifier + quantity administered (e.g., N4 12345678900 ML 10).
  • 837P electronic: Report in Loop 2410, LIN segment — LIN03 qualifier must be N4, LIN04 is the 11-digit NDC. Also populate the CTP segment with UOM qualifier and quantity. All three are required.
  • No hyphens in EDI — submit NDC as a plain 11-digit number (12345678900), never as 12345-678-90.
  • Corrected claim: CMS-1500 → Box 22, Resubmission Code "7" + original ICN. UB-04 → TOB frequency "7" + original TCN in Box 64.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits before resubmitting — deadlines don't pause while tracking down NDC details.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
NDC may not be in their drug file
📞 If the corrected claim still gets N60, the payer's internal drug file may not recognize the NDC — especially for newer drugs, biosimilars, or recently repackaged products.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, date of service, HCPCS billed, NDC submitted, drug name, strength, manufacturer, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask: "Is NDC [XXXXXXXXXXX] recognized in your drug file for HCPCS [XXXXX]? If not, is there an alternate NDC or updated code your system requires for this drug?"
  • Ask if the payer requires NDC registration or pre-loading in their formulary system before claims with that NDC will process.
  • Ask if the denial is a formatting issue — confirm whether they received the NDC with or without hyphens and whether the LIN/CTP segments were both present.
  • 📝 Document: reference number, rep name, date, time, and exactly what they say is wrong or missing.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Attach FDA proof the NDC is valid and active
⚖️ If the payer upholds N60 after a corrected claim and call, file a formal appeal with FDA documentation proving the NDC is valid, active, and correctly reported on the claim.
  • Appeal must include: Provider NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, HCPCS, NDC submitted, drug name, strength, manufacturer, and MAR confirming administration.
  • Key statement: "NDC [XXXXXXXXXXX] is an active, FDA-registered National Drug Code for [Drug Name, Strength] manufactured by [Manufacturer], as confirmed by the FDA NDC Directory. The NDC was correctly reported in Loop 2410 / Box 24A per CMS billing guidelines. We appeal the N60 denial."
  • Attach: FDA NDC Directory printout confirming active status, drug package label, MAR, original + corrected claims, both remittance advices.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with MAC within 120 days. Reference CMS Pub 100-04, Chapter 17. Commercial: check EOB — typically 30–180 days.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your NDC Capture Workflow
NDC must flow from administration directly to the claim
🔁 If N60 appears across multiple claims, your NDC is not being captured at the point of administration and passed to billing. Billers should never be manually looking up or typing NDCs — the drug barcode scanned at admin time must auto-populate into the claim.
  • Capture NDC at point of administration. Build a workflow where nursing or pharmacy scans the drug barcode at administration time — that scan should push the NDC directly into the patient's medication record and then to the claim. Manual entry at billing time is the #1 cause of N60.
  • Validate NDC format in your billing system. Add a field-level validation that confirms the NDC is exactly 11 digits with no hyphens before the claim can be submitted — reject any entry that doesn't match the format.
  • Keep your NDC master file current. When a drug is repackaged or a new manufacturer is added to your formulary, update the NDC in your billing system immediately — stale NDCs trigger N60 even when the drug itself hasn't changed.
  • Add a pre-submission edit for all drug HCPCS codes (J-codes and chemotherapy codes) that flags any claim line missing a value in the NDC field before the claim is released to the payer.
  • Verify NDC against the FDA directory quarterly. Cross-check every NDC in your drug master file against the FDA NDC Directory to confirm active status — flag any inactive NDC for immediate update before it causes a denial cascade.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Reporting an incorrect or fabricated NDC on a drug claim is a False Claims Act risk — the NDC must reflect the exact product administered, not a similar or substitute drug's code.

N60 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

Valid NDC is required for payment of drug claims.

Drug Billing / Data Mismatch · Professional & Facility Claims ·
Common CARC Pairing
CMS-1500 Box 24 & UB-04 (FL43-FL44) CO-16 Claim/service lacks information
What This Means
💡
What This Means

N60 is a payer-generated remark code indicating that a valid NDC is required on the claim in order to process payment for a drug service

ℹ️
Important Distinction
N60 means the claim cannot be paid without a properly submitted, valid NDC. In most cases this resolves with a corrected claim. N60 is often seen in bulk on the first wave of denials after a payer activates NDC enforcement — meaning it may affect multiple claims across multiple dates of service simultaneously.
Where to Report This Information
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional)
Professional claim reporting guidance
  • Box 24D — HCPCS/CPT drug code (J-code)
  • Shaded area 24A–24G — N4 qualifier + 11-digit NDC + unit of measure + quantity
✅ Correct: N412345678901
❌ Incorrect: N4 12345678901
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims)
Facility claim reporting guidance
  • FL - 44 — HCPCS/CPT code
  • FL - 43 — N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM + Quantity
Format: N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM + Qty
Example: ✅ Correct: N412345678901
⚠️
N4 Qualifier Format — Common Sub-Error
The N4 qualifier must appear as a single uninterrupted prefix immediately before the 11-digit NDC number. Even minor spacing or formatting differences between N4 and the NDC value can cause payer edits, clearinghouse rejections, or electronic claim failures.
#
11-Digit NDC Format (5-4-2) — Conversion Guide
Original Format Add Zero To Example Conversion
4-4-2 Front of Labeler Code 1234-5678-90 → 01234-5678-90
5-3-2 Front of Product Code 12345-678-90 → 12345-0678-90
5-4-1 Front of Package Code 12345-6789-0 → 12345-6789-00
Unit of Measure (UOM) Misalignment
💊
Valid UOM Codes — When to Use Each
Reference guide for selecting the correct billing unit of measure
UOM Code Name When to Use Billing Unit
UN Unit Powder-form drugs in a vial that must be reconstituted before administration One unit per vial used
ML Milliliter Liquid-form drugs supplied in a vial or pre-filled syringe Actual milliliters administered
GR Gram Ointments, creams, inhalers, or bulk powders dispensed by weight Actual grams dispensed — primarily retail pharmacy
F2 International Unit Factor VIII Antihemophilic Factor and similar biologics billed in international units Per IU administered
📌
Key Rule
The UOM must match the physical form of the drug as supplied on the date of service — not how you prefer to bill it, and not what a prior claim used.
Why This Happens
⚠️
DATA ENTRY & SELECTION ISSUES
Most common root causes behind NDC-to-HCPCS mismatch denials
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Most NDC mismatch denials occur because the submitted NDC does not align with the billed HCPCS or J-code, or the NDC itself is invalid or incomplete.
1
Wrong NDC Selected
The NDC entered does not belong to the drug actually administered or references a different manufacturer version.
2
10-Digit NDC Not Converted
A 10-digit NDC was submitted without converting it to the required 11-digit (5-4-2) billing format.
3
HCPCS and NDC Do Not Match
The HCPCS or J-code billed does not align with the NDC submitted on the claim.
4
Expired or Inactive NDC
The NDC used is expired, discontinued, or no longer active in the payer's drug file.
5
Missing NDC on Claim
The drug was billed using only a J-code or HCPCS code, but no NDC value was included on the claim.
6
Supplier Change Not Captured
The drug was purchased from a new supplier, but the updated NDC was not captured during administration or claim entry.
How to Fix It — RARC N60: Valid NDC is Required for Payment of Drug Claims
💡 What is RARC N60?
Your claim was denied because a valid NDC (National Drug Code) is missing or invalid on the drug claim. Think of the NDC like a drug's fingerprint — it is the FDA-assigned 11-digit number that identifies the exact drug, manufacturer, strength, and package size administered. Payers require it on every drug claim to confirm what was actually given to the patient. No valid NDC = no payment.
CMS-1500
Box 24A
Shaded area — NDC field
837P EDI
Loop 2410
LIN segment — qualifier N4
NDC Format
11 Digits
No hyphens in EDI
📋 Common Reasons N60 Fires on Drug Claims
Root Cause
What Happened
NDC field left blank
Biller submitted HCPCS only — NDC never entered
10-digit NDC submitted
Package shows 10 digits — leading zero not added
Hyphens included in EDI
NDC submitted as 12345-678-90 instead of 12345678900
Inactive / retired NDC
Drug repackaged — old NDC no longer active in FDA directory
Wrong qualifier used
LIN segment missing N4 qualifier before NDC in 837P
1
Find the Correct NDC for the Drug Administered
Go back to the actual vial or package label
🔍 Pull the medication administration record (MAR) or drug log for the date of service. The valid NDC must come from the exact vial or package administered — not the drug name, not the order, not a lookup table guess.
  • Check the drug label or barcode scanned at administration — the NDC is printed on every FDA-regulated drug package in a 10- or 11-digit format.
  • Verify the NDC is active and valid in the FDA NDC Directory at fda.gov/drugs or ndclist.com — search by NDC number and confirm the listing is not inactive or retired.
  • If the package shows a 10-digit NDC, pad it to 11 digits by adding a leading zero to the correct segment. The three NDC formats are 4-4-2, 5-3-2, and 5-4-1 — each pads differently to reach 11 digits (5-4-2).
  • Confirm the NDC is for the exact manufacturer and package size dispensed — same drug from a different manufacturer has a different NDC and must be reported correctly.
  • If a reference lab or specialty pharmacy provided the drug, obtain the NDC from them directly — do not guess or substitute a similar product's NDC.
2
Add the Valid NDC & Resubmit
Correct format is critical — not just the number
✅ Once you have the valid 11-digit NDC, add it in the correct field and format, then resubmit as a corrected claim. Format errors are just as likely to re-deny as a missing NDC.
  • CMS-1500 (paper): Enter in the shaded area of Box 24A using format: qualifier N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM qualifier + quantity administered (e.g., N4 12345678900 ML 10).
  • 837P electronic: Report in Loop 2410, LIN segment — LIN03 qualifier must be N4, LIN04 is the 11-digit NDC. Also populate the CTP segment with UOM qualifier and quantity. All three are required.
  • No hyphens in EDI — submit NDC as a plain 11-digit number (12345678900), never as 12345-678-90.
  • Corrected claim: CMS-1500 → Box 22, Resubmission Code "7" + original ICN. UB-04 → TOB frequency "7" + original TCN in Box 64.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits before resubmitting — deadlines don't pause while tracking down NDC details.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
NDC may not be in their drug file
📞 If the corrected claim still gets N60, the payer's internal drug file may not recognize the NDC — especially for newer drugs, biosimilars, or recently repackaged products.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, date of service, HCPCS billed, NDC submitted, drug name, strength, manufacturer, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask: "Is NDC [XXXXXXXXXXX] recognized in your drug file for HCPCS [XXXXX]? If not, is there an alternate NDC or updated code your system requires for this drug?"
  • Ask if the payer requires NDC registration or pre-loading in their formulary system before claims with that NDC will process.
  • Ask if the denial is a formatting issue — confirm whether they received the NDC with or without hyphens and whether the LIN/CTP segments were both present.
  • 📝 Document: reference number, rep name, date, time, and exactly what they say is wrong or missing.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Attach FDA proof the NDC is valid and active
⚖️ If the payer upholds N60 after a corrected claim and call, file a formal appeal with FDA documentation proving the NDC is valid, active, and correctly reported on the claim.
  • Appeal must include: Provider NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, HCPCS, NDC submitted, drug name, strength, manufacturer, and MAR confirming administration.
  • Key statement: "NDC [XXXXXXXXXXX] is an active, FDA-registered National Drug Code for [Drug Name, Strength] manufactured by [Manufacturer], as confirmed by the FDA NDC Directory. The NDC was correctly reported in Loop 2410 / Box 24A per CMS billing guidelines. We appeal the N60 denial."
  • Attach: FDA NDC Directory printout confirming active status, drug package label, MAR, original + corrected claims, both remittance advices.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with MAC within 120 days. Reference CMS Pub 100-04, Chapter 17. Commercial: check EOB — typically 30–180 days.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your NDC Capture Workflow
NDC must flow from administration directly to the claim
🔁 If N60 appears across multiple claims, your NDC is not being captured at the point of administration and passed to billing. Billers should never be manually looking up or typing NDCs — the drug barcode scanned at admin time must auto-populate into the claim.
  • Capture NDC at point of administration. Build a workflow where nursing or pharmacy scans the drug barcode at administration time — that scan should push the NDC directly into the patient's medication record and then to the claim. Manual entry at billing time is the #1 cause of N60.
  • Validate NDC format in your billing system. Add a field-level validation that confirms the NDC is exactly 11 digits with no hyphens before the claim can be submitted — reject any entry that doesn't match the format.
  • Keep your NDC master file current. When a drug is repackaged or a new manufacturer is added to your formulary, update the NDC in your billing system immediately — stale NDCs trigger N60 even when the drug itself hasn't changed.
  • Add a pre-submission edit for all drug HCPCS codes (J-codes and chemotherapy codes) that flags any claim line missing a value in the NDC field before the claim is released to the payer.
  • Verify NDC against the FDA directory quarterly. Cross-check every NDC in your drug master file against the FDA NDC Directory to confirm active status — flag any inactive NDC for immediate update before it causes a denial cascade.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Reporting an incorrect or fabricated NDC on a drug claim is a False Claims Act risk — the NDC must reflect the exact product administered, not a similar or substitute drug's code.
Modifier to Know
🏷️
Modifier Reference Guide
Common modifiers and proper usage guidelines
Modifier Description Usage Notes
KO Single drug unit dose formulation Use for single-drug unit-dose packaging.
KP First drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation First drug when multiple drugs are in one unit-dose.
KQ Second or subsequent drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation Each additional drug after KP in multi-drug unit-dose.
JW Drug amount discarded or not administered to the patient Requires a separate line on the same claim. Primary line must show >0 units administered. JW line shows wasted/discarded quantity. Both lines must reflect the same NDC and J-code.
JZ Zero wastage — no drug was discarded Use when no drug was discarded. Required by some payers when JW is not applicable.
💊
JW Modifier — Correct Billing Structure Example
Line 1
Line 1: J-code | 2 ML administered | same NDC | same DOS
Line 2
Line 2: J-code + JW | 0.5 ML discarded | same NDC | same DOS If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
Important: If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that lead to repeat denials
  • Do not resubmit without adding a valid, properly formatted NDC — the claim will deny again with N60
  • Do not use an NDC from a different manufacturer, lot, or package without verifying it was the actual drug administered
  • Do not copy an NDC from a prior claim without confirming it matches the vial used on this specific DOS
  • Do not submit the NDC without the N4 qualifier
  • Do not appeal a N60 denial if you have not yet submitted a corrected claim first
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting the underlying NDC & UOM error wastes timely filing days and may forfeit your right to correct the claim. Always correct first, then appeal only if the corrected claim is also denied.
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
✅
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist

Before submitting any drug claim, confirm:

  • ✅ NDC & UOM captured directly from the administered vial or package label
  • ✅ J-code validated against NDC & UOM using a current, reliable crosswalk
  • ✅ 10-digit NDC converted to 11-digit format (5-4-2) if applicable
  • ✅ N4 qualifier formatted with no space before the NDC number
  • ✅ Manufacturer-specific NDC & UOM confirmed (not from a different lot or supplier)
  • ✅ JW modifier applied on a separate line with administered quantity on primary line (if wastage applies)
  • ✅ NDC & UOM confirmed as active on the date of service
  • ✅ Claim run through edits before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅

Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True

Use only when the claim has already been corrected and still denied
  • A corrected claim has already been submitted and denied again
  • All billing data (NDC, J-code, UOM, quantity, manufacturer) has been confirmed correct against the MAR and vial label
  • The denial reason after correction still cites N60 — indicating a payer-side processing error
🔄

Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)

Recommended first step for most denials
  • Most N816 denials resolve by correcting and resubmitting the claim
  • Do not appeal as a first step - Verify NDC ↔ J-code crosswalk, 11-digit format, N4 qualifier, UOM, and quantity before resubmission
  • Use Resubmission Code 7 on the corrected claim

Most common root causes behind UOM-related drug billing denials
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Most UOM denials happen because the submitted unit of measure does not match the drug form, payer requirements, or NDC file mapping.
1
Missing UOM Code
The UOM field was left blank or populated with a placeholder or default value.
2
Wrong UOM Selected
Example: billing UN for a liquid drug that should be billed using ML.
3
Drug Form Mismatch
The UOM submitted does not match the drug form listed in the payer's NDC drug file.
4
Expired or Discontinued NDC
The NDC submitted is expired, discontinued, or no longer active in the payer's drug file.
5
Missing NDC on Claim
The drug was billed only with a J-code or HCPCS code, but no NDC value was attached to the claim.
6
Supplier Change Not Captured
A new supplier or manufacturer was used, but the updated NDC and UOM were never captured at the point of administration.
How to Fix It — RARC N815: Invalid NDC Unit Count
💡 What is RARC N815?
Your claim was denied because the NDC unit count (quantity administered) is missing, incorrect, or does not align with the billed drug. While the NDC identifies what drug was given, the NDC quantity tells the payer how much of that drug was actually administered. If the unit count is wrong, payers cannot validate dosing accuracy — resulting in denial. Even with a valid NDC, incorrect units will trigger N815.

WHAT NOT TO DO

What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that lead to repeat denials
  • Do not appeal before correcting the UOM (UN or ML) mismatch

  • Do not guess at the manufacturer, quantity, or drug lot always Verify with MR
  • Do not submit a corrected claim with the same incorrect NDC & UOM
  • Do not appeal a N815 denial if you have not yet submitted a corrected claim first
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting the underlying NDC & UOM error wastes timely filing days and may forfeit your right to correct the claim. Always correct first, then appeal only if the corrected claim is also denied.
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
✅
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist

Before submitting any drug claim, confirm:

  • ✅ NDC & UOM captured directly from the administered vial or package label
  • ✅ J-code validated against NDC & UOM using a current, reliable crosswalk
  • ✅ 10-digit NDC converted to 11-digit format (5-4-2) if applicable
  • ✅ N4 qualifier formatted with no space before the NDC number
  • ✅ Manufacturer-specific NDC & UOM confirmed (not from a different lot or supplier)
  • ✅ JW modifier applied on a separate line with administered quantity on primary line (if wastage applies)
  • ✅ NDC & UOM confirmed as active on the date of service
  • ✅ Claim run through edits before submission

✅

Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True

Use only when the claim has already been corrected and still denied
  • A corrected claim has already been submitted and denied again
  • All billing data (NDC, J-code, UOM, quantity, manufacturer) has been confirmed correct against the MAR and vial label
  • The denial reason after correction still cites N815 — indicating a payer-side processing error
🔄

Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)

Recommended first step for most denials

N847 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

(NDC) Billed Is Obsolete

Drug Billing / Data Mismatch · Professional & Facility Claims ·
Common CARC Pairing
CMS-1500 Box 24 & UB-04 (FL43-FL44) CO-16 Claim/service lacks information
What This Means
💡
What This Means

N847 is a payer remark code indicating that the National Drug Code (NDC) submitted on the claim has been identified as obsolete — meaning the NDC existed at one point but has since been retired, replaced, or superseded in the payer's drug file or the FDA NDC database.

ℹ️
Important Distinction
N847 does not mean the drug is not covered or the claim is permanently denied. It means the specific NDC number submitted is no longer recognized. In most cases, the same drug is available under a current, active NDC that the payer will accept. The correction is to identify and submit the correct NDC that was active and in use on the date of service.
Where to Report This Information
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional)
Professional claim reporting guidance
  • Box 24D — HCPCS/CPT drug code (J-code)
  • Shaded area 24A–24G — N4 qualifier + 11-digit NDC + unit of measure + quantity
✅ Correct: N412345678901
❌ Incorrect: N4 12345678901
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims)
Facility claim reporting guidance
  • FL - 44 — HCPCS/CPT code
  • FL - 43 — N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM + Quantity
Format: N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM + Qty
Example: ✅ Correct: N412345678901
⚠️
N4 Qualifier Format — Common Sub-Error
The N4 qualifier must be submitted as a continuous prefix immediately before the 11-digit NDC number. Adding spaces, separators, or formatting characters between N4 and the NDC will result in claim rejection even when the NDC itself is valid.
#
11-Digit NDC Format (5-4-2) — Conversion Guide
Original Format Add Zero To Example Conversion
4-4-2 Front of Labeler Code 1234-5678-90 → 01234-5678-90
5-3-2 Front of Product Code 12345-678-90 → 12345-0678-90
5-4-1 Front of Package Code 12345-6789-0 → 12345-6789-00
Unit of Measure (UOM) Misalignment
💊
Valid UOM Codes — When to Use Each
Reference guide for selecting the correct billing unit of measure
UOM Code Name When to Use Billing Unit
UN Unit Powder-form drugs in a vial that must be reconstituted before administration One unit per vial used
ML Milliliter Liquid-form drugs supplied in a vial or pre-filled syringe Actual milliliters administered
GR Gram Ointments, creams, inhalers, or bulk powders dispensed by weight Actual grams dispensed — primarily retail pharmacy
F2 International Unit Factor VIII Antihemophilic Factor and similar biologics billed in international units Per IU administered
📌
Key Rule
The UOM must match the physical form of the drug as supplied on the date of service — not how you prefer to bill it, and not what a prior claim used.
Why This Happens
⚠️
DATA ENTRY & SELECTION ISSUES
Most common root causes behind inactive, retired, or discontinued NDC denials
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Most discontinued NDC denials occur because the claim references an old, inactive, or retired NDC that no longer matches the drug currently being dispensed or billed.
1
Old NDC Reused
An NDC was copied from a prior claim where a different lot, package size, or manufacturer version was used, and that NDC has since been retired.
2
Manufacturer Changed Packaging
The drug manufacturer updated packaging or labeling and issued a new NDC, but the billing system still contains the retired code.
3
New Supplier Different NDC
The drug was purchased from a new wholesaler or distributor whose product carries a different current NDC than the legacy code stored in the system.
4
Expired or Discontinued NDC
The NDC submitted is expired, discontinued, or no longer active in the payer's drug reference file.
5
Missing NDC on Claim
The drug was billed only with a J-code or HCPCS code, but no NDC value was attached to the claim.
6
Supplier Change Not Captured
A new supplier or manufacturer was used, but the updated NDC was never captured at the point of administration or inventory intake.
How to Fix It — RARC N847: NDC Billed Is Obsolete
💡 What is RARC N847?
Your claim was denied because the NDC submitted on the claim is obsolete (inactive, retired, or no longer valid) in the payer’s drug database or FDA NDC Directory. Even though the drug may still exist, the specific NDC used has been replaced, discontinued, or repackaged. Payers only accept active NDCs tied to the exact product administered — using an outdated code results in denial.
CMS-1500
Box 24A
Shaded area — NDC field
837P EDI
Loop 2410
LIN segment — qualifier N4
NDC Status
Active Only
Inactive codes deny
📋 Common Reasons N847 Fires
Root Cause
What Happened
Retired NDC used
Drug manufacturer discontinued that specific NDC
Repackaged drug
Same drug now assigned a new NDC
Outdated billing system
Old NDC stored in charge master or EMR
Copied from prior claim
Reused historical NDC without validation
Payer drug file mismatch
NDC not recognized in payer formulary
1
Find the Correct NDC for the Drug Administered
Go back to the actual vial or package label
🔍 Pull the medication administration record (MAR) or drug log for the date of service. The valid NDC must come from the exact vial or package administered — not the drug name, not the order, not a lookup table guess.
  • Check the drug label or barcode scanned at administration — the NDC is printed on every FDA-regulated drug package in a 10- or 11-digit format.
  • Verify the NDC is active and valid in the FDA NDC Directory at fda.gov/drugs or ndclist.com — search by NDC number and confirm the listing is not inactive or retired.
  • If the package shows a 10-digit NDC, pad it to 11 digits by adding a leading zero to the correct segment. The three NDC formats are 4-4-2, 5-3-2, and 5-4-1 — each pads differently to reach 11 digits (5-4-2).
  • Confirm the NDC is for the exact manufacturer and package size dispensed — same drug from a different manufacturer has a different NDC and must be reported correctly.
  • If a reference lab or specialty pharmacy provided the drug, obtain the NDC from them directly — do not guess or substitute a similar product's NDC.
2
Add the Valid NDC & Resubmit
Correct format is critical — not just the number
✅ Once you have the valid 11-digit NDC, add it in the correct field and format, then resubmit as a corrected claim. Format errors are just as likely to re-deny as a missing NDC.
  • CMS-1500 (paper): Enter in the shaded area of Box 24A using format: qualifier N4 + 11-digit NDC + UOM qualifier + quantity administered (e.g., N4 12345678900 ML 10).
  • 837P electronic: Report in Loop 2410, LIN segment — LIN03 qualifier must be N4, LIN04 is the 11-digit NDC. Also populate the CTP segment with UOM qualifier and quantity. All three are required.
  • No hyphens in EDI — submit NDC as a plain 11-digit number (12345678900), never as 12345-678-90.
  • Corrected claim: CMS-1500 → Box 22, Resubmission Code "7" + original ICN. UB-04 → TOB frequency "7" + original TCN in Box 64.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits before resubmitting — deadlines don't pause while tracking down NDC details.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
NDC may not be in their drug file
📞 If the corrected claim still gets N60, the payer's internal drug file may not recognize the NDC — especially for newer drugs, biosimilars, or recently repackaged products.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, date of service, HCPCS billed, NDC submitted, drug name, strength, manufacturer, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask: "Is NDC [XXXXXXXXXXX] recognized in your drug file for HCPCS [XXXXX]? If not, is there an alternate NDC or updated code your system requires for this drug?"
  • Ask if the payer requires NDC registration or pre-loading in their formulary system before claims with that NDC will process.
  • Ask if the denial is a formatting issue — confirm whether they received the NDC with or without hyphens and whether the LIN/CTP segments were both present.
  • 📝 Document: reference number, rep name, date, time, and exactly what they say is wrong or missing.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Attach FDA proof the NDC is valid and active
⚖️ If the payer upholds N60 after a corrected claim and call, file a formal appeal with FDA documentation proving the NDC is valid, active, and correctly reported on the claim.
  • Appeal must include: Provider NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, HCPCS, NDC submitted, drug name, strength, manufacturer, and MAR confirming administration.
  • Key statement: "NDC [XXXXXXXXXXX] is an active, FDA-registered National Drug Code for [Drug Name, Strength] manufactured by [Manufacturer], as confirmed by the FDA NDC Directory. The NDC was correctly reported in Loop 2410 / Box 24A per CMS billing guidelines. We appeal the N60 denial."
  • Attach: FDA NDC Directory printout confirming active status, drug package label, MAR, original + corrected claims, both remittance advices.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with MAC within 120 days. Reference CMS Pub 100-04, Chapter 17. Commercial: check EOB — typically 30–180 days.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your NDC Capture Workflow
NDC must flow from administration directly to the claim
🔁 If N60 appears across multiple claims, your NDC is not being captured at the point of administration and passed to billing. Billers should never be manually looking up or typing NDCs — the drug barcode scanned at admin time must auto-populate into the claim.
  • Capture NDC at point of administration. Build a workflow where nursing or pharmacy scans the drug barcode at administration time — that scan should push the NDC directly into the patient's medication record and then to the claim. Manual entry at billing time is the #1 cause of N60.
  • Validate NDC format in your billing system. Add a field-level validation that confirms the NDC is exactly 11 digits with no hyphens before the claim can be submitted — reject any entry that doesn't match the format.
  • Keep your NDC master file current. When a drug is repackaged or a new manufacturer is added to your formulary, update the NDC in your billing system immediately — stale NDCs trigger N60 even when the drug itself hasn't changed.
  • Add a pre-submission edit for all drug HCPCS codes (J-codes and chemotherapy codes) that flags any claim line missing a value in the NDC field before the claim is released to the payer.
  • Verify NDC against the FDA directory quarterly. Cross-check every NDC in your drug master file against the FDA NDC Directory to confirm active status — flag any inactive NDC for immediate update before it causes a denial cascade.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Reporting an incorrect or fabricated NDC on a drug claim is a False Claims Act risk — the NDC must reflect the exact product administered, not a similar or substitute drug's code.
Modifier to Know
🏷️
Modifier Reference Guide
Common modifiers and proper usage guidelines
Modifier Description Usage Notes
KO Single drug unit dose formulation Use for single-drug unit-dose packaging.
KP First drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation First drug when multiple drugs are in one unit-dose.
KQ Second or subsequent drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation Each additional drug after KP in multi-drug unit-dose.
JW Drug amount discarded or not administered to the patient Requires a separate line on the same claim. Primary line must show >0 units administered. JW line shows wasted/discarded quantity. Both lines must reflect the same NDC and J-code.
JZ Zero wastage — no drug was discarded Use when no drug was discarded. Required by some payers when JW is not applicable.
💊
JW Modifier — Correct Billing Structure Example
Line 1
Line 1: J-code | 2 ML administered | same NDC | same DOS
Line 2
Line 2: J-code + JW | 0.5 ML discarded | same NDC | same DOS If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
Important: If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that lead to repeat denials
  • Do not substitute a currently active NDC without confirming it was also active on the date of service — a future NDC billed against a past DOS is also invalid
  • Do not copy a replacement NDC from a different lot, package size, or manufacturer without verifying it matches the drug actually administered
  • Do not carry the obsolete NDC forward to secondary or tertiary claims — correct it on every payer submission
  • Do not appeal before first attempting a corrected claim with the current active NDC
  • Do not appeal a N847 denial if you have not yet submitted a corrected claim first
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting the underlying NDC & UOM error wastes timely filing days and may forfeit your right to correct the claim. Always correct first, then appeal only if the corrected claim is also denied.
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
✅
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist

NDC captured directly from the actual administered vial label on the DOS — not from a prior claim or outer carton

  • ✅ NDC verified as active (not obsolete, deactivated, or withdrawn) on the date of service via FDA NDC database
  • ✅ Billing system NDC defaults reviewed and updated when new drug lots or packages are received
  • ✅ 10-digit NDC converted to 11-digit format (5-4-2) if applicable
  • ✅ N4 qualifier formatted with no space before the NDC number
  • ✅ Manufacturer-specific NDC & UOM confirmed (not from a different lot or supplier)
  • ✅ JW modifier applied on a separate line with administered quantity on primary line (if wastage applies)
  • ✅ NDC & UOM confirmed as active on the date of service
  • ✅ Claim run through edits before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅

Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True

Use only when the claim has already been corrected and still denied
  • A corrected claim with a verified active NDC for the DOS has already been submitted and denied again with continued N847
  • The FDA NDC database confirms the submitted NDC was active on the DOS and is not obsolete
  • The continued denial is due to a payer-side drug file error — payer's file has not been refreshed
🔄

Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)

Recommended first step for most denials
  • Most N847 denials resolve by correcting and resubmitting the claim
  • Do not appeal as a first step - Verify NDC ↔ J-code crosswalk, 11-digit format, N4 qualifier, UOM, and quantity before resubmission
  • Use Resubmission Code 7 on the corrected claim
