🔁 If N60 appears across multiple claims, your NDC is not being captured at the point of administration and passed to billing. Billers should never be manually looking up or typing NDCs — the drug barcode scanned at admin time must auto-populate into the claim.
  • Capture NDC at point of administration. Build a workflow where nursing or pharmacy scans the drug barcode at administration time — that scan should push the NDC directly into the patient's medication record and then to the claim. Manual entry at billing time is the #1 cause of N60.
  • Validate NDC format in your billing system. Add a field-level validation that confirms the NDC is exactly 11 digits with no hyphens before the claim can be submitted — reject any entry that doesn't match the format.
  • Keep your NDC master file current. When a drug is repackaged or a new manufacturer is added to your formulary, update the NDC in your billing system immediately — stale NDCs trigger N60 even when the drug itself hasn't changed.
  • Add a pre-submission edit for all drug HCPCS codes (J-codes and chemotherapy codes) that flags any claim line missing a value in the NDC field before the claim is released to the payer.
  • Verify NDC against the FDA directory quarterly. Cross-check every NDC in your drug master file against the FDA NDC Directory to confirm active status — flag any inactive NDC for immediate update before it causes a denial cascade.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Reporting an incorrect or fabricated NDC on a drug claim is a False Claims Act risk — the NDC must reflect the exact product administered, not a similar or substitute drug's code.
Modifier to Know
🏷️
Modifier Reference Guide
Common modifiers and proper usage guidelines
Modifier Description Usage Notes
KO Single drug unit dose formulation Use for single-drug unit-dose packaging.
KP First drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation First drug when multiple drugs are in one unit-dose.
KQ Second or subsequent drug in a multiple drug unit dose formulation Each additional drug after KP in multi-drug unit-dose.
JW Drug amount discarded or not administered to the patient Requires a separate line on the same claim. Primary line must show >0 units administered. JW line shows wasted/discarded quantity. Both lines must reflect the same NDC and J-code.
JZ Zero wastage — no drug was discarded Use when no drug was discarded. Required by some payers when JW is not applicable.
💊
JW Modifier — Correct Billing Structure Example
Line 1
Line 1: J-code | 2 ML administered | same NDC | same DOS
Line 2
Line 2: J-code + JW | 0.5 ML discarded | same NDC | same DOS If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
Important: If the JW line is the only line, or if the administered line shows zero units, the claim will deny.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that lead to repeat denials
  • Do not resubmit with the same unresolvable NDC — the claim will deny again with N848
  • Do not fabricate or estimate an NDC — submitting a made-up NDC that happens to resolve to a different product creates a false claim risk
  • Do not use a different drug's NDC as a substitute without clinical confirmation that the same drug was administered
  • Do not appeal before first attempting a corrected claim with the current active NDC
  • Do not appeal a N847 denial if you have not yet submitted a corrected claim first
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting the underlying NDC & UOM error wastes timely filing days and may forfeit your right to correct the claim. Always correct first, then appeal only if the corrected claim is also denied.
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
✅
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist

NDC captured character by character from the actual administered vial label — not typed from memory or copied from a prior claim

  • ✅ NDC verified in FDA OpenFDA or AAPC Codify database — confirms it resolves to a real, identifiable product
  • ✅ NDC is exactly 11 digits in 5-4-2 format — no missing, extra, or transposed digits
  • ✅ N4 qualifier present with no space before the NDC
  • ✅ NDC resolves to the same product as the billed J-code via current crosswalk
  • ✅ Manufacturer-specific NDC & UOM confirmed (not from a different lot or supplier)
  • ✅ JW modifier applied on a separate line with administered quantity on primary line (if wastage applies)
  • ✅ NDC & UOM confirmed as active on the date of service
  • ✅ Claim run through edits before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅

Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True

Use only when the claim has already been corrected and still denied
  • A corrected claim with a verified active NDC for the DOS has already been submitted and denied again with continued N847
  • The FDA NDC database confirms the submitted NDC was active on the DOS and is not obsolete
  • The continued denial is due to a payer-side drug file error — payer's file has not been refreshed
🔄

Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)

Recommended first step for most denials
  • Most N847 denials resolve by correcting and resubmitting the claim
  • Do not appeal as a first step - Verify NDC ↔ J-code crosswalk, 11-digit format, N4 qualifier, UOM, and quantity before resubmission
  • Use Resubmission Code 7 on the corrected claim

Invalid Type of Bill

Drug Billing / Data Mismatch · Professional & Facility Claims ·
Common CARC Pairing
CMS-1500 Not Use & UB-04 (FL43-FL44) CO-16 Claim/service lacks information
What This Means
💡
What This Means

The Type of Bill (TOB) field on the UB-04 claim (Form Locator 4) was either left blank, submitted with an invalid code, or contains an incomplete value that does not meet payer requirements. The TOB is a critical 3-digit (or 4-character with leading zero) code that tells the payer exactly what kind of facility submitted the claim, what type of care was rendered, and whether this is an opening, interim, or closing bill in a series.

ℹ️
Important Distinction
Type of Bill (TOB) tells the payer three important things:

1. What type of facility billed the claim
2. What kind of care the patient received
3. What kind of claim is being submitted (original, corrected, void, etc.)

Simple Formula:
TOB = Facility Type + Care Type + Claim Frequency
💡
Easy Tip for Denial AR Users
• If the patient stayed overnight after formal admission, think "Inpatient"
• If the patient came and left the same day, think "Outpatient"
• If the service happened at home, think "HHA"
• If the service was dialysis, think "Dialysis Facility"
• If it was surgery without overnight stay, think "Outpatient Surgery"
Where to Report This Information
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional)
Professional claim reporting guidance
  • Non Billable — Type of Bill (TOB) codes are not used on CMS-1500 professional claims
  • Non Billable — FL4 reporting applies only to institutional UB-04 billing
Professional Claims Guidance
Type of Bill (TOB) codes are institutional billing elements and are not submitted on CMS-1500 professional claims.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims)
Facility claim reporting guidance
  • Field — FL4 Type of Bill (TOB)
  • Format — 4-character alphanumeric code. Position 1 must always contain "0"
  • Position — Upper-left section of the UB-04 directly below FL2 (Patient Control Number) and FL3 (Medical Record Number)
  • Required On — All institutional UB-04 claims including inpatient, outpatient, SNF, hospice, HHA, ESRD, ASC, RHC, and FQHC billing
Type of Bill Example
Location: Upper-left section of the UB-04 claim form
Format: 4-digit numeric TOB
Example: ✅ Correct: 0851
⚠️
Facility Type + Care Type + Claim Frequency
These are the most commonly encountered Type of Bill (TOB) combinations across hospital, SNF, HHA, hospice, ESRD, ASC, clinic, and rehabilitation billing. Always validate the facility type, care classification, and claim frequency digit before resubmission to avoid RTP edits and payer rejections.

Why This Happens

DATA ENTRY & SELECTION ISSUES
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Most TOB denials happen because the claim contains a missing, incomplete, incorrect, or mismatched Type of Bill value.
1
Missing TOB
FL4 was left completely blank during claim submission.
2
Incomplete TOB
Only 2 or 3 digits submitted — TOB submitted as 3 characters instead of 4 — leading zero dropped.
3
Wrong Facility Type
Facility type digit does not match the provider's enrollment type — for example, an ASC billing with a hospital TOB (013X) instead of an ASC TOB (085X).
4
Wrong Bill Classification
Outpatient services billed with inpatient classification — for example, 0111 used for an outpatient infusion that should be 0131.
5
Wrong Frequency Code
Admit-through-discharge claim (frequency 1) submitted when the patient was never discharged — creating a false episode closure.
6
System & Interface Errors
Billing system updated with new TOB values but old TOBs carried forward in templates.

How to Fix It — RARC MA30: Missing / Incomplete / Invalid Type of Bill
💡 What is RARC MA30?
Your claim was denied because the Type of Bill (TOB) in Form Locator 4 (FL-4) of the UB-04 (CMS-1450) is missing, incomplete, or does not match the services, facility type, or billing period on the claim. Think of the TOB as the routing address for your claim — it tells the payer what kind of facility billed, what type of service was rendered, and whether this is an original, replacement, or void submission. If that address is wrong or blank, the payer cannot adjudicate the claim. This is a pure administrative billing error — not a medical necessity or coverage denial — and it is fully correctable.
Claim Form
UB-04
CMS-1450 institutional
Field
FL-4 (Box 4)
Type of Bill — 4 digits
Denial Type
Administrative
Correctable — Resubmit
📋 Common Reasons MA30 Is Triggered — TOB Digit Breakdown
Root Cause
What Happened
TOB field left blank
FL-4 was empty — claim rejected at intake before adjudication
Wrong facility type digit (2nd digit)
e.g., SNF (2XX) billed instead of Hospital (1XX) for the service rendered
Wrong type of care digit (3rd digit)
e.g., outpatient digit on an inpatient admission — 131 used instead of 111
Wrong frequency digit (4th digit)
Replacement claim submitted with digit "1" instead of "7"
CAH billed with wrong TOB
Critical Access Hospital must use 85X — not 13X used for general outpatient
1
Coding Escalation — Validate the TOB
Internal review and root cause identification
🔍 Pull the original claim and remittance. Before contacting the payer, the billing team must own the investigation internally — escalate to a coder or senior biller to confirm the exact TOB error and the correct replacement code.
  • Retrieve the 835 remittance or paper EOB and confirm RARC MA30 is present. The TOB is a 4-digit code in Box 4 (FL-4) of the UB-04 — no blanks, no zeros where digits are required.
  • Validate all four TOB digits: Digit 1 = leading zero (ignored by CMS); Digit 2 = Facility type (1=Hospital, 2=SNF, 3=Home Health, 7=Clinic); Digit 3 = Type of care (1=Inpatient, 3=Outpatient); Digit 4 = Frequency (1=Admit-Discharge, 7=Replacement, 8=Void).
  • Cross-check the TOB against services rendered — common mismatches: outpatient billed as inpatient (131 vs. 111), SNF billed with hospital TOB, or a replacement claim missing the frequency digit "7".
  • Verify payer-specific TOB rules — Medicare Part B inpatient must use TOB 121, not 111. Critical Access Hospitals must use 85X, not 13X. These are not universal defaults.
  • If the correct TOB cannot be determined with certainty, escalate to a Senior Coder or Compliance Officer before resubmitting — patching the wrong digit causes a second denial.
2
Corrected Claim Resubmission
Fix the TOB and resubmit as a replacement claim
✅ MA30 is a correctable billing error — not a coverage determination. A corrected claim with the accurate TOB is the fastest path to payment. Do not submit as a new claim.
  • Update Box 4 (FL-4) on the UB-04 with the verified, correct 4-digit TOB (e.g., 0131 = Hospital Outpatient, 0111 = Hospital Inpatient Admit-Discharge).
  • Set the last digit (frequency) to "7" (Replacement) — for example, 0137 = Hospital Outpatient Replacement Claim. A corrected claim without digit "7" may process as a duplicate and deny again.
  • Enter the original claim number / TCN in Box 64 to link the corrected claim to the original submission. Missing this field causes the payer to treat the claim as new rather than corrected.
  • Add a note in Box 80 (Remarks): "Corrected Type of Bill. Original TOB [XXX]. Correct TOB [YYY]. Resubmitting per RARC MA30 denial."
  • Run a full pre-submission scrub before resubmitting — verify patient demographics, revenue codes, NPIs, diagnosis codes, and service dates are all accurate.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits — Medicare: 12 months from date of service. Most commercial payers: 90–180 days. Corrected claim deadlines may differ from original submission windows.
3
Still Denied? Call Provider Relations
Diagnose payer-side system or policy issues
📞 If the corrected claim is denied again with MA30 — or shows no movement after 30+ days — call the payer's Provider Relations line (not general member services) to determine if there is a payer-side configuration issue, system edit, or policy nuance blocking the TOB.
  • Have ready: Original claim number, corrected claim number, date of service, member ID, TOB used on both submissions, and remittance advice for both denials.
  • Ask the rep: "Is TOB [XXX] valid for this provider type and service? Does your system require a specific TOB for this revenue code or place of service?"
  • Ask whether the corrected claim was received as a replacement (frequency digit 7) — if the payer's system processed it as a duplicate instead, it may have auto-denied without human review.
  • Ask if the payer has a TOB crosswalk or policy document that differs from NUBC standards — request it in writing or ask for a portal link for future reference.
  • If the rep cannot resolve it, escalate on the call to a Claims Supervisor or Provider Relations Specialist with UB-04 expertise. Do not end the call without a resolution path.
  • 📝 Document: Call reference number, representative name, date, and time. This is required evidence if the denial escalates to a formal appeal.
4
Payer Denied Reprocessing — Appeal Required
Formal appeal proving the TOB is correct
⚖️ If the payer upholds the MA30 denial after a corrected claim and provider relations outreach, file a formal appeal. Since MA30 is an administrative denial — not a medical necessity denial — the appeal focuses entirely on demonstrating the TOB was correct and the payer's denial is in error.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, billed amount, and the specific TOB in dispute on both the original and corrected submissions.
  • Key statement: "We are appealing the MA30 denial on the basis that Type of Bill [XXX] is correct and appropriate for the facility type and services rendered. The TOB was complete and valid at submission per NUBC and CMS standards."
  • Attach: Original and corrected UB-04 copies, both EOBs/ERAs, clinical documentation confirming the place and type of service, and the call reference number from Step 3.
  • Reference CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Publication 100-04, Chapter 25 (Completing and Processing the Form UB-04 Data Set) or the AHA UB-04 Data Specifications Manual as authority for the correct TOB.
  • Medicare: File a Redetermination with the MAC within 120 days of the initial denial date. Commercial: Submit per the payer's appeal instructions on the EOB — typically 30–60 days per state regulation.
5
Payer Says Information Not Received on Form — Appeal Required
Prove the TOB was present on the original submission — EDI transmission audit
🔁 This scenario is distinct from Step 4. Here the payer is not saying the TOB was wrong — they are saying the TOB field was blank, missing, or not received on the submitted form. This is frequently a clearinghouse mapping error, a billing system configuration gap, or a payer claims intake failure that dropped the FL-4 data in transit.
  • Request a claim image from the payer as they received it. Compare it side-by-side with your original UB-04 to confirm whether FL-4 was present or dropped during transmission. This is your right as a provider and shifts the burden of proof.
  • Pull the original 837I EDI transmission file and confirm the TOB was submitted in Loop 2300, CLM05-1 (Type of Bill). If absent or blank in the 837I, the issue is internal — fix at the billing system level before resubmitting.
  • Review the 999 Functional Acknowledgment or TA1 Interchange Acknowledgment from your clearinghouse. An interchange-level "Accepted" does not guarantee all segments passed through correctly — check for CLM-segment-level rejections that may have silently dropped FL-4.
  • File the appeal with proof of original submission: Include a printed UB-04 showing the TOB in FL-4, the 837I CLM05-1 segment excerpt with the TOB value, the clearinghouse acknowledgment, and a written statement confirming the data was present at the time of submission.
  • Ask the payer to investigate whether a system intake configuration error caused the CLM05-1 segment to be dropped or ignored during adjudication — identifying a payer-side intake failure may trigger internal reprocessing without a full appeal cycle.
  • 🔒 After resolution: Work with your clearinghouse to add a pre-submission scrub rule that flags any UB-04 institutional claim where FL-4 (TOB) is blank or malformed before release — preventing recurrence across your entire institutional claim volume.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that lead to repeat denials
  • Do not resubmit the claim with the same invalid or incomplete TOB — it will deny again with MA30
  • Do not change the TOB without reviewing all cross-validated fields — a TOB correction that is not reconciled with revenue codes, admission date, discharge status, and occurrence codes will generate secondary denials
  • Do not use frequency code 7 (replacement) without a valid prior claim to replace — submitting a replacement against a claim that was never processed will create a new claim rather than replace the denied one
  • Do not use frequency code 8 (void) unless the original claim was paid and must be fully reversed — a void against an unpaid claim may not process correctly
  • Do not carry an incorrect TOB to secondary or tertiary claims — the wrong TOB on the primary will generate a cascade of secondary denials
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing MA30 before correcting the TOB error wastes timely filing days and is almost never successful — the payer will uphold the denial because the claim data itself is incorrect. Correct the TOB, reconcile all cross-validated fields, and resubmit before considering an appeal.
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
✅
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist

FL4 is populated — not blank, not truncated & TOB is exactly 4 characters and begins with "0"

  • ✅ Position 2 (facility type) Position 3 (bill classification) Position 4 (frequency) accurately reflects where this claim falls in the billing sequence
  • ✅ The full 4-digit TOB combination is a recognized and payer-accepted code — not just mathematically valid
  • ✅ Revenue codes in FL42 are consistent with the TOB
  • ✅ Admission date (FL12) is populated if TOB is inpatient or SNF
  • ✅ Discharge status (FL17) is populated and consistent with the frequency code
  • ✅ Condition code D4 is included when resubmitting a corrected claim (frequency 7)
  • ✅ For interim billing series — prior claims in the sequence are confirmed submitted and received before sending the next interim bill
  • ✅ Claim run through a scrubber with TOB validation before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅

Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True

Use only when the claim has already been corrected and still denied
  • A corrected claim with the verified TOB has already been submitted and denied again
  • You have documentation confirming the TOB is valid for this facility type, care setting, and billing period
  • The continued denial with MA30 is due to a payer-side system mapping error or provider enrollment mismatch
🔄

Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)

Recommended first step for most denials
  • Nearly all MA30 denials are billing errors — missing, 3-digit instead of 4-digit, or wrong facility/classification/frequency digit
  • Do not appeal as a first step — identify the specific TOB error, correct it, and resubmit with Resubmission Code 7
  • If the error is a replacement or void without ICN, add the original claim ICN to FL64 and resubmit

Invalid Admission Date

Facility Billing / UB-04 · Inpatient & SNF
Common CARC Pairing
UB-04 (FL12) CO-16 Claim/service lacks information
What This Means
💡
What This Means

The Admission Date field (Form Locator 12) on the UB-04 claim was either left blank, submitted with an invalid date format, or contains a date that conflicts with other fields on the claim. FL12 is required on all inpatient hospital and SNF claims — the payer cannot determine the start of the benefit period without it

ℹ️
Important Distinction
MA40 does not mean the stay is not covered. It is a data integrity error — the claim cannot be processed until a valid, correctly formatted admission date is present in FL12. This is almost always resolved with a corrected claim, not an appeal.
Where to Report This Information
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional)
Professional claim reporting guidance
  • Non Billable — FL12 Admission Date reporting is not used on CMS-1500 professional claims
  • Non Billable — Admission dates are institutional claim elements specific to UB-04 billing
Professional Claims Guidance
FL12 admission/start-of-care dates are not reported on CMS-1500 claims and do not apply to professional billing.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims)
Facility claim reporting guidance
  • FL12 — Admission / Start of Care Date: Patient admission date for inpatient, SNF, or qualifying facility services
  • Format — MM/DD/YY (6-digit) per UB-04 billing instructions; some payers also accept MMDDYYYY (8-digit)
Fields That Cross-Validate With FL12
FL6: Statement Covers Period (From Date)
FL17: Patient Discharge Status
FL18–FL28: Condition Codes
FL31–FL34: Occurrence Codes / Dates
FL4: Type of Bill
FL67: Principal Diagnosis
⚠️
Admission Date — Common Sub-Error
FL12 is one of the most critical dates on the UB-04 claim because it drives DRG grouping, benefit period calculations, payer edits, and Medicare SNF coinsurance logic. Incorrect admission dates can trigger medical necessity denials, MSP conflicts, or reimbursement calculation errors.

Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Most TOB denials happen because the claim contains a missing, incomplete, incorrect, or mismatched Type of Bill value.
1
Missing TOB
FL4 was left completely blank during claim submission.
2
Incomplete TOB
Only 2 or 3 digits submitted — TOB submitted as 3 characters instead of 4 — leading zero dropped.

Wrong Facility Type
Facility type digit does not match the provider's enrollment type — for example, an ASC billing with a hospital TOB (013X) instead of an ASC TOB (085X).
4

How to Fix It — RARC MA40: Missing / Incomplete / Invalid Admission Date
💡 What is RARC MA40?
Your claim was denied because the Admission Date in Form Locator 12 (FL-12) of the UB-04 (CMS-1450) is missing, incorrectly formatted, logically invalid, or conflicts with other dates on the claim. Think of the admission date as the anchor point of the entire claim — every other date on an inpatient bill (statement period, discharge date, occurrence dates) is cross-validated against it by the payer's adjudication system. If that anchor is wrong, blank, or inconsistent, the claim cannot be processed. This is a pure administrative billing error — not a medical necessity or coverage denial — and is fully correctable with a corrected claim resubmission.
Claim Form
UB-04
CMS-1450 institutional
Field
FL-12
Admission / Start of Care Date
Required Format
MMDDYY
6-digit numeric — no separators
📋 Common Reasons MA40 Is Triggered — Admission Date Errors on the UB-04
Root Cause
What Happened
FL-12 left blank
Field was empty — required for all inpatient TOB types (11X, 12X, 21X, 22X, etc.)
Wrong date format
Date entered as MM/DD/YYYY or with separators — must be MMDDYY (6 digits, no slashes)
Admission date after "From" date in FL-6
FL-12 date is later than the statement period start — payer's logic check fails immediately
Transposed digits / data entry error
e.g., 013124 entered instead of 013124 — month/day swap creates an invalid or future date
Admission date conflicts with FL-6 "From" date
For inpatient claims, FL-12 must match or precede FL-6 "From" — a mismatch fails cross-field edits
1
Coding Escalation — Verify the True Admission Date
Go back to the source record before touching the claim
🔍 Pull the patient's medical record and registration documentation. The admission date in FL-12 must reflect the actual date the patient was admitted to the facility — not the order date, not the pre-admission date, and not the first date of service in a different setting.
  • Retrieve the admission/registration record or face sheet for the encounter — this is the authoritative source for the true admission date for inpatient claims.
  • Confirm the FL-12 format is MMDDYY (6 numeric digits, no slashes or separators). Per CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Chapter 25, the admission date field cannot exceed 8 positions and must be valid if present. Example: January 31, 2025 = 013125.
  • Cross-validate FL-12 against FL-6 (Statement Covers Period From/Through) — the admission date in FL-12 must equal or precede the "From" date in FL-6. A mismatch between these two fields is a leading cause of MA40 denials on inpatient claims.
  • Confirm the TOB in FL-4 requires an admission date — FL-12 is required when the Type of Bill is 11X, 12X, 18X, 21X, 22X, 32X, 33X, 41X, 81X, or 82X. Outpatient TOBs (13X) do not require FL-12, so the denial may also signal a TOB issue.
  • For SNF, home health, or rehab claims, confirm FL-12 reflects the start-of-care date for the episode, not the date of the physician's order — these dates are frequently confused at registration, producing systematic MA40 denials.
  • Escalate to a Senior Coder or Health Information Management (HIM) staff member if the medical record and billing system show conflicting dates before resubmitting.
2
Corrected Claim Resubmission
Correct FL-12 and resubmit as a replacement claim
✅ MA40 is a correctable billing error — not a coverage or medical necessity denial. Once the true admission date is confirmed, correct FL-12 and resubmit as a corrected claim. Do not submit as a new claim.
  • Update FL-12 (Admission/Start of Care Date) with the verified correct date in MMDDYY format (6 numeric digits, no slashes or separators). Confirm the date is not a future date and is not later than the "Through" date in FL-6.
  • Simultaneously review and correct FL-6 (Statement Covers Period) if needed — for inpatient claims, the "From" date in FL-6 must align with or follow FL-12. A corrected FL-12 that still conflicts with FL-6 will trigger a second denial.
  • Set the TOB frequency digit (4th digit in FL-4) to "7" (Replacement) to indicate this is a corrected claim — e.g., 0117 = Hospital Inpatient Replacement Claim. A corrected claim without digit "7" may process as a duplicate and auto-deny.
  • Enter the original claim number / TCN in Box 64 to link the corrected claim to the original. Missing this reference causes the payer to treat the claim as a new submission rather than a correction.
  • Add a note in Box 80 (Remarks): "Corrected Admission Date in FL-12. Original date [MMDDYY]. Correct date [MMDDYY]. Resubmitting per RARC MA40 denial."
  • Run a full pre-submission cross-field validation: confirm FL-12 ≤ FL-6 From date ≤ FL-6 Through date ≤ current date, and that occurrence code dates in FL-31 through FL-34 are also consistent with the corrected admission date.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits before resubmitting — Medicare: 12 months from date of service. Most commercial payers: 90–180 days. Corrected claim deadlines may differ from original submission windows.
3
Still Denied? Call Provider Relations
Diagnose payer-side system edits or date conflict logic
📞 If the corrected claim is denied again with MA40 — or shows no movement after 30+ days — call the payer's Provider Relations or Claims department (not general member services) to identify whether the date is failing a payer-side cross-field edit, enrollment validation, or system configuration rule.
  • Have ready: Original claim number, corrected claim number, date of service, member ID, the admission date submitted on both claims, and both remittance advices showing MA40.
  • Ask the rep: "Is the admission date [MMDDYY] in FL-12 failing a specific cross-field edit? Is it being compared against a coverage effective date, a prior authorization start date, or an eligibility record in your system?"
  • Ask whether the payer's system is flagging a conflict between FL-12 and the member's eligibility period — if coverage was not yet active on the admission date, MA40 may be a proxy denial for an eligibility issue that needs separate resolution.
  • Ask whether the payer requires the admission date to be reported in a specific alternate format (some older payer systems still require MMDDYYYY — 8 digits — rather than the standard MMDDYY — 6 digits) despite CMS guidance.
  • If the rep confirms the date is correct but the system still rejects it, ask for manual reprocessing on the call or escalate to a Claims Supervisor with authority to override the system edit.
  • 📝 Document: Call reference number, representative name, date, and time. This is mandatory evidence if the denial escalates to a formal appeal.
4
Payer Denied Reprocessing — Appeal Required
Formal appeal proving the admission date is accurate and documented
⚖️ If the payer upholds the MA40 denial after a corrected claim and provider relations outreach, file a formal appeal with medical record documentation proving the admission date submitted is accurate and supported by the clinical record.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, billed amount, and the specific admission date in dispute on both the original and corrected submissions.
  • Key statement: "We are appealing the MA40 denial on the basis that the admission date [MMDDYY] reported in FL-12 is accurate, valid, and directly supported by the patient's admission documentation and medical record. This is an administrative billing denial and the admission date was correct and complete at submission."
  • Attach supporting documentation: Original and corrected UB-04 copies, both EOBs/ERAs, the patient's admission/face sheet or registration record confirming the actual admission date, relevant medical record pages documenting the date of admission, and the call reference number from Step 3.
  • Reference CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Publication 100-04, Chapter 25 — which defines FL-12 (Admission/Start of Care Date) requirements — as the governing authority for admission date placement and format on institutional claims.
  • Medicare: File a Redetermination with the MAC within 120 days of the initial denial date on the remittance. Commercial: Submit per the payer's appeal instructions on the EOB — typically 30–60 days per state regulation. Document submission channel, date, and tracking number.
  • Track the appeal deadline and follow up if no decision is received within the payer's standard adjudication window — 60 days for Medicare MACs, 30–60 days for most commercial payers.
5
Payer Says Information Not Received on Form — Appeal Required
Prove FL-12 was present on the original submission — EDI transmission audit
🔁 This scenario is distinct from Step 4. Here the payer is not saying the admission date was wrong — they are saying FL-12 was blank, missing, or not received on the submitted form. This is frequently caused by a billing system field-mapping error, a clearinghouse transmission gap, or a payer claims intake failure that dropped the FL-12 data in transit rather than an error made by the biller.
  • Request a claim image from the payer as they received it — this is your right as a provider. Compare it side-by-side with your original UB-04 to confirm whether FL-12 was populated or dropped during transmission. A blank FL-12 on the payer's image despite it being populated on your submission is definitive proof of a transmission or intake failure.
  • Pull the original 837I EDI file and confirm the admission date was submitted in Loop 2300, DTP segment with qualifier "435" (Admission Date/Hour). If the DTP*435 segment is absent or contains an invalid value, the issue is internal — correct the billing system mapping before resubmitting.
  • Review the 999 Functional Acknowledgment or TA1 Interchange Acknowledgment from your clearinghouse. An interchange-level "Accepted" response does not guarantee all DTP segments transmitted correctly — check specifically for DTP loop-level rejections that may have silently dropped FL-12 data.
  • File the appeal with proof of original submission: Include a printed UB-04 showing the admission date in FL-12, the 837I DTP*435 segment excerpt confirming the date was present in the EDI file, the clearinghouse acknowledgment confirming transmission, and a written statement confirming the data was present and valid at the time of original submission.
  • Ask the payer to investigate whether a system intake configuration error caused the DTP*435 segment to be dropped or ignored during adjudication. Identifying a payer-side intake failure may trigger internal reprocessing without a full appeal cycle — this is worth requesting explicitly before allowing the appeal to run its full timeline.
  • 🔒 After resolution: Work with your clearinghouse or billing system vendor to add a pre-submission scrub rule that flags any 837I institutional claim where the DTP*435 (Admission Date) segment is missing or malformed for inpatient TOB types — preventing the same transmission failure from recurring across your claim volume.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that trigger repeat MA40 denials
These errors commonly cause admission date mismatches, corrected claim rejections, and avoidable timely filing loss.
  • Do not appeal before submitting a corrected claim with the valid admission date
  • Do not submit the corrected claim with the same blank or invalid FL12
  • Do not assume the admission date carried over correctly from a prior claim without verifying the actual FL12 value
  • Do not use the hospital admission date on an SNF claim if the SNF had a separate, later admission date — verify which date applies
  • Do not omit Condition Code D4 on the replacement claim
  • Do not carry forward a placeholder date (e.g., 01/01/00 or 000000) from a billing template
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting FL12 wastes timely filing days. MA40 is almost always a correctable data error — verify the admission date from the ADT system, correct it, and resubmit with Frequency Code 7 and Condition Code D4.
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
✅
PREVENTIVE CHECKLIST
Pre-submission validation checklist

Before submitting any inpatient or SNF claim, confirm

  • ✅ FL12 is populated — not blank, not zero-filled, not a placeholder
  • ✅ Date format is MM/DD/YY (paper) or MMDDYYYY (EDI 837I)
  • ✅ Admission date is confirmed against the face sheet or ADT system record
  • ✅ Admission date is on or before the Statement From date (FL6)
  • ✅ Admission date is on or before the discharge / Statement Thru date
  • ✅ For interim claims — admission date matches the original admission date from the first claim in the series
  • ✅ For corrected claims — Condition Code D4 is included and Frequency Code 7 is in the TOB
  • ✅ Claim run through scrubber with FL12 validation before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅
Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True
Use only after corrected claim submission fails
Appeal only when the admission date has already been corrected, verified against facility records, and the denial still persists due to payer-side processing or validation issues.
  • A corrected claim with the verified admission date has already been submitted and denied again
  • The admission date on the corrected claim is confirmed correct against ADT system records
  • The continued denial is due to a payer-side system or date validation error — not a data issue on the claim
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)
Recommended first action for most MA40 denials
Most MA40 denials are caused by missing or incorrect admission dates and are resolved through claim correction and resubmission.
  • The vast majority of MA40 denials resolve by populating or correcting FL12 and resubmitting
  • Do not appeal as a first step — confirm the admission date from the ADT or face sheet first
  • Use Frequency Code 7 and Condition Code D4 on the corrected claim

M44 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

Invalid Condition Code

Facility Billing / UB-04 · Inpatient & Outpatient
Common CARC Pairing
UB-04 (FL18-FL28) CO-16 Claim/service lacks information
What This Means
💡
What This Means

Condition Codes (Form Locators 18–28 on the UB-04) provide supplemental claim-level information that the payer needs to correctly adjudicate the claim — such as whether the claim is a correction, whether the patient had other insurance, whether an accident was involved, or whether a specific regulatory or billing exception applies.

ℹ️
Important Distinction
M44 does not mean the services are not covered. It means the payer's edit system detected a condition code that is missing, invalid, or conflicts with another field on the claim. In most cases this is resolved with a corrected claim — not an appeal. The specific condition code required depends entirely on the claim scenario, payer, and TOB.
Where to Report This Information
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional)
Professional claim reporting guidance
  • Non Billable — Condition codes are not reported on CMS-1500 professional claims
  • Non Billable — UB-04 condition code reporting requirements do not apply to professional claim forms
Professional Claims Guidance
Condition Codes are UB-04 institutional claim elements and are not submitted on CMS-1500 claims.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility Claims)
Facility claim reporting guidance
  • FL18–FL28 — Up to 11 condition codes can be reported on a single UB-04 claim, with one 2-character alphanumeric code per field
  • Format — Condition codes must align with payer, MSP, discharge, and occurrence-related claim data
Fields That Cross-Validate With FL18–FL28
FL4: TOB-specific condition codes apply
FL12: Accident dates must be ≥ admission date
FL38: MSP codes must match COB data
FL50: MSP codes must match payer
FL58–63: Insurance codes must match insured information
FL17: Hospice/SNF codes must match discharge status
FL66: Some condition codes impact DRG edits
⚠️
MSP Condition Code Validation — Common Sub-Error
If Medicare's Common Working File (CWF) shows an MSP record for the patient's date of service but the claim does not contain the appropriate MSP condition code, the claim may reject or suspend. Include the correct MSP condition code confirming Medicare is secondary, or submit a condition code explaining why another insurer does not apply (such as codes 09, 10, 11, 28, or 29).
#
Invalid Condition Code — Common Sub-Errors
Original Format Condition Name Example
18 Maiden Name Retained Disabled Medicare patient but no LGHP (large group health plan) applies — relevant to MSP working aged / disability rules
11 Disabled Beneficiary but No Large Group Health Plan Patient retains maiden name — name on claim may differ from enrollment records; prevents false identity mismatch denials
20 Beneficiary Requested Billing Patient requested the claim be submitted to Medicare even though coverage is not expected — required before issuing an ABN-based denial
Why This Happens
⚠️
INVALID CONDITION CODE
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Condition code denials occur when required codes are missing, invalid, outdated, conflicting, or not aligned with payer, TOB, or MSP requirements.
1
Missing Required Code
Required condition code omitted — for example, D4 missing on a corrected claim.
2
Invalid Code Entry
Invalid 2-digit code entered due to typo, extra character, or non-existent NUBC code.
3
Conflicting Codes
Mutually exclusive condition codes submitted together causing payer edit failures.
4
Missing MSP Code
MSP-related condition code missing when another primary payer exists.
5
Payer Policy Requirement
Payer-required condition code not added — such as code 20 for ABN billing.
6
Wrong TOB Mapping
Condition code submitted does not apply to the Type of Bill on the claim.
7
Interface Mapping Failure
EHR-to-billing interface failed to populate the required condition code into FL18–FL28.
8
Outdated / Retired Code
Retired or invalid NUBC condition code submitted that is no longer accepted by the payer.
How to Fix It — RARC M44: Invalid Condition Code
💡 What is RARC M44?
Your claim was denied because a Condition Code is missing, wrong, or doesn't apply to the services billed. Think of a Condition Code like a special flag on your claim — it tells the payer about unusual circumstances (like a patient having other insurance or a specific billing situation) that affect how the claim should be processed.
UB-04
FL 18–28
Institutional claims
CMS-1500
N/A
Mostly institutional use
837I
Loop 2300
HI segment
📋 Common Condition Codes That Trigger M44
Code
Meaning
04
Information only claim
07
Treatment of non-terminal condition for hospice patient
08
Billing for same-day services
31
Patient is student (full-time/day)
78
New coverage not implemented by HMO
1
Review the Condition Code Used
Did you use the right flag?
🔍 First — confirm whether a condition code was actually required, which code was used, and whether it matches the claim type and situation being billed.
  • RARC M44 = wrong or invalid condition code. The code submitted either doesn't exist, is outdated, or doesn't apply to the service type billed.
  • Condition codes are claim-type specific. A code valid on an inpatient UB-04 may be completely invalid on an outpatient or professional claim.
  • Check if the code is still active — CMS periodically retires condition codes; using a retired code triggers M44 just like using the wrong one.
  • Escalate to a senior biller or coder to confirm whether any condition code is required for this claim at all — not every claim needs one.
  • Reference the NUBC (National Uniform Billing Committee) official code set for current, valid condition codes and their applicable claim types.
2
Correct the Code & Resubmit
Fix the flag and resend the claim
✅ This is a correctable billing error — not a coverage denial. Replace or remove the invalid condition code and resubmit as a corrected claim for the fastest path to payment.
  • UB-04: Enter the corrected condition code in Form Locators 18–28. If no condition code is needed, leave those fields blank — do not substitute a placeholder.
  • 837I electronic: Report the corrected condition code in Loop 2300, HI segment. Confirm the correct qualifier precedes the code in the segment.
  • If the code was entered in error and no condition code applies, remove it entirely rather than replacing it with another code that may also not apply.
  • Corrected claim codes: UB-04 → set TOB frequency digit to "7" + enter original TCN in Box 64. CMS-1500 → Box 22, Resubmission Code "7" + original ICN.
  • ⚠️ Verify timely filing limits for corrected claims before resubmitting — payer deadlines for corrections may differ from original submission windows.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
Find out exactly what code they expect
📞 If the corrected claim is denied again with M44, call the payer's provider relations line. The issue may be a payer-specific code requirement that differs from standard NUBC guidelines.
  • Have ready: Original + corrected claim numbers, date of service, member ID, the condition code(s) used, claim type (inpatient/outpatient), and both remittance advices.
  • Ask the rep: "Which condition code is required for this claim type and service? Is the code I submitted not recognized in your system?"
  • Ask if the payer has a payer-specific condition code requirement that overrides the standard NUBC code set — some payers require proprietary codes.
  • Ask whether the denial is due to the code being invalid, inapplicable, or conflicting with another element on the claim (e.g., bill type, revenue code, or diagnosis).
  • 📝 Document the call: reference number, rep name, date, time, and the exact code or correction they advise.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Escalate and fight it officially
⚖️ If the payer upholds the M44 denial after a corrected claim and provider relations outreach, file a formal appeal demonstrating that the condition code submitted was valid, appropriate, and compliant with NUBC guidelines for the claim type billed.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, billed amount, and the condition code(s) in dispute.
  • Key statement: "Condition Code [XX] submitted on this claim is valid per the current NUBC code set and is applicable to the claim type and services billed. We appeal the M44 denial as the claim was compliant at submission."
  • Attach: Original + corrected claim copies, both remittance advices, NUBC reference documentation confirming the code's validity and applicability, and payer policy if obtained during the provider relations call.
  • Medicare deadline: File Redetermination with the MAC within 120 days of the denial date. Commercial payers: follow the appeal instructions on the EOB (typically 30–60 days).
  • 📌 Reference: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Pub 100-04, applicable chapter for the service type, and the NUBC Official UB-04 Data Specifications Manual.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Billing Edits
Stop M44 from happening across your entire claim volume
🔁 If M44 is appearing on multiple claims, this is a systemic billing configuration issue — not a one-off mistake. A condition code may be hardcoded incorrectly in your billing system, auto-populated by your EHR, or required by specific payers but missing from your templates.
  • Audit recent claims for the same condition code across multiple accounts. If the same invalid code is appearing repeatedly, it is likely hardcoded or auto-populated incorrectly in your billing system or EHR templates.
  • Review your claim templates by claim type (inpatient, outpatient, SNF, home health, etc.) and confirm condition codes are only populated when applicable — not defaulted on every claim.
  • Cross-reference the NUBC code set annually. Condition codes are updated periodically; a code valid last year may be retired or reassigned this year, triggering M44 on otherwise clean claims.
  • Build a pre-submission edit in your billing system that validates condition codes against the current NUBC-approved list and flags any code that does not match the claim type before submission.
  • Check payer-specific requirements. Some payers require condition codes not in the standard NUBC set — document these as payer-specific rules in your billing system so coders apply them consistently.
  • 🔒 Train your team: Ensure coders and billers understand that condition codes are situational — they should only be added when a specific circumstance applies, never as a default or filler field.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common actions that trigger repeat M44 denials
These errors commonly cause corrected claim failures, invalid condition code edits, and unnecessary claim delays.
  • Do not appeal before submitting a corrected claim with the required condition code added
  • Do not guess the condition code — use the payer's companion guide or call provider services if the required code is unclear
  • Do not submit the same claim again without identifying and correcting the specific condition code issue
  • Do not add a condition code that does not apply to the claim scenario — invalid or inapplicable codes can trigger additional edits
  • Do not omit D4 on a replacement corrected claim — this is the most common repeat M44 error
  • Do not carry a stale or default condition code forward from a billing template without verifying it applies to the current claim
  • Do not apply a retired NUBC condition code — verify the code is current before use
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting the condition code wastes timely filing days. M44 is a data integrity error — identify the specific required code, correct it, and resubmit with Frequency Code 7 and D4 before pursuing an appeal.
CONDITION CODE CHECKLIST
✅
CONDITION CODE CHECKLIST
FL18–FL28 pre-submission validation checklist

Before submitting any institutional claim, confirm all condition code validations are completed

  • ✅ All required condition codes for the TOB and payer have been identified and populated in FL18–FL28
  • ✅ All codes are valid 2-character codes from the current NUBC condition code set
  • ✅ No two mutually exclusive condition codes are present on the same claim
  • ✅ Condition codes are appropriate for the Type of Bill and care setting
  • ✅ MSP screening completed — if a CWF MSP record exists, the appropriate MSP condition code is included
  • ✅ For corrected claims — D4 is in FL18–FL28 and Frequency Code 7 is in the TOB
  • ✅ Payer companion guide reviewed for any proprietary condition code requirements
  • ✅ Billing templates audited to ensure default condition codes do not carry forward incorrectly
  • ✅ EDI 837I Loop 2300 HI*BG segment verified — condition codes are not dropped during claim export
  • ✅ Claim run through scrubber with condition code validation before submission
s
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅
Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True
Use only after corrected claim submission fails
Appeal only when the condition code has already been corrected, validated, and the denial still persists because of payer-side system edits or processing errors.
  • A corrected claim with the verified condition code has already been submitted and denied again
  • The condition code on the corrected claim is confirmed valid and appropriate for the claim scenario
  • The continued denial is due to a payer-side system edit or data error — not a missing or invalid code on your claim
  • Payer contact has confirmed the code is correct and the denial is a system issue on their end
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)
Recommended first action for most M44 denials
Most M44 denials are caused by missing, invalid, or inappropriate condition codes and are resolved through correction and claim resubmission.
  • The vast majority of M44 denials resolve by identifying the missing or invalid condition code, correcting it, and resubmitting
  • Do not appeal as a first step — identify the specific code required using the reference table or payer companion guide
  • Use Frequency Code 7 and Condition Code D4 on the corrected claim
  • If the required code is unclear — call the payer's provider services line before resubmitting

M34 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

Claim Lacks the CLIA Certification Number

Laboratory Billing · CMS-1500 Box 23 / UB-04 FL81 · Professional & Facility Lab Claims
Common CARC Pairing
CO-16 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 23 Lab Claims CPT 80000–89999
What This Means
🧪
What This Means

CLIA means Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments. Any facility — independent lab, physician office lab, hospital outreach lab, or clinic — that performs testing on human specimens for health assessment, diagnosis, treatment, or prevention of disease is required by federal law to hold a current CLIA certificate. When a claim includes laboratory procedure codes (typically CPT 80000–89999), the payer validates the submitted CLIA certification information before processing payment.

ℹ️
Important Distinction
M34 does not mean the lab tests are not covered or medically unnecessary. It is a regulatory compliance and data integrity error — the payer cannot confirm that the performing laboratory is federally certified to conduct the tests billed. This is almost always resolved with a corrected claim supplying the valid CLIA number. Do not appeal before correcting the claim.
Where the CLIA Number Goes on the Claim
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Professional laboratory claim reporting
  • Box 23 — Prior Authorization Number: The CLIA certification number is entered in Box 23 when billing laboratory services on the CMS-1500
  • Enter the 10-character CLIA number with no spaces, dashes, or qualifiers in the printed Box 23 field
  • EDI 837P equivalent: Loop 2300 REF*X4 — qualifier X4 with the 10-digit CLIA number as the reference identification
  • The CLIA number in Box 23 identifies the performing laboratory even if the ordering physician is billing
  • If the performing lab is a reference lab (send-out), the reference lab's CLIA number goes in Box 23 — not the ordering provider's CLIA

Field Label: Prior Authorization Number
CLIA Entry: 14D0000001 (no spaces/dashes)
EDI 837P: Loop 2300 REF*X4*14D0000001~
🏥
UB-04 (Facility / Hospital Lab Claims)
Facility laboratory claim reporting
  • FL81 — Attestation / Code-Code Field: On the UB-04, the CLIA number is typically reported in FL81 using qualifier X4 followed by the 10-character CLIA number
  • Some MACs and payers require the CLIA number in FL67 or payer-specific remark fields — always verify the payer companion guide
  • EDI 837I equivalent: Loop 2300 REF*X4 — same qualifier and format as the 837P
  • For hospital outpatient lab claims billed under the hospital's CLIA, use the hospital's CLIA number
  • For reference lab send-outs billed on a UB-04, use the reference lab's CLIA number

Qualifier: X4
CLIA Number: 14D0000001
EDI 837I: Loop 2300 REF*X4*14D0000001~
⚠️
Box 23 Conflict — Prior Authorization vs. CLIA Number
Box 23 on the CMS-1500 is a shared field used for both prior authorization numbers and CLIA numbers depending on the service type. On laboratory claims, Box 23 must carry the CLIA number — not a prior authorization number. If prior authorization is also required for the laboratory test, review the payer companion guide for dual submission instructions since some payers require a separate loop or note field.
Why This Happens
⚠️
INVALID / MISSING CLIA NUMBER
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
CLIA denials usually occur when the certificate number is missing, expired, incorrectly mapped, or submitted for the wrong performing laboratory.
1
Missing CLIA Number
Box 23 or FL81 left blank during claim entry — most common cause.
2
Auto-Population Failure
Billing system failed to auto-populate the CLIA number on laboratory claims.
3
Expired Certificate
Laboratory CLIA certificate expired before the date of service.
4
Wrong CLIA Number
CLIA number belongs to another lab, another location, or contains a typo.
5
Invalid CLIA Format
Incorrect format submitted with spaces, dashes, or invalid character count.
6
Missing Reference Lab CLIA
Performing reference lab CLIA not populated for send-out testing.
7
Wrong Site CLIA
Corporate CLIA used instead of the site-specific performing lab CLIA.
8
Interface Mapping Error
EHR-to-billing export failed to map the CLIA number into Box 23 or FL81.
9
Field Overwrite Issue
Prior authorization number entered in Box 23 overwrote the CLIA number field.
10
Outdated Claim Template
Template carried an expired or incorrect CLIA number that was never updated.
How to Fix It — RARC M34: Claim Lacks the CLIA Certification Number
💡 What is RARC M34?
Your claim was denied because a CLIA Certification Number is missing from the claim. Think of CLIA like a lab's operating license number — any facility that performs lab tests on human specimens must be certified under the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA). Payers require this number on lab claims to confirm the lab performing the test is legally certified to do so. No number = no payment.

Box 23
CLIA number field
UB-04
FL 51
Attending physician / CLIA
837P EDI
Loop 2300
REF segment (X4)
📋 Common Lab Services That Require a CLIA Number on the Claim
Test / Service
Who Needs CLIA
Blood panels / CBC / metabolic
Any lab performing the test in-house
Urinalysis / urine drug screening
Physician office lab or reference lab
Pap smears / cytology
Lab certified for cytology testing
COVID-19 / infectious disease PCR
CLIA-certified molecular testing lab
Glucose / cholesterol (POCT)

1
Locate Your CLIA Certification Number
It may already be on file — just not on the claim
🔍 Before anything else — find the CLIA number. M34 usually means it was simply left off the claim, not that the lab isn't certified. Check your records before assuming the certification is missing.
  • Check your CLIA certificate — it is physically issued by CMS and should be posted in your lab area. The 10-digit CLIA number is printed on the certificate.
  • Look up your CLIA number instantly on the CMS CLIA database at cms.gov/clia — search by facility name, address, or NPI.
  • Confirm which lab performed the test — if specimens were sent to a reference lab (e.g., Quest, LabCorp), the reference lab's CLIA number goes on the claim, not yours.
  • If your practice performs waived tests only (glucose, strep, flu), you still need a CLIA Certificate of Waiver — confirm you have one and locate that number.
  • ⚠️ If you cannot find a valid CLIA certificate for your facility, stop billing lab claims immediately and contact CMS to apply — performing lab tests without CLIA certification is a federal compliance violation.
2
Add the CLIA Number & Resubmit
Corrected claim — fastest path to payment
✅ This is a simple data entry fix. Add the correct CLIA number in the right field and resubmit as a corrected claim — do not submit as a brand new claim.
  • CMS-1500 (paper): Enter the 10-digit CLIA number in Box 23 (Prior Authorization Number field — used for CLIA on lab claims). Ensure it is formatted correctly with no spaces or dashes.
  • UB-04: Enter in FL 51 per the payer's instructions for institutional lab billing.
  • 837P electronic: Report in Loop 2300, REF segment using qualifier X4 (Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendment Number).
  • Corrected claim codes: CMS-1500 → Box 22, Resubmission Code "7" + original ICN/claim number. UB-04 → TOB frequency digit "7" + original TCN in Box 64.
  • ⚠️ Verify timely filing limits — payer deadlines for corrected claims vary. Do not delay resubmission while waiting for internal confirmations.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
Confirm the number is in their system correctly
📞 If the corrected claim still denies with M34, call the payer's provider relations line. The CLIA number may not be registered in their provider file or may be in the wrong field on the electronic claim.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, date of service, HCPCS/CPT lab code billed, the CLIA number submitted, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask the rep: "Was the CLIA number received on the claim? Is it registered in your provider file for our facility? Which field or segment do you require it in?"
  • Some payers require the CLIA number to be pre-registered in your provider enrollment file — even a correctly placed number on the claim will deny if it isn't on file with the payer first.
  • Ask whether the payer requires the performing lab's CLIA number vs. the billing provider's CLIA number — for reference lab claims this distinction matters and varies by payer.
  • 📝 Document: reference number, rep name, date, time, and the exact field or enrollment step they advise.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Escalate with CLIA certification proof attached
⚖️ If the payer upholds the M34 denial after a corrected claim and provider relations outreach, file a formal appeal attaching proof of active CLIA certification and demonstrating the number was correctly reported on the claim.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, facility name, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, CPT/HCPCS lab code, and the CLIA number in dispute.
  • Key statement: "CLIA Certification Number [XXXXXXXXXX] is active and valid for the test type billed. The number was reported in the correct field per payer and CMS billing guidelines. We appeal the M34 denial as the claim was compliant at submission."
  • Attach: Copy of active CLIA certificate, CMS CLIA database printout confirming active status, original claim, corrected claim, and both remittance advices.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with the MAC within 120 days of denial. Reference CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Pub 100-04, Chapter 16 (Laboratory Services).
  • Commercial payers: check EOB for appeal deadline — typically 30–180 days. Cite the payer's own lab billing guidelines if the CLIA field placement was per their provider manual.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Lab Billing Templates
One template fix stops M34 across every lab claim
🔁 If M34 is appearing on multiple claims, the CLIA number is not hardcoded into your billing system or claim template for lab claim types — or it's populating in the wrong field. This is a one-time fix that stops the denial permanently.
  • Hardcode the CLIA number into your billing system on all lab claim templates — it should auto-populate in the correct field (Box 23 / REF X4) on every lab claim without manual entry. Manual entry = human error = M34.
  • Set up separate templates by performing lab. If you use multiple reference labs, each lab's CLIA number must map to the correct claim template — a single generic template with your facility CLIA won't work for reference lab sends.
  • Audit your payer enrollment files annually. Confirm your CLIA number is on file with every payer you bill lab claims to — re-verify after any facility address change, ownership change, or CLIA renewal.
  • Add a pre-submission edit that flags any claim with a lab CPT code (80000–89999 series) that is missing a value in the CLIA number field before the claim is released to the payer.
  • Track CLIA certificate expiration. CLIA certificates must be renewed every two years — an expired certificate triggers denials just like a missing number. Put the expiration date in your compliance calendar with a 90-day advance reminder.
  • 🔒 Compliance reminder: Billing lab claims without a valid CLIA certificate is a federal violation under 42 CFR Part 493. Ensure your certificate is active, posted, and renewed on time — this is not just a billing issue.
Modifiers Relevant to Laboratory Claims & M34
🧪
Laboratory Modifier Reference Guide
Common modifiers related to laboratory claims, CLIA validation, and M34 denials
Modifier Description How It Relates to M34 / CLIA
QW CLIA-Waived Test Most important modifier for M34. Modifier QW must be appended to CPT codes for tests performed under a Certificate of Waiver. Without QW, the payer may expect a CoC/CoA CLIA number. With QW, the payer knows to validate against a CoW CLIA. Missing QW on a waived test can trigger M34 even when the CLIA number is present.
90 Reference (Outside) Laboratory Required when a provider bills for lab tests performed by a reference (send-out) laboratory. When modifier 90 is present, the CLIA number in Box 23 must belong to the reference lab — not the ordering provider. Forgetting to update the CLIA to the reference lab's number while using modifier 90 is a top M34 cause.
91 Repeat Clinical Diagnostic Laboratory Test Used when the same lab test is repeated on the same day. Each repeated test line still requires the same CLIA number in Box 23 — modifier 91 does not waive the CLIA requirement.
GZ Item or Service Expected to Be Denied as Not Reasonable and Necessary Used when submitting a lab claim without an ABN but the provider believes it may be denied for medical necessity. CLIA must still be present even on GZ-modified claims.
LR Laboratory Round Trip Used for specimen transport claims. The lab performing the test still requires a valid CLIA number on the associated service lines.
59 Distinct Procedural Service Used to unbundle lab services when separately performed. CLIA is required on each unbundled lab service line — modifier 59 does not override the CLIA requirement.
🔬
QW Modifier + CLIA Certificate of Waiver — Paired Requirement
Important: For waived tests, modifier QW and a valid Certificate of Waiver CLIA number must both be present. If either is missing, the claim will deny.

QW without a CoW CLIA number triggers M34. A CoW CLIA without QW may cause the payer's system to expect a higher-complexity certificate and deny for the wrong certificate type.

Always submit both together on every waived test line.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common CLIA billing and compliance mistakes that trigger M34 denials
These errors commonly cause laboratory claim denials, regulatory exposure, and repeat corrected claim failures.
  • Do not appeal before correcting the CLIA number on the claim — M34 is almost always a data correction, not a coverage dispute
  • Do not submit a corrected claim with the same blank, invalid, or expired CLIA number
  • Do not use the ordering physician's CLIA number on a reference lab send-out — the performing lab's CLIA must be used
  • Do not use a corporate or headquarters CLIA number for a satellite testing location that has its own site-specific CLIA
  • Do not begin billing laboratory services before the CLIA certificate is issued — a CLIA application in process is not a valid CLIA number
  • Do not enter dashes, spaces, or extra characters in the CLIA number field — exactly 10 characters, no formatting
  • Do not assume the billing system auto-populates Box 23 correctly — verify the CLIA number in the claim preview before submitting
  • Do not submit a Certificate of Waiver CLIA number for tests that require moderate or high-complexity certification
  • Do not put a prior authorization number in Box 23 without confirming that it does not overwrite the CLIA number requirement for lab claims
⚠️
Critical Compliance Reminder
Billing laboratory services without a valid, active CLIA number is not only a claim denial — it is a federal regulatory violation under CLIA (42 CFR Part 493). Repeated billing under an expired or invalid CLIA can trigger a CMS audit, civil monetary penalties, and exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid. Always verify CLIA status before billing.
CLIA VALIDATION CHECKLIST
✅
CLIA VALIDATION CHECKLIST
Laboratory claim pre-submission validation checklist

Before submitting any laboratory claim, confirm all CLIA validations are completed

  • ✅ CLIA number is populated in Box 23 (CMS-1500) or FL81 with X4 qualifier (UB-04) — not blank
  • ✅ CLIA number belongs to the performing laboratory — not the ordering provider
  • ✅ CLIA number is exactly 10 characters with no dashes, spaces, or special characters
  • ✅ CLIA certificate was active and not expired on the date of service — verified in QCOR
  • ✅ CLIA certificate type (CoW, CoC, CoA) covers the complexity level of the CPT codes being billed
  • ✅ For waived tests — Modifier QW appended to each waived CPT code AND a CoW CLIA number is in Box 23
  • ✅ For reference lab send-outs — Modifier 90 is on the claim line AND the reference lab's CLIA is in Box 23
  • ✅ For multi-site practices — site-specific CLIA used for the location that actually performed the test
  • ✅ Billing system configured to auto-populate the correct CLIA number — verified in claim preview before submission
  • ✅ CLIA expiration date tracked — renewal initiated well before expiration; no billing gap during renewal period
  • ✅ Payer companion guide reviewed — payer does not require CLIA to be pre-loaded in their provider portal
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅
Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True
Use only after corrected claim submission fails
Appeal only when the CLIA number has already been corrected, validated, and the denial still persists due to payer-side provider file or system validation issues.
  • A corrected claim with the valid, active CLIA number has already been submitted and denied again
  • The CLIA number is confirmed active on the date of service via QCOR lookup
  • The CLIA certificate type covers the complexity of the tests billed
  • The payer has confirmed via provider services that the denial is a system-side validation or provider file issue — not a problem with the claim data
  • A copy of the CLIA certificate is available to attach to the appeal as supporting documentation
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)
Recommended first action for most M34 denials
Most M34 denials are caused by missing, invalid, or expired CLIA numbers and are resolved through claim correction and resubmission.
  • The vast majority of M34 denials resolve by populating or correcting the CLIA number in Box 23 or FL81 and resubmitting
  • Do not appeal as a first step — verify the CLIA number via QCOR and correct the claim first
  • Use Resubmission Code 7 on the corrected claim
  • If the CLIA was expired on the DOS — do not resubmit without escalating to compliance first

Missing / Incomplete / Invalid Occurrence Code(s)

Facility Billing / UB-04 · Occurrence Codes (FL31–FL34) · Inpatient & Outpatient
Common CARC Pairing
CO-16 UB-04 FL31–FL34 Inpatient Outpatient SNF HHA
What This Means
📅
What This Means

Occurrence Codes on the UB-04 (Form Locators 31–34) are two-digit codes paired with a date that document specific events, accidents, or conditions related to the patient's claim — such as the date of an accident, the onset of symptoms, the date Medicare was notified of a hospice election, or the start of a home health episode. The claim cannot process correctly until the occurrence code issue is resolved.

ℹ️
Important Distinction
M45 does not mean the services are not covered. It is a data integrity error — the payer's edit system flagged a missing, invalid, or conflicting occurrence code that is required to correctly adjudicate the claim. In nearly all cases this is resolved with a corrected claim. The specific occurrence code required depends entirely on the clinical scenario, payer, and Type of Bill.
Where Occurrence Codes Live on the UB-04
📋
UB-04 Form Locators FL31–FL34
Occurrence code and date reporting
  • FL31–FL34: Each field holds one occurrence code + date pair — up to 4 occurrence codes per claim
  • Each occurrence code is exactly 2 characters (alphanumeric)
  • Each code must be paired with a date in MM/DD/YY format — a code without a date, or a date without a code, will trigger M45 edits
  • EDI 837I equivalent: Loop 2300 HI segment with qualifier BH — format: HI*BH:code:date~
  • Codes are defined in the NUBC UB-04 Data Specifications Manual
  • Order of occurrence codes on the claim does not matter — all available FL31–FL34 fields can be used in any sequence
  • If more than 4 occurrence codes are needed, use FL35–FL36 (Occurrence Span Codes) for date-range events
🔎
Cross-Validation Fields
Related UB-04 validation dependencies
  • FL4 — Type of Bill: Some occurrence codes are TOB-specific, including accident-related billing scenarios
  • FL12 — Admission Date: Occurrence dates preceding admission must align clinically and chronologically
  • FL6 — Statement Covers Period: Occurrence dates must fall within or before the statement period unless documenting pre-admission events
  • FL18–FL28 — Condition Codes: MSP occurrence codes must align with MSP condition code reporting
  • FL50 / FL38: Accident-related occurrence codes must align with payer and responsible party information
  • FL17 — Discharge Status: Hospice occurrence codes must align with discharge disposition and hospice TOB
  • FL35–FL36 — Occurrence Span Codes: Span codes represent date ranges while occurrence codes represent single event dates
UB-04 Occurrence Code Entry Format
FL31: Code | Date Example: 01 | 03/14/25 (Auto accident date)
FL32: Code | Date Example: 11 | 03/14/25 (Onset of symptoms)
FL33: Code | Date Example: 50 | 03/14/25 (Medicare Part A exhausted)
FL34: Code | Date (Leave blank if no fourth code needed)

EDI 837I Format:
HI*BH:01:20250314*BH:11:20250314*BH:50:20250314~
⚠️
Occurrence Code Date Pairing — Common Sub-Error
Every occurrence code submitted in FL31–FL34 must contain a matching occurrence date. Submitting a code without a valid date, or entering a date without an associated occurrence code, commonly triggers M45 edits, RTP status, or electronic claim rejection during payer validation.
Why This Happens
⚠️
INVALID / MISSING OCCURRENCE CODE
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Occurrence code denials usually happen when the code, paired date, format, or clinical event logic does not match payer or NUBC requirements.
1
Missing Occurrence Code
Required occurrence code omitted from FL31–FL34 — most common cause.
2
Missing Paired Date
Occurrence code submitted without its required paired date.
3
Date Without Code
Date populated in FL31–FL34 but no corresponding occurrence code selected.
4
Invalid Date Format
Occurrence date submitted in incorrect paper or EDI date format.
5
Invalid Event Date
Occurrence date falls outside the valid statement or clinical event period.
6
Invalid Occurrence Code
Retired, invalid, or typo-containing occurrence code submitted.
7
Wrong Code Type
Occurrence span code mistakenly entered in the occurrence code field.
8
Missing Accident Codes
Accident-related occurrence codes missing despite injury or trauma diagnosis codes.
9
Hospice / SNF Missing Dates
Required hospice or SNF occurrence codes and qualifying stay dates not submitted.
10
Therapy Date Missing
Therapy plan-of-care occurrence dates not included on the claim.
How to Fix It — RARC M45: Missing / Incomplete / Invalid Occurrence Code(s)
💡 What is RARC M45?
Your claim was denied because an Occurrence Code is missing, incomplete, or invalid. Think of an Occurrence Code like a date-stamped event note on your claim — it tells the payer about a specific event that happened (like an accident or insurance change) and when it occurred. Every occurrence code needs both a code AND a date — one without the other causes M45.
UB-04
FL 31–36
Institutional claims

Meaning
