1
Find the Wrong or Missing Code
Start with the remittance advice
🔍 Pull the EOB or 835 remittance. M45 means something is wrong — your job is to figure out whether the code is missing entirely, has no date, uses an invalid code, or doesn't apply to this claim type.
  • Check FL 31–36 on the UB-04. Each field needs both a code AND a date — submitting one without the other triggers M45.
  • Confirm the code is still active — CMS retires occurrence codes; an outdated code causes M45 just like a wrong one.
  • Verify the code matches the claim type — some codes are inpatient-only, others outpatient-only.
  • Ask a senior coder: "Is an occurrence code required for this visit, and which one?"
  • Reference the NUBC Official UB-04 Data Specifications Manual for the current, valid code list.
2
Fix the Code + Date & Resubmit
Corrected claim — not a brand new one
✅ This is a correctable billing error — not a coverage denial. Fix the occurrence code and/or date, then resubmit as a corrected claim for the fastest path to payment.
  • UB-04: Enter the correct code + date in FL 31–36. Both fields are required — code without date (or vice versa) will re-deny.
  • 837I electronic: Update the Loop 2300, HI segment. Confirm the correct qualifier precedes the code in the segment.
  • If no occurrence code is needed at all, leave FL 31–36 blank — do not substitute a placeholder code.
  • Corrected claim: UB-04 → set TOB frequency digit to "7" + enter original TCN in Box 64.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits for corrected claims before resubmitting — payer deadlines may differ from original submission windows.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
Find out exactly what they expect
📞 If the corrected claim still gets M45, call the payer's provider relations line. The issue may be a payer-specific requirement that differs from standard NUBC guidelines.
  • Have ready: Original + corrected claim numbers, date of service, member ID, occurrence code(s) used, claim type, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask the rep: "Which occurrence code and date format is required for this claim type? Is the code I submitted not recognized in your system?"
  • Ask if the denial is due to the code being invalid, missing a date, or conflicting with the bill type, revenue code, or diagnosis on the claim.
  • 📝 Document the call: reference number, rep name, date, time, and the exact correction advised.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Escalate and fight it officially
⚖️ If the payer upholds the M45 denial after a corrected claim and provider relations outreach, file a formal appeal proving the occurrence code and date submitted were valid and compliant with NUBC guidelines.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, billed amount, and the occurrence code(s) in dispute.
  • Key statement: "Occurrence Code [XX] with date [MM/DD/YYYY] submitted on this claim is valid per the current NUBC code set and applicable to the claim type and services billed. We appeal the M45 denial as the claim was compliant at submission."
  • Attach: Original + corrected claim copies, both remittance advices, and NUBC reference confirming the code's validity and applicability.
  • Medicare deadline: File Redetermination with the MAC within 120 days of the denial date. Commercial payers: follow appeal instructions on the EOB (typically 30–60 days).
  • 📌 Reference: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Pub 100-04 and the NUBC Official UB-04 Data Specifications Manual.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Billing Templates
Stop M45 from happening across your entire claim volume
🔁 If M45 is appearing on multiple claims, this is a systemic template or configuration issue — a wrong code is hardcoded, a date field is being skipped, or occurrence codes are auto-populating from an outdated EHR template.
  • Audit recent denials for the same occurrence code error across multiple accounts. If the same mistake repeats, it's in your template — not a one-off.
  • Check claim templates by type (inpatient, outpatient, SNF, home health). Occurrence codes must always include a date — build that as a required paired field in your system.
  • Update codes annually. NUBC refreshes occurrence codes each year; a retired code auto-populating from an old template will keep triggering M45 on otherwise clean claims.
  • Build a pre-submission edit that validates occurrence code + date pairs before claims go out — flag any code submitted without a corresponding date.
  • Document payer-specific rules. If a payer requires a non-standard occurrence code, save it as a payer rule in your billing system so billers apply it consistently.
  • 🔒 Train your team: Occurrence codes are event-specific — only add them when the real-world event actually happened. Never use them as default fillers.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common occurrence code and date errors that trigger repeat M45 denials
These mistakes commonly cause corrected claim failures, invalid occurrence code edits, and repeat data integrity denials.
  • Do not appeal before submitting a corrected claim with the required occurrence code and date added
  • Do not submit the same corrected claim with the same missing or invalid code
  • Do not enter an occurrence code without its paired date — an unpaired code will deny again with M45
  • Do not enter a date without a corresponding occurrence code — an unpaired date is equally invalid
  • Do not use an occurrence span code number in the occurrence code field (FL31–FL34) — span codes belong in FL35–FL36 with a date range, not a single date
  • Do not guess the occurrence code — use the scenario reference table above or the payer companion guide; incorrect codes cause additional edits
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Appealing before correcting the occurrence code wastes timely filing days and may forfeit your right to correct the claim. M45 is a data integrity error — identify the specific required code and date, correct the claim, and resubmit with Frequency Code 7 and Condition Code D4 before pursuing an appeal.
OCCURRENCE CODE CHECKLIST
✅
OCCURRENCE CODE CHECKLIST
FL31–FL34 pre-submission validation checklist

Before submitting any UB-04 claim, confirm all occurrence code validations are completed

  • ✅ All required occurrence codes for the TOB, payer, and clinical scenario are identified and entered in FL31–FL34
  • ✅ Every occurrence code has its paired date — no unpaired codes or unpaired dates
  • ✅ Dates are in MM/DD/YY format (paper) or MMDDYYYY format (EDI 837I) and Therapy claims include plan of care dates (OC 17/18/19) and treatment start dates (OC 35/44/45)
  • ✅ All dates are sourced from supporting documentation — accident reports, face sheets, therapy plans, hospice certifications, discharge summaries
  • ✅ Occurrence dates are clinically plausible and fall within the valid range relative to the DOS and admission date | Single-date events are in FL31–FL34 (occurrence codes); date-range events are in FL35–FL36
  • ✅ Accident-related claims include the correct accident occurrence code (OC 01–06) matching the type of accident and Hospice claims include both OC 51 (election date) and OC 27 (certification date) and SNF claims include qualifying stay dates (OC 70 or OSC M0) from the prior hospital admission
  • ✅ Claim run through scrubber with occurrence code and date validation before submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct
✅
Appeal Only When ALL of These Are True
Use only after corrected claim submission fails
Appeal only when the occurrence code and paired date have already been corrected, validated, and the denial still persists due to payer-side system edit or adjudication issues.
  • A corrected claim with the verified occurrence code and paired date has already been submitted and denied again
  • The occurrence code and date are confirmed correct against source documentation
  • The continued denial is due to a payer-side system edit error — not a data problem on the claim
  • Payer contact has confirmed the code is correct and the denial is a system issue on their end
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most Cases)
Recommended first action for most M45 denials
Most M45 denials are caused by missing, invalid, or mismatched occurrence codes and dates and are resolved through correction and claim resubmission.
  • The vast majority of M45 denials resolve by identifying the missing or invalid occurrence code and date, correcting the claim, and resubmitting
  • Do not appeal as a first step — identify the required code using the scenario reference table or payer companion guide
  • Use Frequency Code 7 and Condition Code D4 on the corrected claim
  • If the required code is unclear — call the payer's provider services line before resubmitting

M62 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-197

Missing Treatment Authorization Code

Prior Authorization / Pre-Certification · Professional & Facility Claims · CMS-1500 & UB-04
Common CARC Pairing
CO-197 CO-15 CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 23 FL63
What This Means
📋
What This Means

M62 means the payer's system could not find a valid, matching treatment authorization (also called a Prior Authorization or Pre-Auth) number on the claim. Either the authorization number was not submitted at all, it was entered incorrectly, it belongs to a different patient or service, it has expired, or the service billed does not match what was actually authorized. The payer cannot pay the claim until it can verify that the service was approved in advance.

ℹ️
Think of it this way — What is a Prior Authorization?
Before certain procedures, tests, or specialist visits happen, the insurance company requires the provider to ask for permission in advance. That "permission" is called a Prior Authorization (PA). The payer gives back an authorization number — a unique code that proves the service was approved. That number must be reported on the claim in a specific field. M62 fires when that number is missing, wrong, or does not match what the payer approved.
⚠️
M62 Is NOT Always a Billing Error
Sometimes the authorization number is correct but the payer's system has a data entry issue on their end, or the authorization was not properly linked to the claim. Always confirm the auth number before assuming it is a billing mistake.
Where the Authorization Number Goes on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional / Office Claims)
Professional authorization reporting guidance
  • Box 23 — Prior Authorization Number: Dedicated field for the PA number on the CMS-1500. Enter only the authorization number with no extra text or leading/trailing spaces.
  • The authorization number must match exactly as issued by the payer, including letters, dashes, and leading zeros.
  • For multi-date services, verify whether the payer requires a separate authorization per DOS or authorization period.
  • Box 24B — Place of Service: The POS billed must match the setting approved in the authorization request.
  • Box 24D — Procedure Code: CPT/HCPCS billed must match the exact procedure authorized by the payer.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility / Hospital Claims)
Facility authorization reporting guidance
  • FL63 — Treatment Authorization Code: Field used for prior authorization numbers on the UB-04. Formatting requirements may vary by payer.
  • FL4 — Type of Bill (TOB): The TOB must align with the authorized service setting or level of care.
  • FL42 / FL44 — Revenue & Procedure Codes: Revenue and CPT/HCPCS codes must match the services approved under the authorization.
  • FL67 — Principal Diagnosis: Many payers validate the authorization against the diagnosis originally submitted for approval.
✅
Authorization Entry Accuracy — Quick Tip
Many payers treat authorization numbers as case-sensitive values. If the payer issued AUTH-2024-88341 and the claim is submitted as auth2024-88341, the authorization validation may fail. Always copy the authorization number exactly as issued by the payer.
Why This Happens
⚠️
INVALID / MISSING AUTHORIZATION NUMBER
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
Authorization denials usually occur when the auth number is missing, expired, mismatched to the billed service, or not linked correctly by the payer.
1
Missing Authorization
Authorization number never entered in Box 23 or FL63 — most common cause.
2
Incorrect Auth Number
Authorization entered with typo, missing digit, extra spaces, or incorrect formatting.
3
Wrong Patient / Claim Auth
Authorization from another patient or previous claim copied onto the current claim.
4
Communication Breakdown
Authorization obtained but never communicated to billing before claim submission.
5
Expired Authorization
Date of service falls outside the approved authorization validity period.
6
Wrong Procedure Authorized
Authorization approved for a different CPT/HCPCS code than what was billed.
7
Units / Visits Mismatch
Billed units or visits exceeded the quantity approved on the authorization.
8
Provider NPI Mismatch
Rendering or billing provider NPI does not match the provider tied to the authorization.
9
Wrong Place of Service
Authorization approved for a different place of service than what was billed.
10
Different Rendering Provider
Service performed by a covering or substitute provider not tied to the authorization.
How to Fix It — RARC M62: Missing Treatment Authorization Code
💡 What is RARC M62?
Your claim was denied because a Treatment Authorization Code is missing from the claim. Think of it like a permission slip number — before certain services are performed, the payer must approve them and gives you an authorization number. If that number isn't on the claim, the payer has no proof the service was pre-approved and will not pay.
UB-04
FL 63
Treatment Auth. Code
CMS-1500
Box 23
Prior Auth. Number
837I / 837P
Loop 2300
REF segment (G1)
📋 Common Services That Require a Treatment Authorization Code
Service Type
Why Auth Is Required
Inpatient admissions
Payer must approve before or within 24–48 hrs of admit
Elective surgeries
Pre-authorization required before procedure date
Specialty referrals (HMO)
PCP referral auth needed to see a specialist
High-cost imaging (MRI, PET)
Radiology management programs require prior auth
DME / home health / SNF
Post-acute services almost always require auth
1
Check If an Auth Was Obtained
The number may exist — just not on the claim
🔍 Before anything else — check whether a prior authorization was actually requested and approved. M62 only means the number is missing from the claim. The auth may already exist in your system.
  • Search your authorization management system or EHR for the patient, date of service, and service type — the auth number may already be on file.
  • Check the original referral or order — the auth number is often printed on the approval letter or fax from the payer.
  • Confirm the auth covers the exact service billed — procedure code, service dates, and facility must all match the approved auth.
  • If no auth was obtained, determine whether one was actually required for this specific payer, plan type, and service — not every service requires prior auth on every plan.
  • Check the payer's online portal — many payers allow you to look up active authorizations by member ID and service date.
2
Add the Auth Number & Resubmit
Fastest fix if the auth already exists
✅ If the authorization exists but wasn't on the claim, this is a simple data entry fix. Add the auth number and resubmit as a corrected claim — do not submit as a new claim.
  • UB-04: Enter the authorization number in Form Locator 63 (Treatment Authorization Code).
  • CMS-1500: Enter the authorization number in Box 23 (Prior Authorization Number).
  • 837I / 837P: Report in Loop 2300, REF segment using qualifier G1 (Prior Authorization Number).
  • Corrected claim: UB-04 → TOB frequency digit "7" + original TCN in Box 64. CMS-1500 → Box 22, Resubmission Code "7" + original ICN.
  • ⚠️ Confirm timely filing limits for corrected claims — do not let the deadline pass while tracking down the auth number.
3
No Auth on File? Request Retro Authorization
Some payers allow backdated approval
📞 If the service was performed but no auth was ever obtained, call the payer immediately. Many payers allow a retroactive authorization request — especially for urgent, emergent, or clinically necessary services.
  • Call the payer's prior authorization line (not provider relations). Explain the service was rendered and request a retroactive auth review.
  • Have ready: Member ID, date of service, procedure/diagnosis codes, ordering provider NPI, place of service, and clinical notes supporting medical necessity.
  • Ask the payer: "What is your retro auth policy and deadline?" Most payers have a strict window (e.g., 30–90 days from date of service) — act fast.
  • If retro auth is approved, get the authorization number in writing, then resubmit the corrected claim with the number in the appropriate field.
  • 📝 Document everything: call reference number, rep name, date, time, and outcome of the retro auth request.
4
Retro Auth Denied? File a Formal Appeal
Fight it with medical necessity documentation
⚖️ If the payer denies retro auth or upholds the M62 denial, file a formal appeal arguing the service was medically necessary and the lack of prior auth should not override the patient's right to covered benefits.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, billed amount, and procedure/diagnosis codes.
  • Key statement: "The service billed was medically necessary and covered under the patient's benefit plan. The absence of a prior authorization number on the claim does not negate the medical necessity or coverage of the service rendered."
  • Attach: Clinical notes, physician orders, medical necessity documentation, original claim, remittance advice, and any retro auth denial letter received.
  • Medicare: File Redetermination with the MAC within 120 days. Commercial: check EOB for deadline (typically 30–60 days).
  • 📌 For emergent services, cite EMTALA obligations and the payer's own plan language — most plans cannot deny emergent care solely for missing prior auth.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your Auth Workflow
Stop M62 before it hits the payer
🔁 If M62 is appearing across multiple claims, you have a front-end authorization workflow gap — either auths aren't being obtained before service, auth numbers aren't being captured in the patient account, or they're not flowing through to the claim at billing time.
  • Build an auth requirement matrix by payer and service type. Document which payers require auth for which CPT/procedure codes and post it where schedulers and billers can reference it daily.
  • Make auth verification a scheduling checkpoint. Before any appointment is confirmed for an auth-required service, the auth number must be on file — no auth, no schedule confirmation.
  • Store the auth number in the patient account at time of approval so it auto-populates onto the claim at billing — never rely on manual entry at claim creation.
  • Add a pre-submission claim edit that flags any claim for an auth-required service type that is missing a value in the auth number field — catch it before it goes out.
  • Audit auth expiration dates. A valid auth used on a claim after its expiration date will also deny — ensure the auth covers the actual date of service, not just the originally scheduled date.
  • 🔒 Train schedulers and front desk staff: Auth is a revenue cycle responsibility that starts at scheduling — by the time the claim hits billing, it's too late to prevent the denial.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common authorization and referral mistakes that trigger repeat M62 denials
These mistakes commonly cause repeat authorization denials, corrected claim failures, and unnecessary appeal rejections.
  • Do not appeal before first confirming the authorization number and correcting the claim — an appeal on a missing auth will still be denied without proof of authorization
  • Do not resubmit the exact same claim with the same blank or incorrect Box 23/FL63 — the denial will repeat
  • Do not assume the payer has the auth on file without verifying — always confirm via portal or phone before resubmitting
  • Do not use an authorization number obtained for a different service, different patient, or different provider
  • Do not let the timely filing deadline pass while waiting for authorization research — take action in parallel
⚠️
Critical Reminder
Submitting an appeal for M62 without attaching a copy of the authorization approval letter or portal screenshot is the most common reason appeals on this denial are rejected. Always include proof of authorization when appealing.
AUTHORIZATION CHECKLIST
✅
AUTHORIZATION CHECKLIST
Pre-submission authorization validation checklist

Before submitting any authorized service, confirm all authorization validations are completed

  • ✅ Authorization number confirmed on payer portal before claim submission
  • ✅ Auth number entered character-by-character in Box 23 (CMS-1500) or FL63 (UB-04) — no extra spaces, no typos
  • ✅ Date of service falls within the authorized date range
  • ✅ Procedure code on claim exactly matches the authorized procedure code
  • ✅ Place of service / Type of Bill matches the setting that was authorized
  • ✅ Rendering provider NPI matches the provider listed on the authorization
  • ✅ Number of units billed does not exceed the number of units authorized
  • ✅ Authorization was not cancelled or voided before the date of service
  • ✅ Authorization team confirmed auth approval and communicated the number to billing before claim submission
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Use only after authorization accuracy is fully validated
Appeal only when authorization was valid, correctly submitted, and the denial occurred because of payer-side adjudication or system processing failure.
  • A valid authorization was obtained before the date of service and the number was submitted correctly on the original claim
  • You have verified via the payer portal that the auth was active, matched the procedure, provider, and dates — and the claim data was correct
  • The payer denied it anyway — this indicates a payer-side system error and an appeal with the authorization approval documentation should be submitted
  • Always attach the authorization approval letter or portal screenshot to the appeal
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most M62 Cases)
Recommended first action for most M62 denials
Most M62 denials are caused by missing, invalid, expired, or incorrectly submitted authorization numbers and are resolved through correction and resubmission.
  • Most M62 denials are caused by a missing or incorrect auth number in Box 23 or FL63 — fix the field and resubmit with Resubmission Code 7
  • If the service was provided but no auth was ever obtained, work with the clinical team on a retroactive auth request before resubmitting
  • If the auth has expired, request an extension from the payer and resubmit once approved
  • Do not appeal as a first step — correct the root cause first and escalate to appeal only after a corrected claim is also denied

N4 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

Missing Prior Insurance Carrier(s) Explanation of Benefits (EOB)

Coordination of Benefits (COB) · Secondary & Tertiary Billing · CMS-1500 & UB-04
Common CARC Pairing
CO-16 CO-22 COB CMS-1500 UB-04 Box 11 FL50–FL65
What This Means
🧾
What This Means

N4 means the secondary or tertiary payer (the insurance company you are currently billing) is saying: "We can see this patient has other insurance. Before we pay our share, we need to see proof of what that other insurance already paid — or decided not to pay — and why." That proof is called an Explanation of Benefits (EOB), also known as a Remittance Advice (RA). The EOB from the primary payer was either missing from the claim, was attached but had incomplete information, or the data entered in the COB fields on the claim did not match what the secondary payer expected to see.

ℹ️
Key Concept — What is Coordination of Benefits (COB)?
When a patient has more than one insurance plan, the plans have rules about who pays first (primary), who pays second (secondary), and who pays third (tertiary). This process is called Coordination of Benefits (COB). The secondary payer will only process the claim after the primary payer has already made a decision. The EOB from the primary payer is the document that tells the secondary payer: what was billed, what the primary payer allowed, what the primary payer paid, what adjustments were made, and what patient responsibility remains. Without that complete EOB data, the secondary payer cannot calculate their payment obligation — so they deny with N4.
⚠️
N4 Is Almost Always Fixable — It Is a Data Issue, Not a Coverage Issue
N4 does not mean the secondary insurance will not pay. It means the claim is on hold because the COB information is missing or does not match. Correct the EOB data on the claim and resubmit — in most cases the secondary will process and pay their portion.
Where to Report the Primary EOB Data on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (Professional Claims)
Professional COB / secondary billing guidance
  • Box 11 — Insured's Policy Group or FECA Number: Enter the primary insured's policy/group number exactly as issued by the primary payer.
  • Box 11a — Insured DOB & Sex: Must match the primary insured demographics on file with the primary payer.
  • Box 11b — Other Claim ID: Used to report the primary payer claim number or EOB reference number.
  • Box 11c — Insurance Plan Name: Enter the primary insurance plan name exactly as shown on the EOB or insurance card.
  • Box 11d — Another Health Benefit Plan?: Must be marked YES when secondary coverage exists.
  • Box 29 — Amount Paid: Enter the exact dollar amount paid by the primary payer.
✅
CMS-1500 COB Validation Tip
Box 29 must contain the exact primary paid amount in dollars. Leaving Box 29 blank, entering an incorrect amount, or reporting $0.00 when payment was issued is the most common cause of N4 COB denials on CMS-1500 claims.
🏥
UB-04 (Facility / Hospital Claims)
Institutional COB / secondary billing guidance
  • FL50 — Payer Name: Line A = primary payer, Line B = secondary payer, Line C = tertiary payer.
  • FL51 — Health Plan ID: Must contain valid payer IDs recognized by the clearinghouse and payer system.
  • FL54 — Prior Payments: Enter the exact amount paid by the primary or prior payer.
  • FL56 — NPI: Billing provider NPI must match the provider recognized by the primary payer.
  • FL58–FL63 — Insured Information: Patient and insured details must match the primary EOB exactly.
  • FL64 — Document Control Number: Report the primary payer claim number or document control number from the EOB.
  • FL65 — Employer Name: Required when the primary coverage is employer-sponsored or MSP-related.
✅
UB-04 COB Validation Tip
FL54 (Prior Payments) must exactly match the payment amount shown on the primary EOB. Blank payment fields or mismatched payment amounts are one of the leading causes of N4 denials on UB-04 claims.
Why This Happens
⚠️
INVALID / MISSING PRIMARY EOB INFORMATION
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
COB/EOB denials usually occur when primary payer payment details are missing, mismatched, incomplete, or submitted in the wrong payer order.
1
Missing EOB Amount
Box 29 or FL54 left blank — primary payer paid amount not entered on the claim.
2
COB Data Not Entered
Primary EOB received but COB information never transferred into claim fields.
3
Claim Submitted Too Early
Secondary claim submitted before primary payer finished adjudication.
4
Primary Not Billed First
Claim billed directly to secondary without first processing through the primary payer.
5
Payment Amount Mismatch
Paid amount entered does not exactly match the amount on the primary EOB.
6
Wrong Primary Payer Info
Primary payer name or ID does not match the secondary payer's COB records.
7
Wrong EOB Attached
Incorrect patient's or incorrect date-of-service EOB attached to the claim.
8
Zero Pay Explanation Missing
Primary denial or zero-pay reason not communicated correctly to the secondary payer.
9
Incorrect COB Order
Primary and secondary payer sequence submitted incorrectly.
10
Terminated Primary Coverage
Primary insurance terminated but claim still billed as a COB claim.
How to Fix It — RARC N4: Missing Prior Insurance Carrier(s) Explanation of Benefits (EOB)
💡 What is RARC N4?
Your claim was denied because the primary (or other prior) insurance carrier's EOB is missing. Think of it like paying at a restaurant — if someone else is supposed to pay first, the second payer won't cover the bill until they see proof of what the first payer paid (or denied). The EOB is that proof of what the primary insurance already did. Without it, the secondary payer won't process your claim.
UB-04
FL 50–65
Other payer info fields
CMS-1500
Box 11 / 29
Other insurance / amount paid
837I / 837P
Loop 2320
Other subscriber info
📋 Common Situations That Trigger N4
Situation
Why EOB Is Required
Patient has two insurance plans
Secondary payer needs primary's payment/denial details
Medicare as secondary (MSP)
Medicare requires primary payer EOB before processing
Workers' comp or auto insurance primary
Liability payer EOB needed before health plan pays
Medicaid as payer of last resort
All prior payer EOBs must be submitted with claim
Tricare / CHAMPVA secondary
Primary commercial EOB required before Tricare pays
1
Confirm the Patient's Insurance Order
Who is primary — and did they pay first?
🔍 N4 means the payer you billed is not the primary carrier — or they believe another payer should have been billed first. Start by confirming the correct coordination of benefits (COB) order for this patient on the date of service.
  • Review the patient's insurance on file — confirm which plan is primary and which is secondary based on COB rules (birthday rule, employer vs. individual plan, Medicare Secondary Payer rules, etc.).
  • Verify the primary claim was actually submitted and adjudicated before billing the secondary — N4 often fires simply because the secondary was billed too soon.
  • Confirm the primary payer's EOB or 835 remittance is on file for this date of service — check your billing system, patient account, and document storage.
  • If the patient has Medicare as secondary, confirm the primary payer adjudicated first per Medicare Secondary Payer (MSP) guidelines — Medicare will not process until the primary EOB is attached.
  • Ask the patient directly if needed — patients sometimes have coverage through a spouse's employer or a secondary plan they didn't mention at registration.
2
Attach the EOB & Resubmit
Include primary payer details on the corrected claim
✅ Once you have the primary EOB, resubmit the claim as a corrected or crossover claim with the primary payer's payment details populated in the correct fields — the EOB data goes on the claim, not just attached separately.
  • UB-04: Enter primary payer name, paid amount, and adjustment reason codes in FL 50–65 (Other Payer fields). Attach the primary EOB as a paper attachment if submitting paper.
  • CMS-1500: Complete Box 11 (other insurance info) and Box 29 (amount paid by primary). Attach EOB if submitting paper.
  • 837I / 837P electronic: Populate Loop 2320 (Other Subscriber Information) with primary payer paid amount, claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs), and payer ID.
  • Medicare crossover claims often route automatically — if the primary is a Medicare Advantage or major commercial plan, verify the claim crossed over electronically before resubmitting manually.
  • ⚠️ Check timely filing limits for secondary claims — many payers start the clock from the primary EOB date, not the original date of service.
3
Can't Get the Primary EOB? Call the Primary Payer
Track down the missing document
📞 If the primary EOB isn't in your system, call the primary payer's provider relations line to confirm claim status and request a copy of the remittance. Do not wait — timely filing clocks are running on the secondary claim.
  • Have ready: Patient name, member ID (primary plan), date of service, claim number if previously submitted, and the procedure/diagnosis codes billed.
  • Ask: "Was this claim received and adjudicated? Can you send a copy of the remittance or EOB to our provider portal?"
  • If the primary claim was never received, submit it immediately — you cannot bill secondary until primary adjudicates. Track the timely filing deadline for the primary payer too.
  • If the primary denied the claim, you still need that denial EOB — the secondary payer needs to see the denial reason to determine their own liability.
  • 📝 Log the call: reference number, rep name, date, time, and whether the EOB was sent or the claim needs to be resubmitted to primary first.
4
Still Denied? File a Formal Appeal
Escalate with full COB documentation
⚖️ If the secondary payer upholds the N4 denial even after you've provided the primary EOB, file a formal appeal with complete coordination of benefits documentation proving primary adjudication occurred before the secondary claim was submitted.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, both member IDs (primary + secondary), claim numbers, date of service, billed amount, and primary payer paid/denied amount.
  • Key statement: "Primary carrier [Payer Name] adjudicated this claim on [date], paying $[amount] / issuing denial for [reason]. The attached EOB confirms prior adjudication. We appeal the N4 denial as all required COB documentation has been provided."
  • Attach: Primary EOB / 835 remittance, original secondary claim, secondary remittance showing N4 denial, and proof of timely filing to both payers.
  • Medicare MSP appeals: File Redetermination with the MAC within 120 days. Reference CMS Medicare Secondary Payer Manual, Pub 100-05.
  • Commercial payers: follow appeal deadline on the secondary EOB — typically 30–180 days depending on the plan.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your COB Workflow
Stop N4 before it hits the secondary payer
🔁 If N4 appears across multiple accounts, your COB (Coordination of Benefits) process has a gap — secondary claims are going out before primary EOBs are received, or primary payer details aren't being captured and attached correctly at billing.
  • Never bill secondary until the primary EOB is in hand. Build a workflow rule: secondary claim cannot be created or submitted until the primary 835 / EOB is received and posted to the account.
  • Capture COB order at registration. Front desk staff must identify all active insurance plans and record the correct primary / secondary order before the patient is seen — not at billing time.
  • Verify COB at every visit for patients with multiple insurances — coverage order can change with life events (job change, Medicare eligibility, new spouse coverage). Never assume last visit's order is still correct.
  • Add a pre-submission edit for secondary claims that checks whether a primary EOB amount is populated in Loop 2320 (837) or FL 54 (UB-04) before the claim is released — missing value = hold for EOB.
  • Track crossover claims separately. For Medicare/Medicaid crossovers, confirm the claim crossed automatically before manually resubmitting — duplicate submission causes its own denial cascade.
  • 🔒 Train your billing team: COB order determines who gets billed in what sequence — billing secondary first or simultaneously with primary is one of the most common and avoidable causes of N4.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common COB and secondary billing mistakes that trigger repeat N4 denials
These mistakes commonly cause coordination of benefits failures, secondary claim denials, and payer sequencing errors.
  • Do not submit to the secondary payer before the primary payer has fully processed and issued an EOB — the secondary will deny with N4 every time
  • Do not leave Box 29 (CMS-1500) or FL54 (UB-04) blank or enter $0.00 unless the primary truly paid nothing and you have the denial EOB to prove it
  • Do not estimate or approximate the primary paid amount — copy the exact dollar figure from the primary EOB, to the cent
  • Do not appeal N4 before correcting and resubmitting the claim with proper COB data — an appeal without the complete primary EOB information will be denied again
  • Do not assume the clearinghouse automatically forwards the primary EOB to the secondary — in most cases the billing team must manually populate the COB fields from the primary remittance
  • Do not ignore MSP rules — if another payer should be primary, billing Medicare or Medicaid first creates compliance risk beyond just a denial
⚠️
Critical Reminder
The most common N4 mistake is submitting a crossover or secondary claim with Box 29 or FL54 blank because the biller assumed the primary EOB would attach automatically. It does not. Every COB field must be manually verified and populated from the primary remittance before the secondary claim goes out.
COB / SECONDARY CLAIM CHECKLIST
✅
COB / SECONDARY CLAIM CHECKLIST
Pre-submission coordination of benefits validation checklist

Before submitting any secondary or COB claim, confirm all coordination of benefits validations are completed

  • ✅ Primary payer's EOB has been received and is for the correct patient, DOS, and service line
  • ✅ Primary paid amount entered exactly in Box 29 (CMS-1500) or FL54 (UB-04) — matched cent-for-cent to the primary EOB and If secondary payer requires paper EOB attachment — copy of primary EOB is included with the claim
  • ✅ Primary payer name (Box 11c / FL50) and payer ID (FL51) are correct and recognizable to the secondary payer
  • ✅ Primary claim number / document control number entered in Box 11b (CMS-1500) or FL64 (UB-04)
  • ✅ Insured information (Box 11a–11d / FL58–FL63) matches the primary insurance card and EOB exactly
  • ✅ COB order confirmed — primary is actually primary and secondary is actually secondary per Birthday Rule, MSP rules, or plan COB provision
  • ✅ If primary denied the claim — denial EOB is documented and denial reason is communicated correctly on the secondary claim and For Medicare MSP situations — MSP status verified via CMS eligibility portal or HIQA before submission and Secondary payer's timely filing deadline from primary EOB date confirmed — claim is within the window
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Use only after COB data accuracy is fully validated
Appeal only when all COB information was submitted correctly, supporting EOB documentation was attached, and the denial still occurred because of payer-side coordination or adjudication issues.
  • All COB fields were populated correctly on the original claim — Box 29 or FL54 had the exact primary paid amount, payer name and ID were correct, and insured info matched
  • A copy of the primary EOB was attached where required and the claim data matched it exactly
  • The secondary payer denied it anyway — this indicates a payer-side system or COB data issue and an appeal with the primary EOB documentation should be submitted
  • Always attach the complete primary EOB or remittance advice to the appeal — without it, the appeal will be denied
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most N4 Cases)
Recommended first action for most N4 denials
Most N4 denials are caused by incomplete, incorrect, or missing COB information and are resolved through claim correction and resubmission with accurate primary EOB data.
  • Most N4 denials are caused by a blank Box 29 or FL54, or by COB fields that were not populated from the primary EOB — correct the fields and resubmit with Resubmission Code 7
  • If the primary has not yet paid or issued an EOB — wait for primary adjudication, then submit the corrected secondary claim with full COB data
  • If the COB payer order was wrong — correct the order, resubmit to the correct primary first, then bill the secondary after receiving their EOB
  • Do not appeal as a first step — fix the root cause data issue and escalate to appeal only after a corrected claim with full COB data is also denied

N227 SUPPLEMENTAL CO-16

Incomplete Certificate of Medical Necessity (CMN)

Durable Medical Equipment (DME) · Medical Necessity Documentation · CMS-484 / CMS-849 · DMEPOS
Common CARC Pairing
CO-16 CO-50 DME DMEPOS CMS-1500 CMS-484 CMS-849
What This Means
📄
What This Means

N227 means the payer received a claim for a service — most commonly a piece of Durable Medical Equipment (DME) or a supply — that requires a Certificate of Medical Necessity (CMN), but the CMN attached to the claim was either missing entirely, was filled out incorrectly, had blank required fields, had conflicting information, was not signed by the ordering physician, or was signed on a date that does not align with the order or delivery date. The payer cannot process the claim until a complete, valid CMN is on file.

ℹ️
What is a Certificate of Medical Necessity (CMN)?
A CMN is a standardized CMS form completed by the ordering physician that confirms a specific piece of DME or a supply is medically necessary for a specific patient. Think of it as the physician's written sworn statement to the payer that says: "I examined this patient, and based on their diagnosis and clinical condition, they need this equipment." Without a valid CMN on file, the DME supplier has no legal or billing basis to receive payment from Medicare or most payers — even if the equipment is genuinely needed by the patient. The CMN is not just paperwork; it is a coverage requirement.
⚠️
N227 Is a Documentation Denial — Not a Coverage Denial
N227 does not mean the equipment or supply is not covered. It means the paperwork supporting medical necessity is incomplete or invalid. Fix the CMN, get it properly signed, and resubmit — in most cases the claim will process. However, if the CMN cannot be corrected retroactively (e.g., the physician refuses to sign or the clinical criteria are not met), the denial becomes permanent.
Where CMN Information Is Reported on the Claim Form
📄
CMS-1500 (DME Supplier / Professional Claims)
CMN-related claim reporting guidance
  • Box 17 — Referring Provider Name & NPI: The ordering/referring physician listed here must exactly match the physician who completed and signed the CMN.
  • Box 17b — Referring Provider NPI: The ordering physician NPI must be valid, active, and enrolled as an ordering/referring provider with Medicare.
  • Box 19 / Box 23 — Additional Information: Some payers require CMN tracking numbers or order dates to appear in these fields.
  • Box 21 — Diagnosis Codes: ICD-10 diagnosis codes must match the medical condition documented on the CMN.
  • Box 24D — Procedure Code: HCPCS codes billed must be covered under the active CMN on file.
  • Box 24H — EPSDT / Family Plan: If populated, information must remain consistent with CMN documentation.
🩺
CMN Form — Required Sections
Mandatory CMN completion requirements
  • Section A — Patient Information: Patient demographics and insurance ID must exactly match the claim.
  • Section A — Supplier Information: Supplier name, NPI, and PTAN must match CMS enrollment records.
  • Section A — Place of Service: POS documented on the CMN must align with the claim POS billed.
  • Section B — Clinical Questions: Every required question and checkbox must be fully completed.
  • Section C — Narrative / Justification: Complex DME items may require detailed clinical narratives supporting medical necessity.
  • Section D — Physician Signature & Date: Physician signature and signature date must meet payer authentication requirements.
✅
Critical CMN Signature Rule
The physician signature date on the CMN cannot be earlier than the documented face-to-face examination date. If the CMN is signed before the patient evaluation occurred, the CMN becomes invalid and will trigger N227 denial edits even when all clinical documentation appears complete.
Why This Happens
⚠️
INVALID / MISSING CMN
Most common root causes behind this denial
ℹ️
Quick Reminder
CMN denials usually occur when required clinical fields, signatures, dates, diagnosis details, or recertifications are missing, expired, or inconsistent with the claim.
1
Incomplete CMN Fields
Required Section B clinical questions left partially blank on the CMN.
2
CMN Not Obtained
Equipment delivered and billed before obtaining a completed signed CMN.
3
CMN Not Linked
Completed CMN obtained but never attached or linked to the billed claim.
4
Missing Oxygen Test Values
Qualifying oxygen saturation or ABG results missing from CMS-484 oxygen CMN.
5
Missing Length of Need
Estimated length of need not documented on the CMN.
6
Missing Physician Date
Physician signed the CMN but failed to personally date the document.
7
Invalid Signature Timing
CMN signed before the required face-to-face examination occurred.
8
Invalid Signature Type
Stamped or auto-generated signature used instead of an acceptable physician signature.
9
Ordering Provider Issue
CMN signed by PA/NP or provider not accepted for the billed HCPCS code.
10
Diagnosis Mismatch
Diagnosis on the CMN does not match the ICD-10 diagnosis billed on the claim.
11
HCPCS Mismatch
Billed HCPCS code not supported or referenced by the CMN documentation.
12
Provider / Patient Mismatch
Physician, patient name, NPI, or insurance details do not match the claim.
13
Expired CMN
CMN validity period expired before the billed rental or service dates.
14
Missing Recertification
Required recertification CMN not obtained for continued rental billing periods.
15
Equipment Change Not Updated
CMN not updated after equipment upgrade or HCPCS code change.
How to Fix It — RARC N227: Incomplete Certificate of Medical Necessity (CMN)
💡 What is RARC N227?
Your claim was denied because the Certificate of Medical Necessity (CMN) is incomplete. Think of a CMN like a doctor's signed permission form — for certain items like wheelchairs, oxygen, or hospital beds, Medicare and other payers require a physician to certify in writing that the item is medically necessary. If any section of that form is blank, unsigned, or missing, the payer rejects the entire claim.
Primary Use
DME Claims
Durable Medical Equipment
CMS Forms
484 / 10160
Home health / DME
Billed On
837P / 837I
Sent as paper attachment
📋 Common Items That Require a CMN
Item / Service
CMS CMN Form
Home oxygen therapy
CMS-484
Power wheelchairs / scooters
CMS-10160 (POA / Written Order)

1
Pull the CMN & Find What's Incomplete
Every blank field is a denial reason
🔍 Retrieve the CMN that was submitted with the claim and go section by section. N227 means something is missing or incomplete — your job is to find exactly which field(s) are blank, unsigned, or incorrectly completed.
  • Check all four sections of the CMN: Section A (supplier info), Section B (physician answers to clinical questions), Section C (narrative justification if required), and Section D (physician signature + date).
  • The most common incomplete fields are Section B clinical answers left blank and Section D missing physician signature or date — check these first.
  • Confirm the correct CMS CMN form version was used for the item billed — using an outdated form version triggers N227 just like a blank field.
  • Verify the ordering physician's NPI and UPIN are correctly populated — missing or mismatched provider identifiers are a common N227 cause on DME claims.
  • Check that the CMN covers the correct date range — a CMN signed after the service date or with an expiration date before the service date will be rejected as incomplete.
2
Complete the CMN & Resubmit
Go back to the physician — get every field filled
✅ This is a correctable documentation error. Return the CMN to the ordering physician to complete all blank sections, then resubmit as a corrected claim with the fully completed CMN attached.
  • Never alter a CMN yourself. Only the ordering physician (or their clinical staff under physician supervision) can complete Section B and sign Section D — supplier staff completing clinical sections is a compliance violation.
  • Return the CMN to the physician with a clear cover note marking exactly which fields are incomplete and the deadline to return it — be specific, not generic.
  • Once fully completed and signed, resubmit as a corrected claim with the completed CMN attached. For electronic claims (837), the CMN is a paper or portal attachment — confirm the payer's preferred submission method.
  • Medicare DMEPOS: Resubmit to your DME MAC (not the A/B MAC). Attach the completed CMN per the DME MAC's documentation submission instructions.
  • ⚠️ Watch timely filing deadlines — the clock doesn't stop while you're chasing the physician signature. Act within days, not weeks.
3
Still Denied? Call the Payer
Confirm exactly which section they flagged
📞 If the claim denies again with N227 after resubmission, call the payer's provider relations or DME claims line. The payer may have received the CMN but flagged a specific field or format issue that isn't obvious from the denial alone.
  • Have ready: Claim number, member ID, date of service, item billed (HCPCS code), CMN form version used, and both remittance advices.
  • Ask the rep: "Which specific section or field on the CMN was flagged as incomplete? Was the CMN received with the claim or is it missing entirely from your system?"
  • Ask whether a payer-specific CMN format is required — some commercial payers do not accept CMS standard CMN forms and require their own proprietary version.
  • For Medicare DME MAC: ask if the issue is with the CMN itself or with the detailed written order (DWO) — these are separate documents and both may be required depending on the item.
  • 📝 Document: reference number, rep name, date, time, and the exact field or section the payer says is incomplete.
4
Payer Won't Reprocess? File a Formal Appeal
Appeal with the fully completed CMN as evidence
⚖️ If the payer upholds the N227 denial after a corrected claim and provider relations outreach, file a formal appeal demonstrating the CMN is fully complete, properly signed, and meets all payer and CMS requirements for the item billed.
  • Appeal letter must include: Provider/supplier name, NPI, Tax ID, patient name, member ID, claim number, date of service, HCPCS code billed, and CMN form version used.
  • Key statement: "The Certificate of Medical Necessity submitted with this claim is fully completed per CMS guidelines, including all required clinical sections and ordering physician signature. We appeal the N227 denial as the CMN was compliant at submission."
  • Attach: Completed CMN (all sections), ordering physician's signed detailed written order (if applicable), original claim, both remittance advices, and any supporting clinical documentation confirming medical necessity.
  • Medicare DME MAC: File Redetermination within 120 days of the denial date. Reference CMS Medicare Benefit Policy Manual, Pub 100-02, Chapter 15 and the applicable Local Coverage Determination (LCD) for the item billed.
  • Commercial payers: follow appeal deadline on the EOB — typically 30–180 days. Cite the payer's own CMN requirements from the provider manual if the form was completed correctly per their guidelines.
5
Seeing This Repeatedly? Fix Your CMN Intake Process
Stop N227 before the claim ever leaves your office
🔁 If N227 appears across multiple claims, your CMN intake and review process has a gap — CMNs are leaving the physician's office incomplete, or no one is checking them for completeness before the claim is submitted.
  • Never submit a claim with an incomplete CMN. Build a mandatory CMN completeness check into your billing workflow — every section must be reviewed before the claim is released. No signature = no submission.
  • Create a CMN checklist for each item type (oxygen, wheelchair, hospital bed, etc.) that maps every required field for that specific form. Use it as a sign-off before sending the CMN to the physician and again when it's returned.
  • Set physician follow-up reminders. If a CMN is sent to a physician for completion, put a 48–72 hour follow-up in your workflow. Waiting passively costs you timely filing days.
  • Keep CMN form versions current. CMS updates CMN forms periodically — using a superseded version triggers N227 even when every field is filled. Audit your templates at least annually against the CMS DMEPOS website.
  • Separate the CMN from the detailed written order (DWO). Many billers confuse these — Medicare requires both for certain items. Confirm which documents are required per the applicable LCD before submission.
  • 🔒 Train your team: A CMN is a legal medical document — only the ordering physician completes the clinical sections. Supplier staff filling in clinical answers on behalf of a physician is a False Claims Act risk, not just a billing error.
WHAT NOT TO DO
🚫
What NOT to Do
Avoid these common CMN and documentation mistakes that trigger repeat N227 denials
These mistakes commonly cause CMN invalidation, DME documentation denials, and federal compliance exposure.
  • Do not fill in blank Section B clinical questions yourself — only the ordering physician can answer clinical questions on the CMN; any alterations by billing staff make the form invalid and create compliance risk
  • Do not alter the physician's signature date, exam date, or any other date on the CMN — falsifying dates on a CMN is a federal compliance violation
  • Do not deliver or bill for equipment before obtaining a signed, completed CMN — the CMN must be in place before the date of delivery for most payers
  • Do not assume the same CMN covers an upgraded or different piece of equipment — if the HCPCS code changes, a new CMN is required
  • Do not appeal N227 without attaching the corrected, completed CMN — an appeal letter alone without the actual documentation will be denied
  • Do not use a CMN completed by a physician who is not enrolled in PECOS for Medicare claims — confirm PECOS enrollment before submitting
⚠️
Critical Compliance Reminder
Altering or completing physician-only sections of a CMN by billing staff can invalidate the documentation and create significant Medicare compliance risk. Always obtain a properly completed CMN directly from the ordering physician before billing or appealing an N227 denial.
CMN VALIDATION CHECKLIST
✅
CMN VALIDATION CHECKLIST
Pre-delivery and pre-submission CMN validation checklist

Before delivering equipment and before submitting the claim, confirm all CMN validations are completed

  • ✅ Correct CMN form identified for the specific HCPCS code being billed — right form for the right equipment
  • ✅ All Section B clinical questions answered — no blank fields anywhere on the form
  • ✅ Physician signature in Section D is a personal, hand-written or valid electronic signature — not a stamp
  • ✅ Physician's signature date is on or after the face-to-face examination date — never before
  • ✅ Estimated length of need is completed — specific duration entered, not left blank
  • ✅ Patient name, insurance ID, and date of birth on CMN match the claim exactly
  • ✅ Diagnosis code on CMN matches ICD-10 code in Box 21 of the CMS-1500 exactly
  • ✅ HCPCS code covered by this CMN matches the code being billed on the claim
  • ✅ Ordering physician's NPI verified as active in NPPES and enrolled in PECOS as ordering/referring provider (Medicare claims)
  • ✅ CMN is not expired — if ongoing rental, recertification CMN obtained before the prior CMN's expiration date
  • ✅ CMN linked or attached in the billing system before the claim is submitted
Best Practice — When to Appeal vs. When to Correct & Resubmit
✅
Appeal When ALL of These Are True
Use only after CMN accuracy and documentation are fully validated
Appeal only when a complete and valid CMN was already obtained, all claim and physician data were verified as accurate, and the denial still occurred because of payer-side documentation matching or adjudication issues.
  • A complete, valid CMN was on file before the claim was submitted — all sections were answered, physician signature and date were present and valid, and no fields were blank
  • The CMN data matches the claim data exactly — diagnosis code, HCPCS code, ordering physician NPI, and patient demographics are all consistent
  • The ordering physician is enrolled in PECOS and their NPI is active in NPPES
  • The payer denied it anyway — this indicates a payer-side documentation matching error and an appeal with the complete CMN attached should be submitted
🔄
Correct & Resubmit First (Most N227 Cases)
Recommended first action for most N227 denials
Most N227 denials are caused by incomplete CMN documentation, missing physician signatures, expired certifications, or mismatches between CMN and claim data and are resolved through correction and resubmission.
  • Most N227 denials are caused by blank Section B fields, a missing physician signature date, or a mismatch between the CMN and claim data — correct the specific issue and resubmit with Resubmission Code 7
  • If the CMN was never obtained — get a completed, signed CMN from the ordering physician and resubmit (check payer's retroactive CMN policy first)
  • If the CMN has expired — obtain a recertification CMN and resubmit the affected claims
  • Do not appeal as a first step when the documentation issue is on your side — correct the root cause first, then escalate to appeal only if a corrected claim with a complete CMN is also denied
